title: WebSocket stale timeout can settle a newer same-ID request
description:
Audit finding from PR #8936 across completeness, correctness, and implementation quality.

The PR correctly makes a live-socket timeout explicit, but the worked and runnable machines correlate a timeout only by `request-id` plus the socket actor id. That rejects timers from an old connection, not an old registration on the same live socket.

At merged commit 23e25e4040:
- `:register-request` stores `[:in-flight request-id]` and schedules `:ws/request-timeout` carrying only that id and `:source-socket-id`.
- `:clear-request` looks up whichever entry currently occupies that id, removes it, and now dispatches its reply-event a local `:ws/timeout`.
- The spec permits any `=`-comparable id and explicitly recommends reusable per-feature vectors such as `[:feature/load slug]`; uniqueness for a socket lifetime is not a contract.

Concrete failure: request A with id R completes; request B reuses R on the same still-live socket before A's uncancelled deadline; A's timer passes `:current-socket?`, deletes B, and fires B's callback with a premature timeout. Registering B while A is still pending also overwrites A's callback without settling it. Both violate the page's new exactly-once/terminal-outcome promise.

Keep the repair local to the WebSocket pattern: correlate scheduled timeouts to the specific registration they came from and state the duplicate-in-flight policy. Do not build a generic timer-cancellation layer or managed WebSocket abstraction.
acceptance_criteria: A timeout or wire reply can settle only the exact in-flight registration it belongs to; an uncancelled timeout from an earlier same-ID request on the same socket cannot clear or notify a later request. Concurrent duplicate IDs have an explicit policy that does not strand a displaced caller. The spec, runnable example, schema if needed, and focused tests agree, while preserving socket-epoch rejection and the existing local/server provenance shapes. No generic cancellation facility or new public WebSocket abstraction.
notes:
AUDIT PR #8946 (2026-09-02) — REOPENED BECAUSE WIRE REPLIES STILL CORRELATE TO THE REUSED ID, NOT THE REGISTRATION.

The timeout half is sound: `:own-request-timeout?` checks both socket epoch and registration token. The same token never reaches the wire-reply path, though:

- `:register-request` still sends `(assoc body :request-id request-id)` with no registration discriminator.
- `ReplyMessage` carries only `:request-id`.
- `:receive-message` looks up and removes whichever entry currently occupies `[:in-flight (:request-id body)]`, without a token check.

Concrete failure: A is pending under `R`; B re-registers `R`, locally superseding A, and both requests are now on the wire with the identical correlation value. When A's server reply arrives first, `:receive-message` finds B's slot, removes it, and fires B's callback with A's body. B's actual reply later becomes unsolicited. The callback count can remain exactly once while the reply is attached to the wrong registration—the more fundamental correlation failure.

This directly contradicts this bead's acceptance criterion: "A timeout or wire reply can settle only the exact in-flight registration it belongs to." The merged spec instead disclaims which server reply answers which registration and says the reply settles whichever registration holds the slot; that narrows the required end state rather than satisfying it. The two new tests use `:silent-no-echo`, so neither injects A's wire reply after B takes the slot and the missing fence is unobserved.

Completeness: the registration identity protects deadlines only. Correctness: last-write-wins plus an unchanged wire id can deliver stale data as B's successful response. Implementation quality: an explicitly ambiguous request/reply contract is a sharp edge in the recommended reusable-id pattern, and the focused tests avoid the ambiguous branch.

Minimal outcome: preserve exact wire correlation either by ensuring two registrations with one wire id are never concurrently outstanding (for example, reject/serialize the newcomer) or by putting a registration discriminator on the wire and requiring it back; add the A-reply-after-B-registration regression. Keep this local to the example—no managed-WebSocket abstraction or generic cancellation layer.

Duplicate search: `rf2-tb442` owns this exact same-id registration-correlation contract and already names wire replies in its acceptance criteria, so it is reopened rather than duplicated.
close_reason:
Second pass (audit PR #8946), PR #8959. The reopen was about the WIRE-REPLY half of the correlation, and that is what this addressed: :register-request now stamps the registration :token onto the outbound frame as :request-token beside :request-id, schema/ReplyMessage REQUIRES it echoed back, and :receive-message settles the [:in-flight rid] slot only while the echoed token is still the slot's token. A mismatch is treated as an unsolicited reply (nothing cleared, no :reply-event fired, frame still reaches the inbox), not an error. Duplicate-in-flight policy (last-write-wins, displaced caller settled :ws/superseded) is unchanged; the displaced registration now leaves two inert leftovers rather than one -- its armed timer and the reply its request will still draw from the server.

REGRESSION PROVING A WIRE REPLY CAN NO LONGER SETTLE A LATER SAME-ID REGISTRATION: deftest websocket-wire-reply-cannot-settle-a-later-same-id-registration in implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/websocket_cljs_test.cljs. A registers under the reusable id [:feature/load "gamma"] and stays pending; B re-registers the same id (A settled :ws/superseded, A's request still on the wire); A's SERVER reply then arrives carrying A's token. Asserted: the slot still holds B's token, B's callback count is still 1, and A's reply reaches the inbox as an unsolicited vetted frame -- then B's own reply settles B with B's OWN body and B's token. RED BEFORE / GREEN AFTER measured: with :receive-message's token check reverted to (get-in data [:in-flight rid]) and everything else left in place, the focused suite returned captured exit 1 with 4 failures, ALL in that test, on the same 29 tests / 240 assertions -- including 'expected (= {:type :request :tag "B"} (:echo outcome)) / actual (not (= {:type :request :tag "B"} {:type :request :tag "A"}))', which is the defect in one row: B's caller handed A's body as its answer. Restored (verified by git blob hash against the committed object), recompiled, re-run: captured exit 0.

Gates, captured exit codes from the runner: node-test compile 0 (1877 files, 0 warnings); node out/node-test.js 0 (11197 tests, 55483 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors); focused websocket ns 0 (29 tests, 240 assertions); check_doc_slugs.py 0; check_readme_links.py --ci 0. Both link gates exercised against a planted broken target first and returned exit 1 naming the planted file and line, so their greens are measured rather than silent.

EP-0011 CANARY HELD. The app-level/no-uniform-envelope boundary is intact: :request-token is an ordinary unqualified app key on the app's own wire frame, not :work/id or :rf/reply-to. The five 'app-level reply carries no EP-0011 ...' assertions pass, and they are live -- planting the five envelope keys onto the reply body reds all five. ServerReplyOutcome is also a :closed map, so envelope vocabulary on this path is a schema rejection as well.

WIRE COMPATIBILITY, stated because the outbound body changed: a server that ignores :request-token echoes only :request-id, its reply then fails the closed ReplyMessage arm, and the frame takes :refuse-frame -- nothing in the connection moves, the slot is not cleared, no callback fires, and the ingress mints the canonical :rf.error/schema-validation-failure naming the missing key on the very first reply; the request then settles on its own deadline with the documented {:origin :ws/local :ok false :error :ws/timeout}. So it degrades to a loud, terminal, documented outcome, never to silence and never to wrong data. Admitting an untokened reply and correlating by id would have restored the exact ambiguity the field removes. The escape hatch is documented in ReplyMessage's docstring and Pattern-WebSocket item 6: an app whose server cannot echo the field drops it from BOTH ReplyMessage and :register-request and then owes its ids uniqueness for the socket's lifetime. A new boundary case pins this -- a reply omitting only :request-token is refused and the in-flight slot survives it.

Scope kept local to the WebSocket pattern per the bead: one wire field, one required schema entry, one equality check, plus spec/example/skill/README prose. No managed-WebSocket abstraction, no generic correlation or cancellation layer, no new public surface.

SPEC CHANGE OF NOTE: Pattern-WebSocket item 6 previously DISCLAIMED this ('the wire reply settles whichever registration holds the slot'), which narrowed the acceptance criterion rather than meeting it. That disclaimer is removed and item 6 is restructured around both settling paths, with a new anti-pattern for fixing the timer and leaving the reply.

ADJACENT FINDING, not fixed here, may deserve a follow-up bead: the test fixture's register-all! re-declares the two ingress event-handler BODIES inline and runs on every test, so those bodies -- not the example's -- are what the suite exercises. Measured: a fault planted in websocket.messages' :ws.app/request-reply body left the suite fully green. Where the fixture points at an example VAR instead (connection machine, socket actor, schemas, mock transport) the example's own code genuinely is under test and a planted fault reds immediately; everything this PR changes substantively falls in that second group. The fixture docstring now records the distinction.

title: CLAUDE.md prescribes naming remote+branch as the fix for 'Cannot rebase onto multiple branches'; measured insufficient
notes:
MEASURED 2026-09-01 22:4x AUSEST by the acting mayor, in the mayor checkout, six worker worktrees live.

WHAT HAPPENED. Ran the checkpoint sequence's third step in its PRESCRIBED named form - 'git pull --rebase origin main' - and it aborted:

  From https://github.com/day8/re-frame2
   * branch                  main       -> FETCH_HEAD
  fatal: Cannot rebase onto multiple branches.

Tree was clean and undiverged. HEAD == origin/main afterwards and the push landed, so no damage this time - but the rebase silently did not happen, which is the step the sequence exists to perform.

WHY THE PRESCRIBED REMEDY DOES NOT HOLD. CLAUDE.md's Beads-durability bullet says a BARE 'git pull --rebase' takes its target from FETCH_HEAD and therefore aborts this way, and prescribes naming remote and branch. But naming them does not immunise the pull, because a pull is TWO steps: it fetches into FETCH_HEAD, then rebases onto what FETCH_HEAD says. FETCH_HEAD lives in the SHARED common git directory - 'git rev-parse --git-common-dir' returns .git from the mayor checkout, and linked worktrees do NOT get their own copy. So any concurrent fetch from any of the six live worker worktrees rewrites it inside that window, and the rebase step reads the peer's multi-ref version no matter how the pull was invoked. Naming the remote and branch controls only the FETCH half.

SECOND, SMALLER FINDING - the abort was INVISIBLE. It was run as 'git pull --rebase origin main 2>&1 | tail -3 && bd dolt push && git push'. A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's, so tail returned 0 and the && chain continued straight past a fatal abort. This is the same hazard the dispatch template's gate-mechanics block states for gates ('Never pipe a gate through a filter'), reached through git rather than through a gate runner, and it is what made the doc's phrase 'inert only because the push that follows still lands' literally true here.    because 'git rev-parse --git-common-dir' returns the mayor checkout's .git,
   linked worktrees have no FETCH_HEAD of their own and any peer worker's fetch
   rewrites the mayor's. Measured on git 2.53.0.windows.2: 'git rev-parse
   --git-path FETCH_HEAD' resolves INSIDE the linked worktree's own git directory,

title: WebSocket teaching surfaces disagree on timeout delivery and reply-envelope shape
description:
Audit finding from PR #8907 across completeness, correctness, and implementation quality.

The PR correctly synchronizes the three active-exit doors with the runnable WebSocket example, but the request-outcome contract is still internally contradictory on the same edited teaching surface.

At merged commit 9445bfeb3c:
- spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md's worked :clear-request action only dissocs the slot. Item 4 says the caller's reply event never fires on timeout.
- The canonical runnable example examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs does the opposite: action-clear-request reads reply-event, clears the slot, and dispatches one machine-stamped :ws/timeout failure. Existing rf2-b2jpr acceptance and tests explicitly require a live-socket timeout as an explicit terminal outcome.
- Two lines after the stale item 4, the spec says a locally minted loss/timeout failure reaches the caller's reply-event. Thus the page contradicts itself and copying its worked machine restores the caller-hang that the canonical example already removed.
- The edited skill still emits the runnable example's bespoke {:origin :ws/local :request-id ... :ok false :error ...} outcome, while its correlation guidance on the same page mandates the uniform reply envelope with closed :status and :rf.reply/work-id. The runnable schema/RequestOutcome and spec use the bespoke shape. A programmer or AI cannot tell which contract is canonical.

No existing Bead owns WebSocket timeout documentation or this reply-envelope conflict; all-status searches covered websocket timeout, clear-request, reply-event, RequestOutcome, uniform reply, and rf.reply/work-id. rf2-0g60h owns only the fatal-door listing drift, rf2-b2jpr the already-fixed clean-disconnect runtime leak, and rf2-iyjae the already-fixed inbound trust/provenance boundary.

Keep this small: rule the one callback contract and align the runnable example, spec, and skill. Do not build a generalized WebSocket facility or a new reply abstraction.
acceptance_criteria: The spec worked :clear-request, its request-reply sequence, the runnable example/test, and the skill agree whether a live timeout invokes reply-event; no copied canonical form can silently clear a request while leaving its caller waiting. The WebSocket RequestOutcome uses one documented envelope shape across source schema, spec, and skill (either the uniform managed envelope or an explicitly justified pattern-local contract). Loss and timeout remain machine-stamped, server outcomes remain unforgeably distinct, and existing exactly-once/stale-epoch controls stay intact. No new abstraction or compatibility layer.
notes:
MAYOR RULING 2026-09-01 22:07 AUSEST — THE UNIFORM REPLY ENVELOPE IS CANONICAL. Settled from the page's own normative text, not by preference.

BOTH HALVES OF THIS BEAD ARE REAL, and neither is a taste call once you read the sources.

HALF 1 — THE SELF-CONTRADICTION. spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md's item 4 says the caller's reply event never fires on timeout. Two lines later the same page says a locally minted loss/timeout failure DOES reach the reply-event, and the runnable example (examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs) dispatches one. So item 4 and the worked :clear-request action are the wrong side of the contradiction: the example and the page's own later text already agree with each other, and rf2-b2jpr's acceptance requires a live-socket timeout as an explicit terminal outcome. RULED: correct item 4 and the worked action to fire the reply-event. Copying the current worked machine restores the caller-hang the canonical example already removed, which is the whole cost here.

HALF 2 — THE ENVELOPE. skills/re-frame2/patterns/websocket.md:200 already states the rule, with its reason and a citation: 'Because this is the completion of an async request, model it on the uniform reply envelope (Managed-Effects property 9), not a bespoke ack: dispatch the :reply-event with a reply map carrying a closed :status {:ok :partial :error :cancelled :stale} and the request id as :rf.reply/work-id ... so your socket replies read the same as every other async completion in trace/Xray.' Line 64 of that same file, and spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md at 181/505/575, emit {:origin :ws/local :ok false :error :ws/connection-lost} — the bespoke ack the page forbids. RULED: the envelope is canonical and the bespoke shape is the drift. A page carrying its own rule plus worked examples that violate it is worse than either alone, because the reader cannot tell which is the contract.

:origin :ws/local IS NOT DROPPED — it is carried INSIDE the envelope. The same paragraph demands that two producers reaching one reply-event be told apart 'by a provenance key the machine stamps after receipt, never by the body's shape'. That is exactly what :origin is for, and it is the reason the two shapes must not remain alternatives: provenance belongs as a field, never as a rival envelope.

SCOPE, measured rather than assumed: seven files carry the bespoke spelling — spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md, skills/re-frame2/patterns/websocket.md, examples/patterns/websocket/{connection,schema,messages}.cljs and its README, plus implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/websocket_cljs_test.cljs. No framework source depends on it, so this is a teaching-surface correction plus one test, not a runtime migration.

NOT WANTED: any change to the reply-envelope contract itself; a WebSocket-specific exemption from it; a new outcome abstraction; a Playwright spec. Do not widen beyond the WebSocket surface.

---

title: machines tracing: preserve raised-event transitions in the macrostep cascade
description:
## Scope

Make the structured `:cascade` on `:rf.machine/transition` faithfully describe transitions selected by same-macrostep raised/internal events, including synthetic compound/parallel done-state signals. Cover flat, compound, and root-parallel machines plus the Xray consumers of this trace. Keep the state/effect fold unchanged.

## Correctness finding

Raised-event execution is semantically correct, but its inspection record is not. In the flat/compound drain, a dequeued raise is processed through a nested `machine-transition-single`; the resulting snapshot and real effects are retained, but that result's structured cascade is discarded because the loop recurs with `cascade` unchanged. The parallel parent queue retains the rebroadcast result's cascade by flattening it into the accumulator, but records no boundary or trigger event, so those exit/action/entry rows are indistinguishable from the external event's transition.

The outer trace can therefore say an external event moved a machine from A to C while its `:cascade` explains only A to B; the raised event that actually moved B to C is invisible or misattributed. That violates the local “complete configuration walk / one trace, one place” contract and prevents Xray from showing why the final state was reached.

XState v6 gets the important boundary right: one `@xstate.transition` inspection event carries every selected transition definition in its ordered `microsteps` collection, including eventless and internally raised processing. re-frame2 need not copy that wire protocol, but its one-macrostep trace should be equally lossless.

## Evidence

- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/transition.cljc`, `drain-to-fixed-point` around lines 4060-4138: after dequeuing a raised event, `step-result` supplies `snap2` and `fx2`, then the `recur` passes the old `cascade` unchanged. By contrast, the `:always` branch around lines 3988-4039 emits `:rf.machine.microstep/transition` and appends a nested `{:kind :microstep ... :steps ...}`.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/parallel.cljc`, `drain-parent-queue` around lines 1320-1370: raised-event rebroadcast appends `(result/cascade step)` directly into `acc-casc`, losing the event boundary/identity even though the geometry survives.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/lifecycle_fx/registration.cljc` around lines 711-734 describes and emits `:cascade` as the ordered explanation of how the macrostep reached `:after`.
- `spec/005-StateMachines.md`, “The structured transition cascade”, promises a complete configuration walk and says one trace is the place tooling reads to understand the transition. Its closed step vocabulary explains external and `:always` work but has no raised-event boundary.
- `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels/machines/trace_state.cljs` reads only this structured cascade to distinguish handled regions and derive fired edges. It assumes non-`:microstep` rows belong to the dispatched event, which makes the parallel flattening actively misattribute raised work.
- XState v6's official inspection contract says each `@xstate.transition` carries the triggering event, final snapshot, and `microsteps`: https://stately.ai/docs/xstate/v6/inspection . Its execution contract defines one externally observed snapshot after all internal steps settle: https://stately.ai/docs/xstate/v6/how-xstate-runs-machines . Exact source baseline: `xstate@6.0.0-alpha.50` (`0b52534e`), whose `packages/core/src/stateUtils.ts` appends the selected transition set for the seed event, eventless rounds, and internal-queue events to the same macrostep `microsteps` array.

## Steps to Reproduce

### Failure scenario/invariant

Use a machine where external `:go` takes `:idle -> :working` and its action raises `[:settle]`; `:working` handles `:settle` with `:target :done` and entry/exit actions.

1. Dispatch `:go`.
2. Observe the committed snapshot is `:done`; FIFO raise semantics worked.
3. Inspect the single `:rf.machine/transition` trace. `:before` is `:idle` and `:after` is `:done`, but on a flat/compound machine its `:cascade` contains only the `:go` geometry (and any `:always` wrappers), not the `:settle` transition.
4. Repeat in a parallel machine: raised transition rows appear flattened with the external rows, so Xray may light them as if `:go` selected them.

The same omission applies when the runtime synthesizes a raised done-state event after entering an embedded final state.

Required invariant: the macrostep inspection record preserves, in execution order, the event boundary and transition geometry of every handled dequeued internal event needed to explain the final snapshot. An ignored raised event contributes no fictional transition.

## Recommended minimal fix

Extend the existing structured cascade with one nested internal-event boundary rather than adding a second trace protocol. For example:

```clojure
{:kind   :raised-transition
 :source :raise
 :event  [:settle]
 :from   :working
 :to     :done
 :region nil
 :steps  [ ...the nested exit/action/entry and `:always` steps... ]}
```

- Append one such wrapper after each handled dequeue in both the flat/compound and parallel parent queues, in actual FIFO execution order. Preserve nested `:always` structure from that step.
- Use one schema-approved name/shape across both engines; the example spelling is a recommendation, not a request for aliases.
- Keep the outer trace's external `:event`, `:before`, and `:after` as the macrostep headline.
- Keep the current `:microsteps` scalar as the `:always`-iteration count for compatibility unless a separate design explicitly changes it. Do not emit an extra dispatch envelope or notify observers mid-macrostep.
- Teach Xray to traverse the wrapper, attribute nested edges/actions to its internal event, and exclude those rows when determining which regions handled the external event.
- Update Spec 005, the trace schema/ratchet, and focused tool documentation to make the internal-event boundary part of the closed cascade shape.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A focused pure-engine test proves a flat/compound `external -> raise -> transition` macrostep records the external geometry and then one internal-event wrapper with the raised event, from/to state, and nested ordered steps.
- A two-raise chain proves wrappers are ordered by actual FIFO dequeue order; an `:always` transition enabled by a raised transition appears inside/after the correct boundary according to runtime order.
- An ignored or guard-blocked raised event does not fabricate a handled-transition wrapper; a targetless handled raised transition still records its action boundary even when from equals to.
- Root-parallel tests prove raised rebroadcast geometry is grouped under the internal event and Xray no longer counts it as evidence that a region handled the original external event.
- A synthetic embedded done-state signal is represented by the same mechanism, without a special parallel trace dialect.
- Xray projection/view tests show the dispatched event and the internal event as distinct causal transition steps and light the correct graph edges.
- Snapshot, data, effect order, raise FIFO, eventless-before-next-raise ordering, atomic rollback, and subscriber/dispatch behavior are byte/value-identical to pre-change behavior.
- Spec 005, relevant Spec-Schemas/Spec 009 trace rows, runtime comments, and Xray consumers agree on the new closed shape; trace privacy projection still scrubs nested `:data-delta` values.

## Non-goals

- Adopting XState's `@xstate.*` event names or actor inspection protocol.
- Changing transition selection, microstep order, effect order, raise depth limits, or observer notification.
- Adding an actor mailbox, emitted-event channel, or JavaScript transition-function API.
- Recording unhandled internal events as successful transitions.
- Redesigning the public `re-frame.machines/machine-transition` result shape.

## Related/duplicate search

All-status tracker searches covered titles/descriptions containing: `microstep`, `raised event`, `raise`, `cascade`, `structured`, `inspection`, `trace`, `machine transition`, and `XState v6`. No bead owns lossless raised-event macrostep inspection. Closed `rf2-v4xjh` changed the public pure-transition result map and explicitly excluded transition semantics; it does not repair runtime traces. Closed `rf2-sxw06` concerns static Mermaid topology export. Closed `rf2-zk1xu` reconciled Spec 009 tag rows but does not add this missing runtime evidence.

SHAPE SHIPPED. One `:kind :raised-transition` step per HANDLED dequeue, FIFO

   :from :working :to :done :steps [...nested...]}

title: realworld-http: late article delete success overrides the reader's newer route
description:
DISCOVERED-FROM rf2-84iek (PR #8898), named in source by that worker as a suspected same-class defect it deliberately did not fix.

THE SUSPICION (verify at source before acting; this is a CLAIM, not a finding). rf2-84iek corrected three optimistic comment WRITE paths in examples/real-apps/realworld_http/ that mutated shared state without checking the reply belonged to the current route. While doing so its worker observed that :article/author-follow-rollback looks like the same shape: a failed follow on article alpha, settling after navigation to beta, would flip the on-screen author flag for BETA.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED THERE. rf2-84iek non-goals it, and the worker had no reproduced defect for it. It named the suspicion in the source rather than acting on an unverified premise, which is the right call and is why this is a separate bead rather than scope creep on that PR.

WHAT MAKES THIS NON-OBVIOUS, and the reason it should not be fixed by pattern-matching the sibling: rf2-84iek established that gating alone was NOT sufficient for the comment paths. The comments slice is route-owned and resets on slug change, but the comment FORM was not -- so refusing a stale settle left the next articles form permanently locked with its textarea and Post button disabled. The fix needed a gate AND a reset, as two halves of one change. Whoever takes this must ask the same question of the author/follow state: is it route-owned and reset on navigation, or does it ride across? If it rides, a gate alone reproduces that same lock-out bug in a new place.

FIRST STEP IS TO REPRODUCE OR REFUTE. If the author-follow state turns out to be route-owned and already reset by :article/load, there is no defect and saying so with the evidence closes this. Do not fix it on the strength of the resemblance.

SCOPE: examples/real-apps/realworld_http/ plus the existing production-source CLJS suite at implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/realworld_cljs_test.cljs. No framework work, no new mutation abstraction, no Playwright spec.
acceptance_criteria: `:article/delete-success` carries the issuing slug and navigates home only while that slug still owns `[:article]`. A held alpha delete settled after navigation to beta leaves beta current; the same success settled while alpha is current still navigates home. Reuse the existing slug gate and request target shape; no new framework machinery.
notes:
AUDIT PR #8911 (2026-09-01) — REOPENED.

The three db-write gates are correct, route-owned, and well tested. Completeness stops one settle too early: `:article/delete-success` is excluded because it writes no db, yet it dispatches navigation and the source itself acknowledges that a late alpha success sends a reader who has moved to beta home. Navigation is the active route's stateful effect; a stale reply changing the screen is the same ownership violation even though it does not use `:db`.

Correctness scenario: delete alpha, navigate to beta before the server settles, then deliver alpha success. Current code unconditionally navigates home and discards the reader's newer route choice. Nothing needs to be stranded: the server deletion succeeded, beta remains valid, and returning to alpha later will naturally fail/reload. Implementation quality: carry the issuing slug on the success target and gate the navigation with the existing `reply-for-current-slug?`; add the late-success refusal plus current-slug navigation control. No request epoch, cancellation scheme, or new abstraction.

VERDICT (PR #8938, 2026-09-01). DEFECT REPRODUCED, then fixed. The audit note governs and was followed; the description's author-follow framing is the older layer, already discharged by PR #8911.

REPRODUCTION, against unmodified source. Read /article/alpha, press Delete, hold the DELETE open, walk to /article/beta before the server answers, then let alpha's DELETE succeed. Observed: route id :realworld/home, route params {}. The reader is taken off the article they chose and out to the home page. Three assertions red in the new test; the other 55,169 assertions in the node-test lane green — which is exactly why the existing suite passed with this bug.

FIX. `:article/delete`'s `:on-success` now carries the issuing slug, as its `:on-failure` already did, and `:article/delete-success` asks the existing `reply-for-current-slug?` before dispatching the navigation. No request epoch, no cancellation scheme, no new abstraction — the acceptance criteria's shape exactly.

DOES REFUSING STRAND ANYTHING? Checked at source rather than taken from either text. No. `:article/delete` writes no `:db` at all — it fires the request and nothing else, so there is no `:deleting` flag; the Delete button in `article-meta` has no `:disabled` binding and no pending state; `[:article]` is rebuilt wholesale by `:article/load`'s request hat on a slug change. The server deletion succeeded regardless, so there is no retry to lose, and returning to alpha later fails and reloads like any other missing article. This is the difference from rf2-84iek, where `[:comment-form]` was a boot-time singleton riding across the navigation still `:submitting` — that one needed a gate AND a reset; this one needs the gate alone. A gate alone is what landed.

TESTS (2, both in realworld_cljs_test.cljs, in the existing realworld-article-social-cross-slug deftest, reusing the existing held-request harness): the late-success refusal, carrying the same `beta-slice-is-rebuilt` strand control the three sibling refusals use; and the current-slug navigation control, proving a delete settled on its own slug still goes home.

OUT OF SCOPE, untouched: `:editor/delete-success` in article_editor.cljs is a different slice with its own `still-editing?` law; the acceptance criteria names `:article/delete-success` only. Noted here rather than acted on.

GREEN UNDER THE CONTROL: everything else, including the three db-write gates the audit calls correct, their non-vacuity control, and article-detail-delete-test's existing "a successful detail-page delete navigates home".

The alpha→beta case is fixed, but the gate does not actually establish that the issuing slug still owns the ACTIVE ROUTE. `reply-for-current-slug?` compares only the reply slug with cached `[:article :slug]`. Navigating from `/article/alpha` to a non-article route (home, profile, login, editor, etc.) runs that route's own `:on-match` and does not clear the article slice, so its slug remains `alpha`. title: docs(story-mcp): three pages still promise false-empty browser reads
description:
## Scope

Align the three remaining Story-MCP documentation statements for unreachable browser-only capabilities with the shipped `capability-unavailable` error contract. Documentation only: `tools/story-mcp/README.md`, `tools/story-mcp/spec/002-Tool-Registry.md`, and `tools/story/spec/Principles.md`. No runtime, schema, tool, or transport change.

## Correctness finding

PR #8865 correctly rewrote `docs/story/api/mcp-surface.md` to say that the headless JVM cannot inspect the CLJS substrate registry or a11y-panel atom and therefore returns `isError true` / `:rf.error/story-mcp-capability-unavailable`, never a false-empty success. Three committed authorities still state the retired opposite:

- `tools/story-mcp/README.md:18-20`: browser-only surfaces return an explicit empty result.
- `tools/story-mcp/spec/002-Tool-Registry.md:462-463`: `read-a11y-violations` returns an empty list plus a hint.
- `tools/story/spec/Principles.md:168-170`: substrates/a11y violations return empty plus a hint.

The implementation, tool descriptors, focused tests, `tools/story-mcp/spec/API.md`, and the opening host-boundary section of `002-Tool-Registry.md` all enforce the error. The stale prose is operationally material: an empty violations vector means a reached provider observed no findings, while capability absence means the host could not look.

## Deduplication

All-status searches over `read-a11y-violations`, `capability-unavailable`, `false-empty`, `empty list`, and the exact sentences found no issue owning these residual pages. rf2-udumn / PR #8865 owns the public chapter and retired `record-as-variant` residue; its enumerated scope is complete and closed, so this narrowly owns the separate capability-result contradiction.

## Recommended minimal fix

Replace the three stale clauses with one consistent rule: unreachable provider -> machine-readable capability error; empty collection -> a reached provider genuinely reported none. Keep the canonical links rather than adding another catalogue.
acceptance_criteria:
1. README, Tool-Registry §read-a11y-violations, and Story Principles all describe the same `isError true` / `:rf.error/story-mcp-capability-unavailable` result for an unreachable browser provider.
2. Each distinguishes capability absence from a reached provider returning an empty substrate/violation collection.
3. No runtime, descriptor, schema, tool inventory, or transport behavior changes.
4. The applicable documentation link gate passes; tables/links touched are hand-checked where the gate does not cover prose.

title: bug(story-mcp): missing adapter yields a false passing run
description:
## Scope

Make Story-MCP's headless `run-variant` / `preview-variant` path fail clearly when the consumer JVM has not installed a re-frame adapter, and teach the existing consumer-project launch recipe to install the renderer-free `plain-atom` adapter when variants are meant to run. Keep the fix on the existing lifecycle and README surfaces; add no server flag, bridge, default-adapter registry, or new tool.

## Correctness finding

PR #8866 made the project-stories conformance witness non-vacuous and discovered the prerequisite needed to make that witness execute: without `(rf/init! plain-atom/adapter)`, the headless server's setup dispatch reaches no adapter, the script produces no assertion, yet `run-variant` returns the ordinary `:status :pass` envelope over `{}` and `[]`. The PR correctly installs `plain-atom` in its fixture, but the published `tools/story-mcp/README.md` golden-path alias only requires the project's story namespace and lists JVM-loadability/stdout as the two namespace rules. A real consumer following it can therefore receive a success-shaped non-run.

The no-adapter state is directly detectable through the existing `rf/current-adapter-spec` surface, and core already names it `:rf.error/no-adapter-installed`. Preserve Story's intentional rule that an actually executed assertion-free variant is vacuously green; the defect is reporting that verdict when frame allocation never obtained the mandatory state substrate.

## Evidence and deduplication

- PR #8866 / rf2-3n3dk's worker note measured `BARE-APPDB {}` / `BARE-ASSERTIONS []` without `rf/init!`, versus the exact passing assertion after installing plain-atom.
- Its fixture comment now documents the failure and installs plain-atom, but `tools/story-mcp/README.md` lines 54-159 do neither in the user-facing launch recipe.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/adapter.cljc` already makes state-container creation fail with `:rf.error/no-adapter-installed`; `rf/current-adapter-spec` is public.
- rf2-3n3dk owns only the conformance witness and explicitly keeps the server/tool surface out of scope. All-status searches over Story-MCP/run-variant plus adapter, plain-atom, reactive substrate, no adapter, zero assertions, and headless JVM found no issue owning this runtime/recovery contract.

## Recommended minimal fix

At the shared run lifecycle boundary, reject an absent core adapter before allocating/running and return the normal machine-readable MCP error envelope with a concise recovery hint. Update the existing consumer alias example/rules to require `re-frame.substrate.plain-atom` and call `rf/init!` in the preloaded JVM namespace when headless execution is wanted. Pin both failure and recovery in the existing focused tests.

## Non-goals

No automatic substrate choice, browser bridge, adapter registry, blanket assertion requirement, new MCP option/tool, or redesign of Story's vacuous-pass rule.
acceptance_criteria:
1. With no adapter installed, Story-MCP `run-variant` and `preview-variant` refuse before lifecycle execution with `isError true`, a stable machine-readable error, and recovery that names `rf/init!` / the headless plain-atom choice; they never return `:status :pass` for this condition.
2. With plain-atom installed, the existing project-stories fixture still returns its exact setup/script assertion witness and passes.
3. The published consumer-project launch recipe includes the adapter boot prerequisite in a copyable form and distinguishes catalogue-only loading from runnable headless variants.
4. An adapter-installed, assertion-free variant retains Story's intentional vacuous `:pass`; no new assertion requirement or default adapter is introduced.
5. A focused negative control removes the fixture boot (or invokes an isolated no-adapter fixture) and observes the explicit error; restoration is green.
close_reason:
FIXED in PR #8899 (branch worker/storymcp-6j0yl, head ff7410799d). All AC met.

AC1: tools.lifecycle -- the owner run-variant and preview-variant already share for blocking invocation and error normalization -- gains no-adapter-error, a PRE-flight refusal composed into both handlers' or chains beside the existing arg-shape and substrate guards. It returns nil when an adapter is installed and otherwise isError true with core's OWN id for this condition, :rf.error/no-adapter-installed (the id re-frame.substrate.adapter's require-adapter! throws, catalogued in spec/009), plus :tool and :recovery :init-an-adapter-in-the-preloaded-namespace. The human sentence names rf/init! and the renderer-free plain-atom choice, and says catalogue reads keep working. The refusal carries NO :status at all, so it can never be mistaken for a run outcome. Detection is the existing public surface rf/current-adapter-spec, exactly as the item directed. No server flag, bridge, default-adapter registry or new tool.

AC2: the project-stories fixture already installs plain-atom (PR #8866), so it is unaffected -- end-to-end-project-stories.cjs captured exit 0, the rf.assert/path-equals witness minted, aggregate status pass.

AC3: tools/story-mcp/README.md gains a subsection under Loading your project's stories -- a copyable app.stories.cljc showing the plain-atom boot, and prose separating catalogue-only loading (needs nothing more) from runnable headless variants (needs the adapter). spec/002-Tool-Registry.md gains a section for the contract, spec/API.md carries it on the host boundary and on both lifecycle tools' Errors lines, and the run-variant and preview-variant descriptors now advertise it to agents (tool-descriptors.edn regenerated; --check in sync, 19 tools).

AC4: untouched and pinned. run-variant-happy still asserts the SAME fixture variant is vacuously :pass WITH an adapter installed, and the new negative control sits directly beneath it so the two states read as different rather than merged. snapshot-identity is deliberately unguarded -- it hashes the declared tuple and runs no lifecycle.

AC5: lifecycle-tools-refuse-with-no-adapter removes the fixture's adapter boot through core's test-only cold-start seam, observes the explicit error on BOTH tools, restores in a finally, and asserts the restored run is green again.

BONUS FINDING, fixed here rather than deferred: end-to-end-story.cjs -- the CATALOGUE conformance harness -- launched story-mcp bare and then asserted at steps 5-6 that preview-variant and run-variant came back green. That green was the same NON-RUN this bead is about: the identical false green rf2-3n3dk removed from the sibling project-stories harness, which that fix did not reach. Its launch now carries the adapter boot as a clojure.main -e init-opt in the shape the README documents; the trailing nil in that init-opt is load-bearing because -e prints a non-nil result and stdout is the JSON-RPC wire. Step 6's vacuous pass is now honest. stdio-roundtrip.js calls preview-variant only on an unknown variant so with-variant short-circuits first, and end-to-end-flag-gates.cjs drives only the write tools; both re-run green.

GATES, all on the final rebased base (origin/main c65367cfc1), each exit captured on the runner's own command line: story-mcp JVM suite exit 0 (279 tests / 1476 assertions), with a planted :recovery fault returning exit 1 naming the plant at the same 279/1476 counts; clojure -M:gen --check exit 0 (in sync, 19 tools); end-to-end-project-stories.cjs exit 0, and with the fixture's rf/init! removed it returns exit 1 with the client receiving the new refusal where it previously received a green run -- the end-to-end proof the defect is closed; end-to-end-story.cjs exit 0 (it was exit 1 before the harness repair); stdio-roundtrip.js exit 0; check_doc_slugs.py exit 0 with a planted broken anchor going red; check_readme_links.py --ci exit 0 with a planted broken target going red. Every plant restored and each restore verified by git blob hash against the committed object, not by diff.

JUDGEMENT on the shared theme with rf2-6j0yl: TWO defects, not one. Kept as two vocabularies deliberately -- the capability error means this host has no bridge to that provider (permanent, unfixable by the caller, recovery read-from-a-browser-local-story-host), while this refusal means the host could run it but the app has not chosen its substrate (fixable boot omission). Folding them into one id would tell a consumer following the README that their own launch is unfixable, and would blur exactly the vacuous-green line this bead says to preserve.

title: bug(realworld-http): optimistic comment replies can settle into a different article route
description:
## Scope

Keep RealWorld HTTP comment mutations owned by the `/article/:slug` page that issued them. Scope is `examples/real-apps/realworld_http/comments.cljs` plus the existing production-source CLJS suite. Reuse the `:comments :slug` fact and `reply-for-current-slug?` introduced by PR #8845; no framework or mutation abstraction work.

## Correctness finding

PR #8845 correlates article/comments READ replies, but the optimistic comment WRITE callbacks in the same file remain slug-free and mutate the one shared comments/form state unconditionally.

- `:comment-form/submit` reads the current slug for the POST path, but emits `:on-success [:comment-form/submit-success temp-id]` and `:on-failure [:comment-form/submit-error temp-id]`. A reply from alpha after navigation to beta can reset beta's current draft/form on success or surface alpha's failure on beta.
- `:comment/delete` likewise sends `:on-failure [:comment/delete-rollback prior]`. If alpha's DELETE fails after beta has loaded, the rollback inserts alpha's saved comment into beta's comments vector.
- None of those terminal handlers consults the new `reply-for-current-slug?` gate. The new source commentary says every reply target carries the requested slug and every terminal handler gates its write, but that is true only of the two reads.

This is not hypothetical request-id protection: these writes carry no shared cross-route request id that would suppress a late terminal reply. The current main still has the slug-free target vectors above.

## Reproduction

Load alpha, begin either an optimistic comment submit or delete with its HTTP reply held, navigate to beta and settle beta's comments load, then deliver alpha's terminal reply. Alpha submit failure writes beta's form error; alpha delete failure inserts alpha's comment into beta's list. The beta route and `[:comments :slug]` remain beta throughout.

## Minimal fix

Carry the issuing slug in the submit success/failure and delete rollback target vectors, and gate each state-changing terminal handler with the existing comments-slice correlation predicate before touching comments or form state. The delete success handler is a no-op and needs no machinery. Keep temp-id/prior payloads for their current optimistic reconciliation jobs.

## Non-goals

No generic route-owned mutation layer, request cancellation scheme, cache, comment-form redesign, or changes to managed HTTP. Do not broaden this into unrelated article social controls without a reproduced defect.

## Duplicate search

All-status searches covered cross-slug comments, comment submit/delete rollback, late comment replies, route correlation, `comment/delete`, and the RealWorld handler names. No owner was found. `rf2-iy3d6` deliberately scoped itself to route-driven reads and explicitly listed optimistic comment behavior as a non-goal, so this is a discovered follow-up rather than a duplicate.
acceptance_criteria:
- A focused production-source CLJS test holds an alpha comment submit or delete reply, navigates to and loads beta, then delivers alpha's submit success/failure and delete failure; beta's comments slice and current form remain byte-for-byte unchanged.
- The request target vectors carry the issuing slug, and all state-changing terminal handlers refuse a slug that differs from `[:comments :slug]` via the existing correlation helper.
- Current-slug controls prove submit reconciliation and delete rollback still work normally; the gate must not swallow every reply.
- The focused RealWorld CLJS suite and examples compile gate pass. No framework API or new abstraction is added.
notes:
## Resolution (PR #8898)

Fixed as specified. The three optimistic comment WRITE settles now carry the
issuing slug and gate on the existing reply-for-current-slug? predicate against
[:comments :slug]:

  - :comment-form/submit-success  [slug temp-id reply]
  - :comment-form/submit-error    [slug temp-id reply]
  - :comment/delete-rollback      [slug prior reply]

:comment/delete-success writes nothing, so it took neither slug nor gate, as the
item anticipated. Verified by census: the gate expression now occurs exactly 5
times in comments.cljs -- the two route-driven reads plus these three.

### The judgement the item left open: what a late write owes its route

A dropped READ is simply discarded; a dropped WRITE can strand optimistic state.
Walked each path:

  - submit-success: drop the whole write. The optimistic temp card was ALREADY
    discarded when :comments/load reset the slice on the slug change, and the
    comment really is saved server-side, so returning to the article re-reads it.
  - submit-error: drop the whole write. Same -- the temp card it would have
    yanked out is already gone.
  - delete-rollback: drop the whole write. Alpha's list was reset on the way out,
    and the server still holds the comment (the DELETE failed), so a return
    re-reads it. Re-inserting into another article's list would FABRICATE a
    comment that article never had.

### One fact had to be added, and it is load-bearing

[:comments :data] is route-owned already, but [:comment-form] is NOT: it is a
boot-time singleton set once by :comment-form/initialise from :app/initialise,
and the article route's on-match is only [[:article/load] [:comments/load]]. So
the form rode across a navigation still :status :submitting -- and the textarea
AND the Post button are both :disabled while submitting. Gating alone would have
left the destination article's comment form PERMANENTLY LOCKED: a worse bug than
the one reported, and invisible to a test that only asserts the slice.

So :comments/load now also resets [:comment-form] when it takes on a NEW article
identity, reusing the refresh? decision it already computes two lines up. A
same-slug refresh leaves the form alone, so a background re-load never eats an
in-progress draft. No new key, no new event, no new abstraction. Gate and reset
are two halves of one fix; either alone is wrong.

### The commentary trap

Confirmed at source: the block comment added by #8845 asserted that every reply
target carried its slug and every terminal handler gated its write, which was
true only of the two reads -- the file asserted the invariant it violated. It now
names exactly which five settles are correlated, names the two deliberate
NON-members, and states that the gate gives ROUTE identity rather than request
identity (so an alpha-beta-alpha return readmits an old alpha reply; deliberate,
since a per-request epoch was an explicit non-goal).

### Out of scope, deliberately, and now named in the source

The article SOCIAL controls in the same file are ungated and remain so per this
item's non-goal: :article/author-follow-synced, :article/author-follow-rollback
and :article/delete-failed all write [:article :data ...] unconditionally from a
button press. :article/author-follow-rollback looks like the same class of defect
(alpha's failed follow could flip the author flag on the article now on screen),
but no defect has been reproduced against it, so it was left alone and instead
called out by name in the correlation-gate comment so no future reader mistakes
it for covered. Worth a bead if the mayor wants it chased.

### Tests and gates

Six new cases in the existing production-source CLJS suite
(implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/realworld_cljs_test.cljs, deftest
realworld-comment-mutations-cross-slug): three cross-slug refusals asserting the
whole comments slice and whole form map; a non-vacuity control proving all three
settles still do their ordinary optimistic job on the current slug; a strand
control pinning that the destination form arrives usable and can post its own
comment; and a same-slug-refresh control. The pre-existing stale-index rollback
test moved to the new arity.

Gates, captured exits:
  - npm run test:cljs, split into its two phases and run foreground:
    compile exit 0; full suite exit 0, 11105 tests / 54792 assertions,
    0 failures 0 errors. Re-run after rebase onto the final base.
  - npm run test:examples-compile: exit 0, all 56 swept builds, zero warnings
    (:examples/realworld is the build carrying this file).
  - No markdown in the diff, so neither doc-link gate applies.

Sabotage witness: disabling the gate in :comment/delete-rollback alone turned the
focused suite RED (exit 1) with exactly the reported symptom -- the other
article's comment spliced into the current list -- at the same 18 tests / 343
assertions as the control, then restored, blob hash identical to the committed
object.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #8898. The three optimistic comment WRITE settles (comment-form/submit-success, comment-form/submit-error, comment/delete-rollback) now carry the issuing slug and gate on the existing reply-for-current-slug? predicate; comment/delete-success writes nothing so it needed neither. Each late write is DROPPED outright -- nothing is stranded, because the slice reset on the slug change already discarded the optimistic card and the server holds the truth. One fact had to be added and it is load-bearing: the comment form is a boot-time singleton the route never revisits, so it rode across a navigation still :submitting, and since the textarea and Post button are both disabled while submitting, gating ALONE would have locked the destination form permanently. comments/load therefore also resets the form on a NEW article identity, reusing the refresh? decision it already computes; a same-slug refresh leaves an in-progress draft alone. The false #8845 commentary claiming every target carried its slug and every handler gated is corrected: it now names the five correlated settles, the two deliberate non-members, and the route-identity (not request-identity) strength of the gate. Six new cases in the existing production-source CLJS suite, including a non-vacuity control and the strand control. Gates: test:cljs compile exit 0 and full run exit 0 (11105 tests / 54792 assertions, 0 failures 0 errors) re-run on the post-rebase base; test:examples-compile exit 0 across all 56 builds with zero warnings. Sabotage witness: removing the delete-rollback gate turned the focused suite red with exactly the reported symptom, then restored to an identical blob hash. No framework change, no new abstraction.

title: bug(skills): implementor filing recipe uses two labels that do not exist upstream
description:
The implementor local filing recipe (skills/re-frame2-implementor/references/cardinal-rules.md, section 8) ends its gh issue create example with:

    --label spec-gap,from-implementor

Neither label exists in day8/re-frame2. Measured live 2026-09-01 from a worker checkout: gh label list --repo day8/re-frame2 returns exactly ten labels (bug, documentation, duplicate, enhancement, good first issue, help wanted, invalid, question, wontfix, nightly-red) and neither spec-gap nor from-implementor is among them.

gh resolves --label names to ids BEFORE the createIssue mutation, so the whole call dies at pre-flight:

    could not add label: spec-gap not found     (exit 1)

Reproduced accidentally while executing the recipe end to end under rf2-2zkrz: the real gh ran instead of a stub, and this is exactly where it stopped. No issue was created -- the pre-flight failure is what saved it, which is also the evidence that filing never reaches the create step.

So the recipe still cannot file even with rf2-2zkrz landed. That bug was the temp-path handoff and its non-goals explicitly fence labels, so this was left standing and filed instead.

Disposition is a real ruling, not a mechanical fix -- pick one:
  1. create the two labels upstream (they are reasonable routing labels for spec gaps from ports), or
  2. drop --label from the recipe entirely, or
  3. point it at an existing label (documentation, or enhancement).

The migration skill recipe (skills/re-frame-migration/references/issue-filing.md) passes no --label at all and is unaffected.

Worth noting the class: nothing gates the recipe against the live repo, which is the same shape of defect as rf2-2zkrz -- the recipe reads correctly and does not run.
notes:
--- MAYOR RULING 2026-09-01 17:55 AUSEST: TAKE OPTION 2, DROP --label ENTIRELY. DISPATCHABLE. ---

Of the three dispositions this item offers, take option 2. Reasons, in the order they decided it:

THE SIBLING RECIPE ALREADY PROVES IT WORKS. skills/re-frame-migration/references/issue-filing.md
passes no --label at all and files successfully. That is not an argument by analogy, it is a working
precedent in this repository on the same surface, and it means option 2 costs nothing that is
currently being had.

OPTION 1 BUYS ROUTING CONVENIENCE WITH REPOSITORY CONFIGURATION, and nobody has asked for the
routing. Creating spec-gap and from-implementor upstream is an operator action, it makes the recipe
depend on repo state that no gate maintains, and it would put us back here the first time a label is
renamed. It is also the option that cannot be taken by a worker, so choosing it would convert a
dispatchable item into another operator hold.

OPTION 3 IS WORSE THAN NO LABEL. A spec gap reported by a port is neither documentation nor
enhancement, and a wrong label routes worse than an absent one -- it puts the issue in a queue whose
readers will not act on it, which is a silent failure rather than a visible gap.

NOTHING IS FORECLOSED. Dropping the flag leaves label-based routing available the moment somebody
wants it; the labels can be created and the flag re-added in one small change. That asymmetry is why
the smallest option is also the safest here.

EXPLICITLY NOT WANTED, so the next worker does not build it: do NOT add a gate that validates recipe
labels against the live repository. The item is right that nothing gates the recipe against the live
repo, and right that this is the same shape as rf2-2zkrz -- but the remedy there was a behavioural
fixture over the shipped recipe with a stubbed tool, which is cheap and offline. A gate that reaches
the real forge on every PR buys a rarely-changing fact at the cost of network flakiness in CI, and
that is the gold-plating the stance rejects. If a check is wanted at all, it belongs in the same
offline fixture #8892 added to check_skill_mcp_drift.py, asserting only that the recipe passes no
flag whose value it cannot know is valid.

SCOPE FOR THE DISPATCH: remove --label and its two values from the implementor recipe in
skills/re-frame2-implementor/references/cardinal-rules.md section 8. Confirm at source first that
the two labels really are absent from the repository, since that premise is what makes this a bug
rather than a preference. Re-run the census the item implies -- other pages may carry the same flag.
close_reason: Fixed by PR #8907 (worker/textfix-3), taking the mayor's ruled option 2. PREMISE CONFIRMED AT SOURCE AT TIP, which is what makes this a bug rather than a preference: gh label list --repo day8/re-frame2 returns exactly ten labels (bug, documentation, duplicate, enhancement, good first issue, help wanted, invalid, question, wontfix, nightly-red), and a direct API lookup for each of the two returns HTTP 404 while the control lookup for bug resolves. CENSUS RE-RUN at tip over tracked files, line-level AND flattened so a line-broken occurrence cannot hide, each control-checked against a known hit: the flag appears in five files -- three are an unrelated bench script's own flag (bench/hicasso seam_ladder.cjs and two docs/design/hicasso studio pages), one is prose in the migration recipe warning against interpolating it, and cardinal-rules section 8 was the ONLY filing recipe that passed it. spec-gap survives only as the issue TITLE prefix spec-gap(EP-NNN): and in prose; neither is a label. LANDED: the flag and its two values removed from the section 8 recipe, plus a short note saying why there is no label so the next author does not helpfully add one back. Two consequential edits kept the page self-consistent: section 9's approval draft no longer asks the engineer to review a label set that cannot exist, and the reviewer-pass bullet cites --repo and --search rather than a flag the recipe now refuses to pass. NOT BUILT, per the ruling: no gate validating recipe labels against the live repository. GATES: check_doc_slugs.py exit 0 (covers skills/, proven by plant to read this worktree), check_readme_links.py --ci exit 0. Neither reads inside fenced code blocks and the removed line was inside one, so their green says nothing about the change itself; the recipe block was hand-checked for continuation-backslash correctness after dropping the final flag.

title: mayor method: frozen clocks are ambiguous, not a signature of imminent completion
description:
OPERATIONAL, filed by the mayor 2026-09-01 15:10 AUSEST for Mike's call. Not a code defect.

SYMPTOM. Three background workers report 'running' in the agent listing while every independent signal says they are idle:
  - a95b2faa (rf2-ni0ko, PR #8872): last commit 2h ago, worktree clean, local tip == remote tip, no reply to a direct message sent ~30 min ago.
  - a458d57b (rf2-g1m2q, PR #8876): last commit 79 min ago, no file write since 13:51, worktree clean, tip == remote, no reply to a direct message.
  - abed3ebfd (rf2-j3tud fix worker): its PR MERGED two hours ago and its remote branch was deleted; zero unmerged patches; no write for 80+ min; no reply to a stop-and-report sent ~50 min ago.

COST, and it is not just slots. PR #8876 reads 85 checks / 0 non-terminal / 0 failing — the current band exactly. It clears every clause of the merge criterion EXCEPT the draft flag, which only its author can flip. PR #8872 is complete too but computed against the pre-#8868 matrix (84), so it needs a rebase as well as a ready mark. So two finished changes are stranded behind an interlock whose protected party may no longer exist, and the effective fleet is 3 of 6.

WHY THE MAYOR HAS NOT ACTED. Three candidate remedies, each reserved:
  (a) Flip the draft flag myself. The interlock exists so the merge loop cannot land a change out from under a live worker; overriding it on an INFERENCE that the worker is dead is exactly the proxy the reaping rules exist to forbid, one surface over.
  (b) Stop the agents (TaskStop), which would establish they are not live and discharge (a) honestly — but destroys any unwritten report, and the reports are the outstanding deliverable.
  (c) Dispatch around them to keep 6 ACTIVE. Done once already this session and it worked, but it grows the registered-agent count without bound if agents keep going quiet, and it is the wrong move if the cause is machine contention.

DIAGNOSIS IS UNRESOLVED and that is why this is filed rather than fixed. The competing explanation is loops.md section 2's wedge: a heavyweight gate that stalls with no progress, no exit file and no error, which would also explain why messages are not drained (they land at the receiver's next tool round, and a wedged tool call never reaches one). Machine reads 58 chrome and 11 node processes against 1 java — real browser-lane activity, but attributable to the three ACTIVE workers, so it neither confirms nor refutes the wedge.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: whether the harness's 'running' state distinguishes a live turn from an agent stuck in a hung tool call, and whether there is a liveness probe cheaper than a message that a wedged agent cannot answer.
acceptance_criteria:
- Both method pages describe frozen tip/fetch/write/message observations as non-discriminating: compatible with long foreground work/final hygiene and also with a stopped or wedged worker, never a positive signature of either state.
- A direct live-progress signal remains preferred; without one, the guidance is to declare a window and re-read without acting on the clocks alone.
- The five-worker/sixth-worker outcome count is stated consistently across both pages and matches the recorded incident.
- The fix-dispatch re-draft/verify rule and conservative never-flip-on-inference rule remain intact; no dashboard or new activity sweep.
notes:
METHOD REREAD 2026-09-01 15:16:13 AUSEST: the GENERAL rule this incident exposed is now written up in PR #8885 — docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md, section 'Publishing the change'. It records that the draft interlock fails in BOTH directions (stale-open on a fix dispatch, stuck-closed on a silent author), says explicitly not to flip the flag on an inference, and settles the resolution as a read rather than an inference: the agent's own report, or the operator's decision to stop the agent, which settles liveness by making it false.

THIS ITEM IS NOT THEREBY CLOSED. The doc change captures the rule; the operator question it names is still open and still Mike's — which of the three remedies to take here, and whether the harness's 'running' state can distinguish a live turn from an agent stuck in a hung tool call. Two finished changes remain stranded meanwhile.
UPDATE 2026-09-01 15:49 AUSEST — the problem has GROWN in two directions, and neither was visible when this was filed.

(1) FOUR dormant, not three. ab64ac300 (rf2-k2d2t, PR #8882) has joined them: its PR has carried two clj-kondo failures untouched for over an hour, which is the same shape as the others — registered running, nothing moving. Registered agents now number NINE against five genuinely active.

(2) IT HAS PROPAGATED INTO THE BACKLOG. Two open beads are now fenced behind the two stranded DRAFTS, so the cost is no longer just the stuck changes:
  - rf2-yasvj waits on PR #8876 (classifier-skills) merging.
  - rf2-0g60h waits on PR #8872 (ws-fatal) merging.
Neither can be dispatched, and neither fence can clear by any action available to me, because the merge criterion refuses a draft and only the author can lift that flag. A fence whose release condition is held by an agent that has stopped is not a queue; it is a dead end.

SALVAGE TEST RUN, and the answer is reassuring: NOTHING is at risk. ws-fatal, classifier-skills and urldecode all read local tip == remote tip, and routing-encoding shows no remote ref only because its branch was deleted on merge — git cherry reports zero unmerged patches against main, so its work is contained there. Every dormant agent has its work either merged or pushed. What is stranded is the READY MARK and the REPORTS, not the code.

That bounds the decision usefully: stopping these agents would cost the unwritten reports and nothing else. It does not make the call for you, but the downside is now measured rather than feared.
THE COST IS NOW A TRACKER LIE, 2026-09-01 15:55 AUSEST. Both stranded drafts have CLOSED beads whose work is NOT on main — rf2-g1m2q (PR #8876) and rf2-ni0ko (PR #8872) each read CLOSED while git cherry reports one patch with no upstream equivalent.

This is the documented consequence of beads closing on PR-OPEN rather than on merge, which is normally benign because changes merge within the hour. Here two of them cannot merge at all, so the tracker permanently asserts work the trunk does not have.

AND IT IS INVISIBLE BY CONSTRUCTION. The backlog reread reads OPEN items; nothing re-reads a closed one. So these two will not surface in any loop again: they are not a closure that REVERTED (that at least reappears in the open list), they are a closure that was never true. If those PRs are eventually abandoned, two closed beads silently describe absent work and the next person to touch that surface finds the defect still there with a closed item saying it was fixed.

NOTE THE SYMMETRY, because it is exactly inverted from the finding merged this session as PR #8888. That addition taught the backlog loop to catch an OPEN item that is already DONE. This is a CLOSED item that is UNDONE. Both are the tracker disagreeing with the tree; only one direction is now covered, and the uncovered direction is the one no loop reads. Raised for the next method-reread rather than acted on here.

NOTHING IS LOST EITHER WAY: both branches are pushed, so the code survives regardless of what is decided about the agents.
NEGATIVE RESULT 2026-09-01 16:20 AUSEST — MESSAGING DOES NOT REACH THESE AGENTS, and this rules out the most comfortable explanation.

Three direct messages have now gone to dormant agents (a458d57b, a95b2faa, a861d3726). ZERO replies. The third is the informative one: a861d3726 was messaged within MINUTES of its PR merging, proactively, precisely to stop it becoming another two-hour zombie — while it was presumably still mid-turn and had every reason to answer. It has now been running 52 minutes since, has not replied, and is dormant number five.

WHAT THAT ELIMINATES: "the message arrived after the agent had already stopped" was the kind explanation, and it does not survive this. The message was early, the agent was fresh, and nothing came back.

WHY IT MATTERS TO THE METHOD RATHER THAN JUST TO THIS BOARD: the stranded sweep leans on message-first as its liveness discriminator — send one, because a reply distinguishes alive from finished where a transcript cannot. Against this failure that discriminator is not merely slow, it is INOPERATIVE. A message queues for delivery at the receiver a tool round, and an agent that never reaches another tool round never drains it. So the one probe the method offers is exactly the probe this condition defeats, and its silence is indistinguishable from an agent that is busy working.

The practical consequence for anyone reading this later: do not spend further messages on an agent already showing the pattern (registered running, tip unmoved, no writes, work pushed). One is worth sending. The second and third are not, and I sent them.

FLEET STATE: 11 registered, 6 genuinely active, 5 dormant. The ceiling is not yet binding because idle agents contend for nothing, but the registered set now grows monotonically.

--- MAYOR MEASUREMENT 2026-09-01 16:45 AUSEST ---

The dormant set has grown from three to FIVE, and the two drafts it strands are now measured rather than described:

  PR #8876 (worker/classifier-skills-g1m2q, rf2-g1m2q): 85 checks, 0 non-terminal, 0 failing.
    FULLY GREEN AT BAND. It is blocked by nothing except the draft flag its author never unset.
    Last updated 03:58Z; measured at 06:45Z, so roughly 2h45m stranded.
  PR #8872 (worker/ws-fatal-ni0ko, rf2-ni0ko): 84 checks, 0 non-terminal, 0 failing.
    Green, but at band-minus-one -- it branched before the job that moved the band to 85 landed,
    so clause 5 needs a rebase before it can be judged. That rebase is work no live agent will do.

DOWNSTREAM COST, enumerated: four ready beads are fenced behind those two changes.
  Behind #8876: rf2-yasvj (retire the stale "skills_structural does not yet fire" caveats) and
                rf2-qxg24 (surface-review conformance-security classifier pair).
  Behind #8872: rf2-0g60h (spec/Pattern-WebSocket worked example still teaches the leak).
  Plus rf2-g1m2q and rf2-ni0ko themselves read CLOSED while their work is not on main.

WHY THE MAYOR HAS NOT ACTED: the publishing section of the dispatch template rules that a stuck-CLOSED
draft is NOT settled by flipping the flag on an inference -- "it looks done" is the same proxy the
reaping rules refuse. It is settled by a read: the agents own report, or the operators decision to stop
that agent, which settles liveness by making it false. Neither has arrived, so both changes wait.

NEGATIVE RESULT ON THE ONE PROBE THE METHOD OFFERS: three direct messages to dormant agents have produced
zero replies. The most recent was sent PROACTIVELY within minutes of that agents PR merging, while it was
presumably still mid-turn -- which eliminates "the message arrived too late" as the explanation. A message
queues for the receivers next tool round, and an agent that never reaches another tool round never drains
it. So message-first, the stranded sweeps liveness discriminator, is INOPERATIVE against this failure
rather than merely slow, and its silence is indistinguishable from an agent that is busy working.
Practical advice: one message is worth sending; the second and third are not.

NOTHING IS AT RISK. Every dormant agents work is merged or pushed. What accumulates is the registered
agent set, two finished changes, and four fenced beads.

--- STRANDED SWEEP 2026-09-01 16:49 AUSEST: the harness liveness probe is defeated by this failure ---

Ran the full loops.md ss4 sweep from the worktrees. Result: NOTHING TO SALVAGE, NOTHING TO REDISPATCH.
All five dormant worktrees have local HEAD == origin HEAD and clean status; routing-encoding has no
origin branch at all but git cherry against main returns "-", i.e. its commit is already patch-equivalent
on the trunk. So step 3 of the sweep has no work in it: every commit is durable, three of the five are
already merged.

CLOCKS, run properly rather than reasserted:
  fetch-head read twice, 16:46:49 and 16:49:06 (2m17s apart), per-worktree copy:
    ws-fatal 14:00:59 frozen | classifier-skills 13:50:48 frozen | routing-encoding 13:45:31 frozen
    urldecode 14:40:15 frozen | ssr-form2 15:35:03 frozen
    CONTROL, same instrument, same two reads: runrecipes moved 16:26:17 -> 16:47:30 with its tip
    advancing 3a52bc795c -> a776ebb49f. So the instrument works and the stillness is real, which a
    single read could never have established.
  write clock at TWO spans (5 min and 60 min) on the three oldest: all zero at both. Their creation
  times are 12:53, 13:18 and 13:31, so the 60-minute span sits well inside the trees own age and the
  zero is a genuine no-writes rather than the checkout-age artefact the method warns about.

THE FINDING THAT IS NEW, AND IT IS ABOUT THE SWEEP ITSELF:

loops.md ss4 step 3 endorses asking the harness whether an agent is RUNNING, and calls it "decisive in
one direction: an agent under an exhausted allowance dies within seconds of being resumed, so minutes of
running is positive evidence the allowance came back."

That reading does not survive THIS failure mode. All five of these agents report RUNNING -- for between
1h11m and 3h01m -- while every other clock says idle and their trees say finished. So "running" is
positive evidence of life ONLY in the narrow post-resume context the method describes, where the
alternative is near-instant death. Read generally, which is how the rule is written, it inverts: it
becomes the single most reassuring signal on the board and it IS the symptom.

That matters because the probe is cheap and the method presents it as the fast path -- a mayor reaching
for it first, as designed, gets told all five are alive and stops sweeping. The per-worktree fetch-head
clock read twice is what actually discriminated here, and it is the slower, less obvious instrument.

NOT FIXING THE DOCUMENT FROM THIS LOOP -- the posture loop flags drift, the method-reread loop repairs
the text. Recorded here so the repair has its measurement when that loop next runs.

--- COUNT CORRECTION + NEW ARRIVAL 2026-09-01 17:08 AUSEST ---

CORRECTION TO MY 16:45 NOTE. That note said "four ready beads are fenced behind those two changes" and
then enumerated THREE (rf2-yasvj, rf2-qxg24 behind #8876; rf2-0g60h behind #8872). The count and its
breakdown disagreed. The breakdown was right and the count was wrong: it was three, not four. Stating
it plainly because the number is the thing an operator would act on, and because a total that does not
match its own list is exactly the error I keep a note about.

IT IS NOW GENUINELY FOUR, by arrival rather than by recount. rf2-bbe91 (P3, wire the MIG-23 cold-start
fixture into the skills-structural CI job) modifies .github/workflows/test.yml, and its own description
says so: "Hot-zone: touches .github/workflows/test.yml -- sequence accordingly." #8876 modifies the
SAME job in the SAME file, so bbe91 cannot be dispatched while #8876 sits unmerged.

CURRENT FENCED SET, enumerated and counted from that enumeration:
  Behind #8876 (85 checks, 0 non-terminal, 0 failing -- fully green at band, author dormant ~3h):
    rf2-yasvj, rf2-qxg24, rf2-bbe91   = 3
  Behind #8872 (84 checks, green but band-minus-one, needs a rebase no live agent will do):
    rf2-0g60h                          = 1
  TOTAL FENCED READY BEADS = 4
  Plus rf2-g1m2q and rf2-ni0ko, which read CLOSED while their work is not on main.

THE TREND IS THE POINT, not the number. Two of these four did not exist when the drafts stranded; they
arrived afterwards and landed on the same hot file. A stranded change in a hot-zone file does not hold a
fixed queue -- it ACCRETES one, because every later item touching that file must sequence behind it. So
the cost of this hold grows on its own without anything new going wrong.

A SIXTH INSTANCE MAY BE FORMING. PR #8892 (worker/issuebody-2zkrz) has been green at band for about
25 minutes and remains a draft; its worktree tip has not moved and its fetch-head clock has been frozen
at 16:23:12 for 43 minutes, measured twice. I am NOT recording it as stranded: the method names exactly

FOUR OF THE FIVE AGENTS I CLASSIFIED AS DORMANT HAVE NOW COMPLETED, ALIVE, WITH FULL REPORTS.

three hours into foreground gates reaches one rarely -- but I converted "slow" into "inoperative",

WHAT I ACTUALLY MEASURED WAS RIGHT; THE CONCLUSION DRAWN FROM IT WAS WRONG. The frozen fetch-head
clocks, the zero writes at two spans, the unmoved tips -- every one of those readings was accurate.
They are also the EXPECTED readings for a healthy worker inside a long foreground gate, which is what

THE METHOD ALREADY SAID SO AND I UNDER-WEIGHTED IT. loops.md ss4: "An unchanged tip says nothing on
its own -- a worker inside a long gate commits nothing by design, so a still tip is the EXPECTED
