title: spec(Conventions): roster :rf/settle-flows in the reserved :rf/* row
description:
rf2-kh73v added a second member to `re-frame.events/reserved-event-ids`: `:rf/settle-flows`, the framework-private flow-settle event the `:fx` walk enqueues after `:rf.fx/reg-flow` / `:rf.fx/clear-flow` (Spec 013 §Sequencing — settling on the dispatching frame).

spec/Conventions.md line ~46 is the normative reserved-namespace roster and its `:rf/*` row names the framework-wide pattern events individually, including `:rf/set-db` at length. `:rf/settle-flows` is not there.

Deliberately NOT taken by rf2-kh73v: spec/Conventions.md is a hot-zone one-toucher and is outside that item's enumerated scope (which named Spec 013, the API/core guides and the cart example). Filed rather than smuggled in.

Note the entry is not simply another `:rf/set-db`. `:rf/settle-flows` is reserved but NEVER REGISTERED — not in the registrar, not in the EP-0023 image standard registry. It resolves through the router's unresolved-handler seam (`router/framework-private-handler-metas`), which is what keeps it off `registrar/registrations :event` and therefore out of every app's event catalogue. It is listed in `reserved-event-ids` for a different reason than `:rf/set-db` is: the registrar is consulted BEFORE the seam, so an app `(reg-event :rf/settle-flows …)` would silently shadow the framework's settle and strand every flow-lifecycle effect. The roster entry should say that, not imply a second registered standard.

Applications must not depend on the id; the observable contract is the settle boundary, not the transport. Spec 013 §Sequencing states this already — Conventions just needs the roster row to agree.
notes:
VERDICT 2026-09-01 AUSEST (worker, PR #8902). PREMISE HELD, TAKEN.

VERIFIED AT SOURCE, not assumed. :rf/settle-flows exists at tip in
implementation/core/src/re_frame/events.cljc (the reserved-event-ids value, the
settle-flows-event-id def, the handler and its handler-meta), fx.cljc:842 and
router.cljc:493. A fixed-string census of the id across ALL tracked markdown
returned ZERO hits, so Conventions did not merely omit it from one row - the id
appeared nowhere in the doc corpus. The census instrument was controlled: the
same flattened, whitespace-insensitive search returned 53 files for
rf/reg-machine, so the zero is a real zero and not a bad pattern.

THIS WAS A DANGLING CROSS-REFERENCE, not a cosmetic omission - which the item
did not know and which raises its value. spec/013-Flows.md:474 deliberately
does NOT name the private id, and instead says its "id is nonetheless reserved
(per Conventions Reserved namespaces) so an application registration cannot
shadow it". Spec 013 was delegating the reservation to a roster that was
silent, so at tip NO normative document recorded that the id is reserved.

THE ROSTER ENTRY DOES NOT IMPLY A SECOND REGISTERED STANDARD, per the item's
explicit instruction. It states the distinction: unlike :rf/set-db it is
reserved but NEVER registered - no registrar row, no EP-0023 image-standard row
- because it is materialised through the router's unresolved-handler seam, so
it never reaches an application's event catalogue, tooling projection or
generated code. It is reserved for a DIFFERENT reason: the registrar is
consulted BEFORE that seam, so an app reg-event on the id would silently shadow
the settle and strand every flow-lifecycle effect, and fails loud instead. The
row also carries Spec 013's own caution that applications must not depend on
the id, the observable contract being the settle boundary and not the
transport. Spec column gains 013.

The row already had vocabulary for this case - :rf/head and :rf/public-error
are described in it as "reserved-but-not-registered" - so the entry mirrors an
existing shape rather than inventing one.

ONE THING CONSIDERED AND DELIBERATELY NOT DONE. Conventions rule 3 in the same
section reserves the bare :rf/* root for framework-wide pattern events that no
single AREA owns, and a reader could ask whether a flow-settle event should
have been :rf.flow/settle. It is defensible as-is: the event is defined,
enqueued and resolved entirely in core (events.cljc, fx.cljc, router.cljc), not
in the flows artefact, so it is core-owned like :rf/set-db rather than
area-owned. Recording the question rather than reopening a shipped id.

title: ci(http): no lane runs a solo-namespace ordering, so latent load-order hook dependencies are ungated
description:
DISCOVERED-FROM rf2-zvbm9 (PR #8889), reported by that worker as an observation it deliberately did not file itself.

THE FINDING (verify at source before acting): the jvm-http CI job runs a bare "clojure -M:test", i.e. the full-suite ordering only. rf2-zvbm9 was a namespace that passed in that ordering and failed when run ALONE, because it depended on a late-bind hook published by a namespace load that an alphabetically earlier test namespace happened to perform. No gate would have caught it, and none will catch the next namespace that acquires the same kind of latent dependency.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ONE BUG: the failure is silent and it accumulates. A namespace acquires an unnoticed dependency on somebody else load-ordering before it, the suite stays green, and the defect only surfaces when someone runs that namespace alone — which is exactly what a developer does when iterating, so the cost lands on the person least equipped to explain it. The specific hook here fails OPEN too: extract-paths returns an empty map when unbound rather than erroring, so the classification silently does nothing.

SCOPE IS A JUDGEMENT AND NOT OBVIOUS — this is filed to be RULED ON as much as fixed. Running every namespace solo multiplies the lane cost; running none leaves the hole. Candidate shapes worth weighing before building anything: a nightly rather than per-PR solo sweep; solo runs for a named set of namespaces with known late-bind dependencies; or making the hook fail LOUD when unbound, which converts a silent misclassification into an error and may remove the need for a solo lane at all. The last one is the smallest change and may be the right one — the stance prefers it over new CI machinery.

NOT URGENT: the specific instance is fixed by #8889, which requires the schemas namespace in the fixture that needed it.
notes:
MAYOR RULING, 2026-09-01: make the hook fail LOUD when unbound. Do NOT build a solo-namespace lane, nightly or per-PR, and do not add a named-set sweep.

The bead names three shapes and already leans at the right one. Confirming it as the ruling: extract-paths returning an empty map when unbound is a fail-OPEN, and that is the actual defect - the silent misclassification, not the absence of a lane. Convert it to an error. A namespace that has acquired a latent load-order dependency then fails immediately and says so, on the developer's own solo run, which is where the cost currently lands and where the message is most useful.

This is the smallest change, it removes a silent failure mode rather than adding machinery to detect one, and it may make a solo lane unnecessary - which is the point. New CI machinery to catch a class of bug that a two-line fail-loud converts into an ordinary error is exactly the over-engineering the stance rejects, and it would put a recurring toll on every PR forever.

If, having made the hook loud, you find a case it cannot reach, file that as its own bead with the case - do not widen this one into a lane.
close_reason:
Fixed in PR #8943 (branch worker/cilanes). Followed the ruling exactly: the hook now fails LOUD when unbound, and NO CI machinery was added — no solo lane, no nightly, no named-set sweep.

THE DEFECT. privacy-body/extract-paths (implementation/http/src/re_frame/http/privacy_body.cljc) returned an empty marks map when the late-bind schema-walker hook was unbound. An unbound hook means the marks are UNKNOWN, not EMPTY, and answering {} for it is the fail-OPEN the ruling names: a :decode schema marking a slot :sensitive? classified nothing and the secret rode the trace verbatim, green either side of it. rf2-zvbm9 was exactly that — four assertions reading their own secret back, visible only in a solo-namespace run because the full-suite ordering happened to load re-frame.schemas first.

THE LOUDNESS IS GATED ON WHETHER A MARK IS DECLARED, AND THAT MATTERS — an unconditional throw would have been wrong in both directions, checked at source rather than assumed. (1) day8/re-frame2-schemas is a TEST-ONLY dep of the http artefact, and the artefact resolves malli.core directly (decode.cljc, which WARNS rather than throws when Malli is absent), so an app can legitimately use a Malli :decode with no schemas artefact at all; an unconditional throw breaks every such app on every successful response, and on the production accept-failure path (transport.cljc, not debug-gated) too. (2) In-tree, http-decode-test, http-managed-test and http-empty-body-parity all use vector :decode schemas WITHOUT requiring re-frame.schemas, so an unconditional throw reddens all three on a solo run for schemas carrying no marks at all.

So extract-paths separates the two cases with declares-marks?, a presence probe asking only whether the schema's EDN form writes a :sensitive? / :large? PROP anywhere — a MAP KEY, so a field merely named :sensitive? is not a mark. It reads no Malli semantics, resolves no registry, derives no paths: not a second walker (the ns doc forbids one), it only decides whether the shared walker is REQUIRED. Declares no mark → {} as before, and a schemas-less app is untouched. Declares a mark with the hook unbound → throws :rf.error/schemas-artefact-missing via the canonical error/throw-error! builder, naming the require that fixes it. Probe and walker agree on the opaque cases (keyword registry ref, compiled m/schema object): both read them as markless leaves, so neither throws.

REUSING THE EXISTING ERROR ID leaves spec/009-Instrumentation.md — hot-zone — untouched; the id is already catalogued there. The contract is recorded in its owning tracked record, spec/014-HTTPRequests.md §Privacy, as a new rule 5 (old rule 5 Composition becomes 6; nothing in the repo references these by number, checked).

GATES, captured exits on the final rebased base: implementation/http 'clojure -M:test' exit 0, 514 tests / 3901 assertions (was 508 / 3883 — the six new tests are §7 of http_privacy_body_test, pinning the throw for both mark axes and the four no-throw cases); scripts/check_doc_slugs.py exit 0 for the spec edit. Both gates were exercised against a planted fault and came back red naming what was planted; restores verified by git BLOB hash against the committed object.

NO CASE FOUND THAT THE LOUDNESS CANNOT REACH, so no follow-up bead was filed. One adjacent surface was checked and deliberately LEFT: resources/classification.cljc's validation-failure-params-marks has the same {}-when-unbound shape but is not a live fail-open — it runs only on a validation failure, which requires the schemas artefact to have validated in the first place, so the unbound branch is unreachable, and its surrounding comment states that posture deliberately.

title: flake(http): supersede-stale poll-until backstop times out under CI load, redding unrelated PRs
description:
implementation/http test `re-frame.http-reply-lowering-test/supersede-distinct-work-ids-and-canonical-stale-trace` (http_reply_lowering_test.clj) fails intermittently on loaded CI runners with `poll-until timed out — supersede-stale`, reported as `0 failures, 1 errors` and exit 1 from `clojure -M:test` in implementation/http.

## Observed

- 2026-09-01, PR #8873 (a routing-only diff that cannot reach this code path): `:elapsed-ms 30022`, i.e. the full 30 s backstop elapsed. Re-running the identical tree on a fresh CI head was green with no code change.
- The test`s own source comment records a PRIOR occurrence of the same class and the mitigation taken then: the backstop was raised from 5 s to 30 s because "the async supersede landed AFTER the window, timing the machine, not the canonicalisation (it redded unrelated PRs, e.g. #6817)".

So the 5 s -> 30 s raise reduced the rate but did not remove the failure mode; 30 s is now demonstrably marginal too.

## Why it matters

This test is inside a surface-gated job, and implementation/http declares day8/re-frame2-routing as a {:local/root} dependency, so ANY routing-only change schedules the http job. A flake here therefore reds PRs whose diff provably cannot reach the code under test, and each red costs a diagnosis dispatch. PR #8873 cost exactly one.

## Shape of the problem, not a prescribed fix

The wait is already signal-based rather than a fixed sleep (`poll-until` on a predicate over delivered replies plus a `:rf.http/stale-suppressed` trace row), which is the right structure — the remaining `:timeout-ms` is a pure backstop. The question is whether the supersede round-trip can be made deterministic at the test boundary (await the transport reply and the trace row on a latch rather than polling), so the backstop is unreachable rather than merely generous. Raising the bound a third time is the option to weigh against that, not the obvious answer.

Deliberately NOT diagnosed here: whether the timeout indicates real contention in the supersede path under load, or purely runner scheduling. Worth one look before choosing a remedy — a genuinely slow supersede under load would be a product finding rather than a test one.

## Non-goals

- No change to supersede/stale-suppression semantics; those are what the test correctly pins.
- Not a licence to delete or weaken the assertion.
notes:
VERDICT (PR #8889, branch worker/http-robust-o9e15): FIXED, and the theory recorded on this bead and in the test source was WRONG.

FINDING 1 - the stale-suppression trace is NOT async. handlers/managed-handler calls registry/supersede! and then transport/emit-superseded-stale-trace! inline in the fx phase, so the :rf.http/stale-suppressed row has already landed before the SECOND dispatch-sync returns. Probed: present with ZERO wait. The source comment claiming a real async round-trip (transport reply -> reply lowering -> app dispatch -> stale trace) was factually wrong and is removed.

FINDING 2 - the failure mode is ABSENCE, not lateness. registry/supersede! returns nil when nothing is in flight under the request-id. The test gate was a CountDownLatch(1) whose FIRST act inside the handler was its own .countDown, so the following .await returned immediately and the gate never held request #1 at all. Request #1 was free to finish its whole loopback round trip in the gap between the two dispatch-sync calls; two app replies were then delivered, no supersede ever happened, and poll-until sat out its full backstop waiting for a row that could not arrive. That is why the 5s -> 30s raise reduced the rate without removing the mode, and why a third raise cannot help: no bound is large enough for an event that is never emitted.

REPAIR - a new start-held-server! holds every exchange until the TEST releases it, so #1 cannot finalise before #2 is issued and the supersede becomes a property of the ordering rather than of machine speed. The stale row is then asserted SYNCHRONOUSLY (the 30s poll is gone entirely), and the one genuinely async step, the surviving request app reply, is awaited on a CountDownLatch the reply handler itself counts down. The sibling supersede-suppresses-prior-app-reply carried the identical no-op gate and the identical latent race and moves to the same harness.

PRODUCT FINDING - none. This bead deliberately left open whether the timeout indicated real contention in the supersede path under load. It does not: the supersede path is correct and synchronous, and the test simply was not exercising it when the race was lost. The one seam worth recording is that a superseded attempt TRANSPORT completion offers no observable completion signal a test can await, which is why the repair holds the server rather than awaiting the abort.

EVIDENCE (a flake is not proved gone by one green, so stated in tiers). STRONGEST: the same planted 300ms pause widening the gap between the two dispatch-sync calls, applied to both structures. Old structure = exit 1, poll-until timed out - supersede-stale, :elapsed-ms 30017, 0 failures 1 errors - matching the CI signature of :elapsed-ms 30022 on PR #8873. New structure = exit 0, 25 tests 137 assertions. ARGUMENT: the timed wait for the stale row became a synchronous assertion. WEAK: five consecutive solo runs, exit 0 and a stable 137 assertions each.

GATES on the final rebased base, all captured exit codes: full suite (= jvm-http in test.yml, clojure -M:test from implementation/http) exit 0, 508 tests 3883 assertions; solo re-frame.http-reply-lowering-test exit 0, 25 tests 137 assertions. Sabotage control planted at http_reply_lowering_test.clj:640 drove exit 1 naming the planted value at the planted line, which also establishes the gate read this branch checkout. Restores verified by git blob hash.

Test-only change: no production source touched, no assertion weakened, no spec change. Related: rf2-zvbm9 rode the same worker; the two turned out INDEPENDENT.
AUDIT PR #8889: REOPENED. The held-server ordering correctly removes the original race, but the regression still does not prove that the one delivered app reply belongs to the superseding issuance. Both server responses are identical, while both tests assert only reply count 1 and :status :ok; canonical replies carry :rf.reply/work-id, so a broken path that delivers issuance 1 while losing issuance 2 can satisfy the advertised request-#2 claim. The final Thread/sleep 200 is also only a timing window for absence of a delayed second delivery. Minimal completion: assert the delivered reply work-id is [:rf.work/http :search 2 1] and make the existing harness's no-second-delivery observation deterministic. Keep the held-server harness; no production change or new abstraction.

VERDICT (PR #8923, branch worker/httpwid-o9e15, 2026-09-01 20:52 AUSEST): AUDIT COMPLETED. Both things the PR #8889 audit asked for are done, test-only, held-server harness kept, no production change, no new abstraction.

PREMISE HELD AT TIP. Verified before editing: both supersession tests asserted only reply count 1 and :status :ok (the stale-trace test asserted only the count -- not even :status), both closing Thread/sleep 200 lines were present, and canonical replies do carry :rf.reply/work-id (already pinned at success-reply-is-canonical). Nothing had been fixed in the interval.

AUDIT LITERAL WAS RIGHT. Read from the code rather than the note: reply.cljc work-id builds [:rf.work/http logical-id (or issuance 1) (or attempt 1)], logical-id = the caller's :request-id when non-nil (here :search); registry/next-issuance! bumps issuance per fresh request under one request-id, and neither request retries. So the superseding attempt is exactly [:rf.work/http :search 2 1], as the audit quoted.

THREE DEVICES, NONE OF THEM A CLOCK.

(1) ISSUANCE IDENTITY. Both tests now assert the DELIVERED reply's :rf.reply/work-id is [:rf.work/http :search 2 1]. Issuance is the only fact distinguishing the two byte-identical server responses, so this is what convicts a path that delivers issuance 1 and loses issuance 2.

(2) THE SUPERSEDE IS AN ORDERING, read while both exchanges are still HELD: the :search in-flight slot already holds issuance 2. registry/supersede! cleared issuance 1 out of it and fired its abort-fn INLINE during the second dispatch-sync's fx phase; that abort-fn wins the once-only :finalised? CAS and routes through dispatch-aborted!, where :request-id-superseded is in reply-suppressing-abort-reasons -- no app dispatch, and the won CAS makes issuance 1's later transport completion bail at already-replied?. There is therefore NO LATER MOMENT at which a second reply could originate. That is the real content of the no-second-delivery claim; the 200ms window was allowing for an event that cannot occur.

(3) A FIFO DRAIN BARRIER replaces Thread/sleep 200. dispatch-sync seeds at the FRONT of the frame's queue and then runs the drain loop to fixed point (router.cljc drain-block!), so every envelope enqueued before it has been PROCESSED by the time it returns. Honest scope: the barrier is a barrier for anything already enqueued; the guarantee against a genuinely later delivery is device (2), not any wait. Both are now stated in the source.

ALSO: registry/reset-issuance-counters-for-test! (an existing test-only helper, already used by http_managed_test.clj) now runs at the top of each test. issuance-counters is a process-global defonce and http_managed_test.clj ALSO uses :request-id :search, so the issuance literals held only because eviction happened to clear the counter -- a latent load-order dependency of exactly the kind rf2-ohfym observes the single full-suite jvm-http lane cannot see. The reset makes the new literals independent of what ran first. Group 3's second test also gains the :status :ok assertion it lacked.

GATES on the final rebased base (163aefb4c4, merge base 3cc654e45c), every exit code captured on one command line and quoted from the .exit file: full suite (= CI jvm-http, clojure -M:test from implementation/http) exit 0, 508 tests 3890 assertions; solo re-frame.http-reply-lowering-test run FIVE consecutive times, exit 0 each, a stable 25 tests / 144 assertions each. Baseline was 137 solo / 3883 full; the seven new assertions are the whole delta. The namespace was run solo deliberately, per rf2-ohfym: a full-suite ordering can supply a load-order dependency the namespace does not declare.

THE CONTROL BIT WHERE IT HAD TO. A plant that reds everything would not demonstrate the audit's gap, so the control makes the harness genuinely deliver issuance 1: one registry/reset-issuance-counters-for-test! inserted BETWEEN the two dispatch-sync calls, re-minting the superseding request as issuance 1. The supersede still happens (it keys on request-id, not issuance), one reply is still delivered, and it is still :status :ok. Exit 1, 25 tests 144 assertions, 2 failures 0 errors -- same assertion count as the clean run, so nothing was crashed out.
  RED (both new): "the surviving in-flight request is issuance 2..." (device 2) and "the delivered reply belongs to the SUPERSEDING issuance (2)..." (device 1), both actual [:rf.work/http :search 1 1].
  GREEN under the same plant -- the assertions that existed BEFORE this PR: reply count 1, ":status :ok", "the superseding request #2 is the live in-flight request", and the whole of supersede-distinct-work-ids-and-canonical-stale-trace. That green-beside-red IS the audit's finding, reproduced.

A FIRST SABOTAGE ATTEMPT CAME BACK GREEN and was treated as a reason to stop, not to proceed: the plant had landed AFTER both dispatch-sync calls, where both issuances were already minted, so it was inert. Moved between the two dispatches, it bit. Restores after every plant verified by git BLOB hash against the committed object (e27fd9f7aa3b14dd8011e275d1314bef137e50a5) -- line endings are translated in this checkout, so a byte digest of the working file would not be sound. The red also establishes the gate read this branch's checkout, since the fault existed nowhere else.

NOT DONE, DELIBERATELY: no production change was needed and none was made; implementation/http/src is untouched. The adjacent rf2-ohfym (jvm-http runs no solo-namespace lane, .github/workflows, hot-zone) stays open and untouched -- but its concern is answered for THIS namespace by the counter reset plus the five solo runs recorded above.
close_reason: PR #8923 (draft->ready): audit completion. Both supersession tests now pin the DELIVERED reply's :rf.reply/work-id to [:rf.work/http :search 2 1] (verified against reply.cljc work-id, not the note - the audit literal was right), and the Thread/sleep 200 quiescence windows are replaced by two non-timed devices: an in-flight-slot ordering assertion read while both exchanges are still HELD (proving supersede! cleared issuance 1 and won its once-only :finalised? CAS inline, so no later delivery can originate) and a dispatch-sync FIFO drain barrier for anything already enqueued. reset-issuance-counters-for-test! added so the issuance literals do not depend on JVM load order. Test-only; held-server harness kept; no production change. Gates on the rebased base: full suite exit 0 (508/3890), solo namespace exit 0 x5 (25/144 each). Control: a plant re-minting the superseder as issuance 1 reds BOTH new work-id assertions while the pre-existing count-and-:status assertions stay GREEN - the audit's gap reproduced.

title: spec/Pattern-WebSocket worked-example listing still teaches the :ws/fatal in-flight leak
description:
rf2-ni0ko composed fail-in-flight onto the :ws/fatal transition in examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs, so every door out of :active reachable from :connected now settles :in-flight exactly once.

spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md's worked-example listing was NOT updated (hot-zone, outside that bead's fence) and still shows the unrepaired shape:

  :ws/fatal    {:target :failed
                :action :record-error}

That is precisely the shape rf2-ni0ko's witness proves strands every in-flight slot and its waiting :reply-event, including across a later manual :ws/connect out of :failed. A consumer copying the spec's recommended listing inherits the leak.

Nothing in the spec is FALSE today — its stated invariant (§5 item 5, and the 'Leaking in-flight requests when the socket drops' pitfall) is scoped to the DROP door, not to every door out of :active — so this is teaching-drift, not a contradiction. Two other pre-existing divergences in the same listing are worth folding in while there: it carries no :ws/disconnect transition at all (rf2-b2jpr added one with :action :fail-in-flight), and it still shows :on-socket-lost with the fail-and-clear INLINED rather than routed through the fail-in-flight helper rf2-b2jpr factored out.

Also skills/re-frame2/patterns/websocket.md line ~114 shows ':ws/fatal {:target :failed}' with no action at all, and its parent-level :on summary row omits :ws/disconnect.

Suggested shape: update the listing's :ws/fatal row to the composed action, add the :ws/disconnect row, and show :on-socket-lost delegating to the shared helper — plus a sentence generalising the invariant from 'when the socket drops' to 'every door out of :active that destroys the socket'. spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md is HOT-ZONE: sequence, don't parallel.
notes: FENCED 2026-09-01 15:32 AUSEST by the mayor: sequenced behind PR #8872 (rf2-ni0ko) MERGING. This item corrects a worked-example listing that teaches the :ws/fatal in-flight leak; #8872 is the change that FIXES that leak, so the doc must describe the repaired behaviour and cannot be written accurately before it lands. spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md is also hot-zone one-toucher. CAUTION for whoever picks this up: #8872 is currently a DRAFT whose author has been unresponsive for over two hours (see rf2-m7sto), so this fence may be held by a change that is not progressing — re-check #8872's state rather than assuming it is merely in flight.
close_reason: Fixed by PR #8907 (worker/textfix-3). FENCE RELEASED, confirmed at source: PR #8872 (rf2-ni0ko) is MERGED, mergedAt 2026-09-01T08:01:11Z, and its commit is on origin/main -- so the caution note about an unresponsive draft author no longer applies. Treated as TEACHING-DRIFT, not a contradiction, exactly as the bead frames it: the page's stated invariant was drop-scoped (section 5 item 5 and the socket-drops pitfall) and the listing agreed with it, so nothing was false. The correction brings the listing level with the shipped example and generalises the teaching to every door out of :active -- which is what the example now implements and what the page's own :spawn bullet already implied (any transition that exits :active destroys the actor), so no normative claim was invented beyond what the pattern already asserts. LANDED in spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md: one fail-in-flight helper factored out as the example does, composed by :on-socket-lost (also bumps retries), :fail-in-flight (clean :ws/disconnect) and the new :on-fatal-error (also records the error); the :ws/disconnect row the listing never carried, at the :active parent level where the in-flight obligation lives, plus a line in the standard-transitions block; a note saying why :ws/auth-failed correctly keeps plain :record-error, since :register-request is bound only on :connected so :in-flight is provably empty by the time that door can be taken; and :origin :ws/local in the minted failure body, which section 5 and the two-producers paragraph already stated but the listing omitted. skills/re-frame2/patterns/websocket.md got the same treatment at its own level of abbreviation -- it showed :ws/fatal with no action at all and omitted :ws/disconnect from the parent-level :on summary row -- plus one anti-pattern for the door-by-door version of the bug. DELIBERATELY OUT: the shipped example also carries :ws/disconnect on :reconnecting and :failed; those doors carry no in-flight obligation because :in-flight was settled on leaving :active, so neither listing gains them. MACHINE-SPELLING CARVE-OUT HONOURED: the file contains exactly one line matching rf/make-machine-handler and zero matching rf/machine-, and that line is untouched (rf2-wrzfb holds those). GATES: check_doc_slugs.py exit 0, proven by plant to read this worktree -- four faults planted in PROSE across both pages returned exit 1 naming each by file and line, then restored and verified against the pre-plant git blob hashes 5830a4a864779e5e26f1ec25367b92b78cfa9a12 and d8cfa28c9293fb2e7798f7eee6ca94077b9c6955. check_readme_links.py --ci exit 0. Structure was hand-checked instead: paren/bracket/brace balance of every clojure fence in both pages, balanced before and after; table column counts uniform at 2; and no heading, anchor or link target added, moved or removed.

title: changed-surfaces: migration_v1_codemod arm misses implementation/core changes its :integration lane now depends on
description:
Surfaced by the rf2-8odvg/rf2-36u96 worker (PR #8857) as an out-of-scope finding it correctly declined to act on; OWNING ITEM: rf2-36u96, which created the dependency.

FINDING (worker's, unverified by the mayor — treat as a claim and check at source): the `migration_v1_codemod` classifier arm in .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh fires on `migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod/*` only. PR #8857 wired `clojure -M:integration` into the jvm-migration-v1-codemod job, and that integration lane reaches implementation/core through a :local/root. So a change confined to implementation/core does NOT arm the codemod job even though the job now depends on that code — the classic surface-armed gate that is skipped on the very push that breaks it (loops.md clause 2 names this shape: a gate skipped on the breaking commit while the trunk rollup reads green throughout).

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED IN #8857: widening the arm means touching .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh AND its pinned mirror implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs — the one-toucher-by-construction pair (CLAUDE.md 'Minimise merge conflicts when dispatching'). A change that alters what the classifier OUTPUTS must move both halves in ONE commit, because the test pins those outputs. The worker was fenced out of that pair and stopped and reported rather than crossing, which was correct.

BEFORE DISPATCHING: verify the arm's current pattern at source, and confirm the :integration lane really does reach implementation/core (read the codemod deps.edn's :integration alias). #8857's own report notes that rf2-36u96's description was ALREADY wrong about scripts/test-jvm-tools.sh's roster, so this bead's premises deserve the same scepticism.

SCOPE IF IT HOLDS: widen the arm so implementation/core changes arm the codemod job, moving script and mirror in one commit; no new job, no new gate.
notes:
VERDICT 2026-09-01 — the bead HOLDS on both halves. Fixed in PR #8867 (branch worker/classifier-arm-fk5jy, commit ea167a2b94).

PREMISE (a) VERIFIED — the arm's actual pattern. Read at source rather than taken from the bead's wording. In .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh, 'migration_v1_codemod=true' appears in exactly ONE arm — 'migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod/*)' — plus mark_all(). No arm earlier in the same case statement matches an implementation/core/... path (the nearest, the per-feature list, enumerates sibling artefacts and the exact files implementation/deps.edn, shadow-cljs.edn, package.json — not implementation/core/*). The job's gate in test.yml is 'if: needs.detect_changed_surfaces.outputs.migration_v1_codemod == 0x27true0x27' with NO implementation_jvm fallback, so nothing else could have armed it.

PREMISE (b) VERIFIED — the :integration edge reaches implementation/core. migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod/deps.edn declares, under the :integration alias, 'day8/re-frame2-core {:local/root "../../../implementation/core"}', and its own comment says it outright: 'only this alias pulls implementation/core'. test.yml's jvm-migration-v1-codemod runs 'clojure -M:test' AND 'clojure -M:integration' as two separate steps (the second added by rf2-36u96 / PR #8857).

MEASURED BEFORE THE FIX (classifier run on this trunk):
  implementation/core/src/re_frame/core.cljc -> migration_v1_codemod=false, implementation_jvm=true, tools_jvm_machines_viz=true
POSITIVE CONTROL on the same instrument, same run:
  migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod/src/re_frame/migration/reg_event_codemod.clj -> migration_v1_codemod=true, implementation_jvm=false
So the false was a real negative, not a classifier that had stopped classifying.

THE FIX. One boolean, 'migration_v1_codemod=true', added to the existing 'implementation/core/*)' arm — which already carries three reverse edges of exactly this shape under rf2-wq17m, whose own comment says every reverse edge in the file is spelled out the same way. No new job, no new gate, no workflow-file edit, no dependency-graph scheme.

SCOPE JUSTIFICATION (why core and no wider): implementation/core/deps.edn puts only ':paths ["src"]' and two mvn coordinates on its BASE classpath. Its cross-artefact :local/root edges (schemas, machines, routing, flows, http, ssr, epoch, resources, test-quiet) all sit under ALIASES, and a :local/root dependency never activates its target's aliases. Core's own tree is therefore the whole of what the :integration lane reaches.

ONE-WAY EDGE, pinned in both directions: core changes now arm the codemod lane, but a codemod-only diff still must not arm implementation_jvm (the codemod is downstream of core). Verified after the fix: the codemod's own source still classifies implementation_jvm=false.

ONE-TOUCHER PAIR honoured — .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh and implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs move in ONE commit. Derived at start-up that nobody else was live on the pair: 0 of 7 open PRs touched either file.

CONTROL (the deliverable). Pin added first, script un-widened: gate went RED, captured exit 1, naming exactly the planted assertion ('a core change arms the v1 codemod lane over the :integration edge (rf2-fk5jy)'). That red is also the proof the gate read the worker's own checkout, since the pin exists in no other tree. After widening: captured exit 0, and the pass count moved 291 -> 292 rather than collapsing.

GATE. The covering gate is CI job js-harness-self-tests -> 'npm run test:scripts' from implementation/, which is UNGATED (no needs: detect_changed_surfaces, no if:) so it runs on every PR; the mirror is picked up by that script's scripts/*.test.cjs glob and spawns the REAL classifier bytes. Full run after the fix: captured exit 0, 122 test files, 0 fail, 209s. All exit codes captured with redirect + echo on one command line in one shell, never through a pipe.

SIDE FINDINGS (not actioned here, flagged for the mayor):
1. test.yml's job NAME for jvm-migration-v1-codemod still reads 'JVM migration/from-re-frame-v1/codemod (clojure -M:test)' though the job has run two aliases since #8857. Cosmetic, and the file is hot-zone, so left alone.

title: patterns/websocket: :ws/fatal out of :active strands in-flight requests (same class as rf2-b2jpr)
description:
rf2-b2jpr routed clean :ws/disconnect through the shared fail-in-flight helper so leaving :active settles every in-flight request exactly once. One door out of :active still bypasses that invariant: :ws/fatal {:target :failed :action :record-error} (examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs, :active :on). Fired from :connected with a non-empty :in-flight, it destroys the socket actor and strands every slot exactly as the clean-disconnect bug did — the scheduled timeout carries the destroyed socket id, :current-socket? rejects it after teardown, and the slot plus its waiting :reply-event survive forever, including across a later manual :ws/connect out of :failed.

Mitigating context: nothing in the example currently dispatches :ws/fatal — it is the documented app-level escape hatch (spec/Pattern-WebSocket.md, ':active / * --:ws/fatal--> :failed'), so the leak is reachable only by consumer code using the pattern as written. :ws/auth-failed -> [:failed] is provably safe by contrast: :in-flight only fills in :connected, and every door out of :active from :connected settles it once this is fixed.

Fix is small now the helper exists: compose fail-in-flight with :record-error on the :ws/fatal transition (one action that does both), plus a wrapper deftest mirroring websocket-clean-disconnect-fails-in-flight-request with :ws/fatal as the exit door. Same fence as rf2-b2jpr: examples/patterns/websocket/connection.cljs + implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/websocket_cljs_test.cljs.

title: reg-interceptor registration coords never reach the interceptor-exception trace (Xray chip gap for the supported authoring form)
description: The Xray Epoch INTERCEPTOR (exception) row's jump-to-source chip reads :source-coord off the :rf.error/interceptor-exception trace tag; the router takes it from the interceptor map's :source-coord (interceptor.cljc error-record). reg-interceptor (the ONE supported authoring form, EP-0022) captures registration coords into the REGISTRY meta (interceptor_registry.cljc reg-interceptor* -> source-coords/merge-coords), but descriptor->interceptor lowers {:before/:after} descriptors through ->interceptor* WITHOUT threading those coords onto the built value — so an interceptor authored the supported way never gets the exception-row chip; only a VALUE registered at the migration boundary carrying its own :source-coord does. Until rf2-93sxp the ->interceptor macro was the de-facto route to a coord-carrying value (tests and the standard_epochs testbed used it); with the macro gone (PR #8791) those sites author with reg-interceptor descriptors and the testbed's exception-row chip degrades to plain text (the INTERCEPTORS registry-read step's chip is unaffected — spec 021:426 documents it off handler-meta). Candidate fix: descriptor->interceptor stamps :source-coord from the registration meta's coords (registry resolver, one site), making the chip work for the authoring form everywhere. Touches interceptor_registry.cljc + tests; check spec/009 and tools/xray/spec/021 wording. Named as within rf2-93sxp's non-goals ('no redesign of source-coordinate diagnostics'), hence this follow-up.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #8817: resolve-ref threads the reg-interceptor registration meta's coords onto every resolved interceptor value as :source-coord (registration-coords helper; value's own coord wins; programmatic/framework/production paths stay coord-free), so a descriptor-authored interceptor's :rf.error/interceptor-exception trace now carries the registration coord the Xray exception-row chip reads. Regression pinned on the actual failing path (descriptor-authored throw -> trace :source-coord tag) plus factory/programmatic/framework/migration-precedence arms; control shown red with the threading removed, restore blob-hash-verified. tools/xray spec 021 unchanged - it already documents this behaviour; no spec/009 change needed.

title: schemas: malli.error's message table survives Closure after the humanizer gating — ruling wanted on an out-of-graph mechanism
description:
Follow-up from rf2-tiymn (PR pending). Measured 2026-08-30 on the matched schemas-bundle A/B, all gzipped, control 86851 B:

- unconditional humanizer publication (trunk before rf2-tiymn): margin 41595 B
- publication gated on interop/debug-enabled? (what rf2-tiymn lands): margin 40885 B (-0.7 KB). The :schemas/humanize-explain! keyword and malli.error/humanize's code leave the probe; malli/error.cljc drops 12.0 -> 10.5 KB optimized.
- adapter's [malli.error] :require deleted outright (counterfactual, not landed): margin 38333 B (-3.3 KB). Every malli.error literal gone.

The 2.5 KB between the last two is malli.error's `default-errors` message table (built through PersistentHashMap.fromArrays) plus its random-uuid negation prefix: top-level defs whose initialisers Closure cannot prove pure, so it keeps them with no reader. Gating cannot reach it; only taking malli.error out of the build's module graph does, and the library cannot do that for a consumer without a build-side knob (a dev-only :preloads ns that publishes the humanizer, a :reader-features conditional require, or an :ns-aliases stub). rf2-tiymn's brief ruled out a new knob and its non-goals rule out a dynamic loader, so the residue is recorded in Spec 010 §Bundle cost and priced inside the gate's margin.

Question for the mayor: is 2.5 KB gzipped per schemas consumer worth a consumer-side dev-only preload (the humanizer moves to a re-frame.schemas.malli.humanize ns wired via :devtools :preloads, with the JVM keeping the automatic publication)? If not, close this as recorded-and-accepted; Spec 010 already says what stays and why.
notes: Figure consistency (2026-08-31): the three margins above in bytes are 41595 B = 40.6 KB (unconditional), 40885 B = 39.9 KB (gated, what PR #8788 lands), 38333 B = 37.4 KB (require deleted, counterfactual). Spec 010 §Bundle cost and PR #8788 quote the same three in KB. Repeat builds of one tree vary by tens of bytes gzipped (raw identical), so the last two digits are noise.
close_reason: REJECTED AS GOLD-PLATING by the mayor 2026-08-31 00:56:58 AUSEST, on the read-only triage at 5d35356469 and a read of PR #8788: the branch already records the residue and its cause (default-errors via PersistentHashMap.fromArrays) at spec/010-Schemas.md:735, prices it inside the +39.9 KB margin, and re-derives the bundle band. The only thing left is a consumer-side dev-only :preloads knob for about 2.5 KB gz, a second wiring path through the template shadow-cljs.edn, the setup skill and the how-to for every consumer, against the stance. Recorded and accepted; reopen only if Mike wants the knob.

THE RULE (binding): a docstring carries (a) what the var is or returns; (b) the contract - takes, returns, promises, effects, ordering, failure behaviour, in full for a public var, and for a private var what it does plus the one non-obvious invariant behind its shape; (c) one sentence of why; (d) where the argument lives, as a repo-relative path into docs/design/hicasso (architecture.md, studio/<page>.md, decisions.md HD-NNN). Links are repo-relative paths, NEVER [[wikilinks]] - 892 exist in src and nothing resolves them; check each retained path exists by hand and say so in the PR body. A measured figure stays only with its page named beside it. A source comment stays only where it protects nearby code from a plausible-but-wrong edit (a local correctness proof); module history, benchmark narrative, rejected alternatives, HD derivations and explanations of other namespaces' mechanisms do not. Content rule, not a number: no 40-line cap, no 1:1 enforcement, no link checker, no script. Untouched: retained-inventory's :what strings and the rf2:builder-bypass-ok block.

MOVE vs DELETE: durable design reasoning with no home in docs/design/hicasso is MOVED there - measurements and traces to studio/, rulings and rejected alternatives to decisions.md, mechanism reasoning to architecture.md; prose a design page already carries, superseded prose and change-narration is DELETED. Known for these files: controlled.cljs ns duplicates studio/controlled-input-two-implementations.md (full matrix and measured rows already there) - delete, cite the page. Check the others against the studio/ and decisions.md pages they name before moving anything. The PR body names, per essay, the path it moved to or "deleted - duplicated at <path>" / "deleted - superseded".

WORKED EXAMPLES (shape to copy; full text in rf2-6c12m.4 notes part 2): the collector ns docstring 392 -> 12 lines (what it owns, why those share a namespace, one design-record path); commit-basis 58 -> ~18 lines (three terms, why three, the .19 reincarnation counter-example kept as the one-sentence why, one architecture.md path); cold-read! 59 -> 9 lines (contract, fallback, why the memo is per read with the figure and its studio page).

ACCEPTANCE: (1) opening each file shows code and a compact namespace map, not an essay; (2) public inputs, outputs, effects, ordering and failure behaviour remain stated at the var; (3) local correctness proofs stay beside the code; history, measurements and cross-module explanation do not; (4) every retained design path resolves (checked by hand) and there is one authoritative explanation per argument; (5) node-test and browser-test compile and the files' focused suites pass, foreground, to completion; (6) scripts/check_doc_slugs.py green for any moved material, check_provenance_pins.py where commit hashes move; (7) the PR body names where each essay went or why it was deleted.

title: hicasso guide ch04: the owned-literal alternate-spelling claim is not delivered by the taught plain merge
description: docs/core/hicasso/04-controlled-inputs.md §Forward caller attributes safely (lines ~116-119 at 1af79839db) claims: 'A caller cannot replace the field's value, checked state, handler, key, or revision by supplying an alternative spelling such as :onInput or "value"; the controlled contract binds to the React slot reached by the authored literal.' That guarantee was only ever enforced by the :& merge key's owned-literal law (merge-caller denied a remainder on the canonical SLOT). The taught spelling — a plain merge with owned keys last — never delivered it: {:onInput f :on-input [...]} survives the merge as two map keys, both land on React's one onInput slot in convert-entry, and which wins is map iteration order. rf2-6c12m.12 removed :& (so no spelling delivers it now) and chose NOT to add a slot-collision refusal in convert-props — the epic's direction is fewer refusals and trust the programmer, and ch02 §Forward attributes with owned keys last already says 'Forward maps should use the same kebab-keyword spelling as Hiccup; a foreign props object's "className" string is a different merge key.' DO: bring ch04's sentence in line with ch02 — the owned literal wins by presence when the caller forwards the SAME key; an alternate spelling of the same slot is a different key, so forward maps in the same kebab spelling (or dissoc the alternates). Guide-only; dw-guide's fence (docs/core/hicasso/**). Check check_guide_samples.py's digest roster if a fenced block moves.

title: hicasso: commit basis - drop the generation term if the frame epoch already covers it (verify first)
description:

(collector.cljs:1008); flush! is reached only via mark-dirty!, whose two callers are the cell watch (:681) and the microtask rewire (:768). The watch fires because a reaction input moved, and every frame-state install already bumps frame-commit-epoch at both write chokepoints (core/src/re_frame/frame.cljc:1734-1749, 1821, 1956, 1981) - so on the watch path the generation never moves without the frame epoch moving first. On the rewire path the affected cell exists and its own re-stamp moves the boundary snapshot; there (max (inc epoch) (commit-basis ...)) (:1031-1033) is load-bearing only through inc - max cannot add correctness to a monotone term. The rest of the machinery (disposal hook, first-registration!, registry epoch, microtask rewire, acquire-cell! re-wire guard :956) each closes a named failure and should stay.

title: loops.md: FETCH_HEAD absence does not prove that no fetch ever ran
description:
FOUND BY THE MERGED-PR AUDIT OF PR #8721.

THE DEFECT. docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md now says each linked worktree gets its own fetch-head copy "the first time anything fetches from it", and that an absent file says "nothing has ever fetched from that tree". The first half of the correction is measured and sound: in the current repository, git rev-parse --git-path FETCH_HEAD resolves to a private metadata path for every linked worktree, and exactly four of seven linked worktrees have the file, matching the PR. The absolute inference from absence is not sound.

THE DIRECT COUNTEREXAMPLE IS PART OF GIT'S NORMAL INTERFACE, not a hypothetical deletion. Git 2.53's git fetch -h documents --[no-]write-fetch-head: a fetch can deliberately update refs without writing FETCH_HEAD. That is directly relevant to this paragraph's automated poller case. Such a poller can fetch forever while the per-worktree file remains absent. Therefore absence proves only that no fetch has written this clock in that worktree (or that the file is no longer there); it does not prove that no fetch has ever run.

IMPACT. The safe, load-bearing direction survives: movement is still proof that a writing fetch ran, while stillness proves nothing about liveness. The defect is confined to the new interpretation of absence, but that interpretation is the point of PR #8721 and can send a reader looking for the wrong history on an externally created tree.

MINIMAL REMEDY. Qualify the two new sentences in place: a linked worktree gets this file when a fetch writes FETCH_HEAD there, and absence means no fetch has written this particular clock. Briefly state that a poller configured not to write FETCH_HEAD is invisible to the clock. Preserve the four-of-seven measurement, the movement/stillness asymmetry, and the rest of the paragraph. Do not add machinery or a policy gate for this prose correction.
acceptance_criteria: docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md no longer says every fetch necessarily creates FETCH_HEAD or that file absence proves no fetch ever ran. It preserves the measured four-of-seven observation and the rule that movement is positive proof while a non-moving clock cannot establish liveness. The repair remains prose-only.
close_reason:
FIXED — PR #8722 merged, closed by the mayor at tip e5429f3862, verified at source.

THE PREMISE WAS CHECKED BEFORE THE EDIT, not taken from the bead. git 2.53.0 here, and 'git fetch -h' lists --[no-]write-fetch-head, so a fetch can update refs without writing the clock. The finding is correct and the over-claim was mine, made in PR #8721 forty minutes earlier.

WHAT LANDED, one file, +18/-15, prose only, no machinery and no gate as the bead directed:
  * 'the first time anything fetches from it' -> 'the first time a fetch WRITES that clock there', with 'a fetch ORDINARILY writes as it reads' opening the sentence.
  * absence 'says only that nothing has ever fetched from that tree' -> 'says less than it looks like saying: only that no fetch has written that clock there, which is not the same as no fetch having run, because the write is suppressible by a flag on the fetch itself — a poller configured that way is invisible to this test altogether.'
  * the guidance moved with it: absence is now a reason to reach for another signal rather than a history of the tree, while staying a hint about a tree you did not create.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA, CHECKED MECHANICALLY rather than asserted: 'first time anything fetches from it' 0, 'ever fetched from that tree' 0, 'four of seven' 1, 'Movement is proof of life' 1, 'stillness restores the ambiguity' 1, 'the write is suppressible' 1. Every criterion the bead stated is met and the load-bearing direction is untouched.

THE FLAG IS DESCRIBED BY WHAT IT DOES RATHER THAN BY ITS SPELLING — 'suppressible by a flag on the fetch itself'. A literal option name in this document would be a measured constant of the kind the method-reread loop watches go stale, and it buys nothing a reader of that paragraph needs.

title: method: the write-clock clause needs the worktree's age, and the obvious way to get it is wrong on exactly the worktrees that matter
description:
MEASURED 2026-08-22 10:03 AUSEST at tip 78c229ce28, on two live worktrees, controlled in both
directions. Found by the mayor while using its own clause.

THE CLAUSE THIS IS ABOUT. docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md, the stranded-sweep write-clock bullet,
carries a sentence added earlier today (rf2-1yct's sibling repair, commit c2a1246061): the clock
"says 'no activity' in three voices and you can only tell them apart with a control", one of the
three being "a span shorter than the worktree's own age".

SO THE CLAUSE DEPENDS ON KNOWING THE WORKTREE'S AGE, AND NAMES NO WAY TO GET IT. The obvious way
is to stat the worktree directory. On this platform's coreutils that is `stat -c %y`, "time of
last modification" -- and a directory's modification time is bumped by the worker writing inside
it.

MEASURED, TWO WORKTREES, ONE LIVE AND ONE INERT:

  pasteros (live worker, mid-edit)
    %y (last modification) 2026-08-22 10:03:23
    %w (birth)             2026-08-22 09:54:25
    -> the two disagree by nine minutes, and %y was moving between successive reads

  specsize (inert since 03:18, checked out at 00:28)
    %y 2026-08-22 00:31:35
    %w 2026-08-22 00:28:02
    -> the two agree to within the 3.5 minutes the checkout itself took

THE FAILURE IS INVERTED, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH A CLAUSE RATHER THAN A SHRUG. %y gives the
RIGHT answer on precisely the worktrees where the age does not matter -- the inert ones, where
nothing has written since checkout -- and the WRONG answer on the live one, where it is the whole
question. A mayor reading %y on a live worker sees a directory "seconds old", concludes the span
is longer than the worktree's age, and fires the no-discrimination warning on every live worker
while never firing it on a dead one. That is the opposite of what the clause is for.

AND IT IS SILENT. Nothing errors; both numbers are well-formed timestamps in the same format, and
on the first worktree a mayor happens to check -- typically an idle one -- they agree. This is the
same instrument class the document already names: an instrument that answers plausibly and wrongly
when misused, whose all-clear is complete and well-formed.

THE REPAIR, and it should be SHORT. One clause on the existing write-clock bullet naming the
distinction: the age you need is the CREATION time, not the last-modification time, and a
directory's modification time is bumped by the very writes you are trying to detect. The document
is OS-neutral by its own header's rule, so name the DISTINCTION (creation versus last
modification) rather than any particular tool's flag; `%w` versus `%y` is this platform's
spelling, not the rule.

A SECOND OPTION WORTH CONSIDERING and rejecting or taking on its merits: the dispatch record
already carries a creation timestamp for every worktree, because the mayor writes one at dispatch
time. Reading the age from the record the mayor itself wrote is more robust than asking the
filesystem at all, and needs no OS-specific spelling. If that is the better clause, say so and
write that instead.

BOUNDS. docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md only, and only the existing write-clock bullet. One or two
sentences. No new section, no new bullet, nothing moved. Generic: no OS-specific flag as the rule,
nothing repo-specific, no operator's name, no absolute paths.

FENCE: none on this file. A peer worker (pasteros, rf2-4j1v) is live in the same TREE but on a
different file, docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md -- no overlap. Re-check at
dispatch time.

Took the filesystem-distinction shape, rejected the dispatch-record shape (the method mandates no timestamp in that record, and 'one worker is not one worktree' means a worker-built gate tree has no dispatch line at all -- the sweep starts from the worktrees precisely because the records are incomplete). Gates: slug 0/1/0 baseline/sabotage/restored, strict build 0/0/0; both 0 again after rebase onto the final base. Control: broken in-page anchor planted mid-line on a line this change authored; slug gate named it by file/line/anchor. Measured that --strict exits 0 on that same plant while printing it at INFO.

title: method: 'Pasting a block' still claims SEVERAL blocks travel verbatim, and the markers are one short
description:
FOUND BY THE rf2-mmwt WORKER (gateblock) OUTSIDE ITS FENCE, correctly not actioned, and verified
against my own sweep of the same file taken before the fix.

rf2-mmwt marked '## Quality gates -- how a gate is run' as the gate-mechanics block, which took
docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md from ONE in-section paste marker to TWO. The
remaining defect is the quantifier that sits above them.

'## Pasting a block' opens: "Several blocks below travel VERBATIM into every dispatch." Three
things in that file are in fact pasted into a brief -- the common preamble, the worktree boundary
block, and now the gate-mechanics block -- but only two carry a marker. '## Common preamble'
carries none.

WHY IT IS THE SAME DEFECT AND NOT A SECOND ONE. The section's own rule is "Anchor the extraction
to CONTENT, never to line numbers", so the markers ARE the roster. A plural claim standing one
ahead of the markers leaves a mayor extracting mechanically unable to tell whether it has them
all -- which is exactly the failure rf2-mmwt was filed for, in its milder form. It is milder
because the preamble is a fenced ```text block whose whole content is the brief skeleton, so it
reads as obviously pasteable in a way a prose section does not.

THE SHAPE I WOULD PREFER, and the worker executing this should overrule it if the file argues
otherwise: replace the bare plural with the roster -- name the three blocks in that opening
sentence -- rather than adding a third marker. Naming them closes the count permanently and gives
the content-anchored extraction its list in one place, where a third marker leaves the reader
still counting. If a marker on the preamble reads better in context, say why and do that instead.

BOUNDS. dispatch-prompt-template.md only. One sentence, or one sentence plus a marker. No new
section, no restructuring, nothing moved between sections. The document is generic by its own
header's rule: nothing OS-specific, repo-specific or operator-specific.

FENCE: SEQUENCE BEHIND PR #8694 (rf2-mmwt), which edits this same file and is open with its
rollup still building at the time of writing. Same file, so parallel is a guaranteed conflict.

docs/the-mayor-method/ before dispatching.

MID-LINE, an end-of-line anchor matches nothing where line endings are translated) and
mkdocs build --strict (this tree is NOT in mkdocs.yml's exclude_docs). Note that --strict does not
gate anchors, so the plant goes against the slug gate. docs/the-mayor-method/ is one of two trees

title: ci(lint): lint.yml's own comments understate it — the surface omits two armed paths, and a non-linter job rides the same classifier
description:
FOUND BY THE METHOD REREAD LOOP 2026-08-22, tip c2a1246061, by testing a claim I have been putting
into dispatch briefs against lint.yml's CODE rather than its COMMENT. Two inaccuracies, both in the
file's description of itself. Neither changed a dispatch outcome; both are fail-open in the
direction that makes a worker skip a gate that would have armed.

*** 1. THE `Lint surface:` COMMENT UNDERSTATES THE CLASSIFIER BY TWO ENTRIES. ***

The comment (around :45) reads "Lint surface: implementation/, tools/ (minus template/resources/),
examples/, testbeds/." The classifier it describes (around :59) reads:

  implementation/*|tools/*|examples/*|testbeds/*|.clj-kondo/*|.github/workflows/lint.yml

So `.clj-kondo/*` and `.github/workflows/lint.yml` arm the lint surface and are named nowhere in
the prose. A worker editing the shared clj-kondo config, or lint.yml itself, and reading the comment
to decide coverage would conclude lint does not arm — when it does. That is the fail-open direction:
understating coverage sends a worker to skip a gate, exactly as CLAUDE.md already warns that
"understating coverage misreports as surely as overstating it".

*** 2. THE FILE CALLS ITSELF A THREE-LINTER GATE AND HAS SIX JOBS, ONE OF WHICH RIDES THE SAME
CLASSIFIER AND IS NOT A LINTER. ***

The header says "Multi-linter CI gate. Three complementary linters run as parallel jobs" and then
describes clj-kondo, Splint and ESLint. The jobs are: detect, clj-kondo, splint, eslint,
api-manifest, provenance-pins-corpus, lint-required.

`api-manifest` ("Public-API manifest drift-check") is gated on `needs.detect.outputs.lint_surface
== 'true'` — the SAME classifier as clj-kondo and Splint. So a change to implementation/ or tools/
arms a public-API manifest drift-check as well as three linters, and the header does not say so. A
worker reading it to decide what its diff arms gets three names and four gated jobs.

(`provenance-pins-corpus` is gated on `github.event_name != 'pull_request'`, so it never runs on a
PR at all — worth stating for the same reason, since its name suggests otherwise.)

WHAT THIS DID NOT BREAK, stated so the priority is not read as higher than it is. My briefs said
"lint.yml's surface is implementation/, tools/, examples/, testbeds/, so docs/ is outside it and its
expensive jobs skip job-side." That CONCLUSION is correct and I re-verified it: on a pull request
touching only docs/, lint_surface and js_surface are both false, so clj-kondo, Splint, ESLint and
api-manifest all skip, provenance-pins-corpus does not run on PR events, and lint-required
aggregates all-skipped to a pass. The reasoning was incomplete; the answer was right.

THE REPAIR: bring both comments into line with the code. Name `.clj-kondo/*` and
`.github/workflows/lint.yml` in the Lint-surface comment, and correct the header so it describes
what the file runs — three linters PLUS a manifest drift-check on the same classifier, plus a
corpus job that skips on PRs. Prose only; no workflow behaviour changes and no job moves.

SAME CLASS AS AN ALREADY-ACCEPTED REPAIR: commit e324988e13 (rf2-0tkx / rf2-xomo) was
"docs(claude)+test(classifier): make the pair's self-description true". This is that, one file over.

HOT-ZONE — SEQUENCE IT. `.github/workflows/*` is on CLAUDE.md's hot-zone list, so this is never
parallel with another workflow change. It is prose-only and not urgent; there is no reason to run it
against a busy fleet.

GATE NOTE FOR WHOEVER TAKES IT: editing `.github/workflows/lint.yml` ARMS THE LINT SURFACE — the
classifier names that exact path, which is the second half of finding 1. So this change gates
itself, and the honest check is that clj-kondo and Splint actually run on the PR rather than skip.
close_reason:
FIXED by PR #8692 (branch worker/lintdesc-63il), merged and fast-forwarded onto main at ac8637b308.
One file, .github/workflows/lint.yml, +35/-4, COMMENTS ONLY — verified mechanically before merging:
zero job keys added, and zero added lines that are not comments.

*** MY FILED REPAIR WAS WRONG AND THE WORKER REPLACED IT. This is the part worth keeping. ***

I filed "append `.clj-kondo/*` and `.github/workflows/lint.yml` to the Lint-surface comment". That
would have introduced a NEW error, in BOTH directions:
  - still omitting TEN patterns — the arming set is five `case` arms and sixteen patterns, including
    .splint.edn, spec/API.md, both api-manifest EDN files, skills/*, docs/core/*,
    docs/*/concepts.md, spec/Privacy.md, docs/api/*, docs/story/api/*;
  - and newly claiming clj-kondo LINTS a YAML workflow and an EDN config directory, which it does
    not.

THE REAL DEFECT IS ONE LEVEL DEEPER THAN I DIAGNOSED: ONE PHRASE NAMES TWO DIFFERENT SETS. The
`Lint surface:` paragraph was not describing the classifier arm at all — it describes the `--lint`
TARGET paths and says so ("excluded by virtue of the explicit `--lint` paths below"), and as an
account of THOSE it was accurate. The next paragraph then uses "the lint surface" for the ARMING
set, and the job is named "Detect lint surface" with output `lint_surface`. Two sets, one phrase.
The worker separated the senses and named the `case` arms as the authority, so a copied list cannot
drift again — which is a better repair than any list would have been.

FINDING 2 HELD AS FILED, plus two I did not name: ESLint keys on `js_surface`, so the three linters
do not share one classifier either; and provenance-pins-corpus is absent from the Lint-required
aggregator's `needs:`.

AND MY BEAD MISCOUNTED ITS OWN EVIDENCE: the finding-2 heading says the file "HAS SIX JOBS" while
the prose beneath it enumerates seven. Seven is correct.

*** THE SELF-GATING PREDICTION WAS CONFIRMED LIVE, WHICH IS THE HALF I MOST WANTED. *** Because the
classifier names .github/workflows/lint.yml explicitly, this comments-only change ARMS ITS OWN LINT
SURFACE. On the PR: clj-kondo RAN (success), Splint RAN (success), Public-API manifest drift-check
RAN (success), ESLint SKIPPED, Provenance pins (full corpus) SKIPPED. The worker's local replay of
the detect classifier predicted exactly that (lint_surface=true, js_surface=false). So finding 1's
mechanism is established by observation rather than by reading, and provenance-pins-corpus really
never runs on a PR.

SABOTAGE, AND THE HONEST NEGATIVE IS THE MORE VALUABLE OF THE TWO. Both plants were on targets
verified unique first and restored with git hash-object verified against blob 44ef4c13bd.
  - Plant 1, inside one of the NEW COMMENTS: both gates stayed green, exit 0 and exit 0. That
    proves the LIMIT, not the coverage — YAML discards `#` lines before any parser reads them, so
    NO GATE IN THIS REPO CAN SEE THE TEXT THIS PR CHANGES. The prose is machine-unverifiable and
    rests on the source reading instead. The worker said so plainly rather than presenting a green
    as coverage.
  - Plant 2, an unmatched quote in the `name:` VALUE: check_workflow_yaml.py exit 1 naming
    lint.yml line 7 column 65, and check_workflow_job_timeouts.py exit 2 on its documented
    parse-error arm. So a green from those two is a real read of that worktree.

BEHAVIOUR-UNCHANGED PROVEN STRUCTURALLY, NOT VISUALLY: yaml.safe_load of origin/main vs HEAD
compares EQUAL (exit 0), with a mutated-copy control confirming the comparison discriminates.
check_workflow_yaml.py 0, --self-test 0 across 5 cases, check_workflow_job_timeouts.py 0 across
117 jobs in 11 files.

GATES DELIBERATELY NOT NOMINATED, with the reasoning read rather than assumed: check_doc_slugs.py,
check_readme_links.py and mkdocs build were all declined because this path is outside all three
roots and is not markdown, so each would have exited green having inspected nothing.

ONE PROCESS NOTE. This worker ended a turn with "I'll wait for the watcher's completion notification
rather than polling further" — the commonest strand shape on this project. It was messaged for a
status and had in fact already stopped its watchers and finished; nothing was lost and no work was
redone. Recording it because the recovery cost one message, exactly as the method says it does.

description:

THE MEASUREMENT. A broken in-page anchor was planted mid-line in a page under docs/. Two gates
were run on it:

  python scripts/check_doc_slugs.py    -> exit 1, naming the file, the line and the anchor
  python -m mkdocs build --strict      -> exit 0

THE REASON, read out of mkdocs.yml rather than inferred. The validation block sets exactly one
key:

  validation:
    links:
      unrecognized_links: warn

There is NO `anchors` key, so anchor validation sits at the MkDocs default, and `--strict`
promotes WARNING but not INFO. The file's own comment block already documents this promotion
mechanism for the two `links` levels — it is why `unrecognized_links` was raised to `warn` under
rf2-5exqc — but it stops at links and says nothing about anchors.

THIS IS REDUNDANCY MISSING, NOT COVERAGE MISSING, and the priority reflects that. In-page anchors
under docs/ ARE gated: check_doc_slugs.py catches them, and it runs in test.yml's
verify-readme-links job on every PR, which carries no surface guard. Nothing is currently
shipping unchecked.

WHY IT IS STILL WORTH RECORDING: it is a FAIL-OPEN GATE NOMINATION waiting to happen, which is the
class this project already spends words on. CLAUDE.md's Build & Test section carries a careful pin
beginning "Link validation is split across two gates, and the split does not follow the job name",
and it nominates gates by path. A reader of that passage would reasonably take `mkdocs build
--strict` to cover anchors on a page inside docs_dir — it is the strict site build over exactly
that tree. It does not, and a brief nominating it alone for an anchor change gets a green that
inspected nothing. The method's own rule is "never nominate a gate that does not cover the surface
being edited", and this is a case where the non-coverage is invisible from the gate's name, its
scope and its output.

THE REPAIR, and it is one clause in prose that already exists — do NOT add a section:
in CLAUDE.md's link-validation paragraph, say that `mkdocs build --strict` does not gate in-page
ANCHORS at all (it reports them at INFO, which --strict does not promote), so check_doc_slugs.py
is the only anchor gate for pages under docs/. Optionally note the same asymmetry beside the
existing `unrecognized_links` comment in mkdocs.yml, which is where the mechanism is already
explained.

A SECOND OPTION EXISTS AND IS NOT BEING RECOMMENDED WITHOUT A RULING: setting
`validation.anchors: warn` in mkdocs.yml would make the strict build gate anchors too. That is a
behaviour change to a shared build rather than a documentation fix, it would red the build on any
pre-existing broken anchor across the whole site, and the coverage it adds is redundant with a
gate that already runs on every PR. It should not be done as a side effect of this bead.

else editing it.

description:
FOUND BY THE rf2-sxhu WORKER (asyncsettle, PR #8675) as a sibling of the fault it was fencing, reported outside its fence and correctly left. IT POINTED AT ONE LINE (~541) AND CALLED IT 'the same shape'. I re-derived it at source and the pointer is right about the FILE and wrong about the SHAPE, which changes the repair — recording the correction here rather than inheriting the characterisation.

THE FILE: implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/hicasso/identifier_prefix_ssr_dom_cljs_test.cljs, six deftests, four of them async adoption rows.

WHAT rf2-sxhu's FILE HAD: a .catch arm that called (done) alongside a finally that also called it — a DOUBLE-FINISH — plus cleanup skipped on the rejection path.

WHAT THIS FILE HAS IS THE OPPOSITE HALF. There is no .catch anywhere in it. Measured with a working control in both directions: grep -c '\.catch' returns 0 on this file and 4 on server_render_ssr_dom_cljs_test.cljs at 2d064aec99, the base rf2-sxhu repaired. So the pattern reaches this corpus and the zero is a reading.

THE SHAPE AT ALL FOUR SITES:

  (-> (sup/adopted! handle)
      (.then (fn [ok] ... (try ...assertions... (finally (stop!) (mount/release! handle) (done))))))

  adoption promise   fulfilment handler   finally
  :353               :354                 :397
  :416               :417                 :448
  :492               :493                 :540-544   <- the ~541 the worker pointed at
  :578               :579                 :603

SO ON A REJECTION NOTHING RUNS AT ALL. The .then handler is skipped, the try is never entered, the finally never fires — and therefore (done) is never called, (stop!) never stops the mismatch watcher, and (mount/release! handle) never releases the root. Three consequences, and the first is why this is worth a bead rather than a note:

1. THE FAILURE IS OPAQUE. The row does not fail; it HANGS to the async timeout, and the message names the timeout rather than the rejection. rf2-sxhu's sites at least reported something.
2. THE WATCHER AND THE ROOT LEAK INTO THE NEXT ROW, which is the same second fault rf2-sxhu names, so the following row's census is measuring residue.
3. THE REJECTION IS NEVER REPORTED, so what the adoption actually threw is lost.

:540-544 is the site whose finally spans five lines because it releases TWO roots (ha and hb) — it is the two-simultaneous-roots row, and it is the one where a leak costs most.

WHAT THE REPAIR PROBABLY WANTS, but the worker decides: PR #8675 introduced a shared settle-row! helper in the sibling namespace that carries one .then with BOTH handlers (mutually exclusive, so a throwing body cannot also reach the rejection arm), release and done beyond both, done in a finally, and a :row label carrying what the hand-written messages did. Whether that helper is lifted into the shared support namespace or the pattern is re-applied locally is a judgement about how many callers it will end up with — do not lift it on the strength of two files without saying why.

ACCEPTANCE: each of the four rows settles exactly once on fulfilment or rejection, reports the rejection with enough to identify the row, stops the watcher and releases every handle on both paths. A deliberate rejected-adoption control that fails before the repair and proves the FOLLOWING row sees no retained root, frame or listener. No assertion changes — prove that mechanically, by extracting the balanced (is ...) forms from both revisions and diffing, as PR #8675 did.

FENCE: keep it to this one test namespace. rf2-sxhu's own widening note is the precedent and its reasoning applies — bounded repair bounds the change, not the search — but the search has been done here and it returned this file.

title: hicasso: PR #8672's adopted-DOM async witnesses double-finish and leak on rejection
description:
MERGED-PR AUDIT #8672 (completeness / correctness / implementation quality).

The product-door byte premise and the adopted-DOM/control readings are strong, but the two new async rows in implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/hicasso/server_render_ssr_dom_cljs_test.cljs have an unreliable failure path.

At merge a8641fdc3c, the-door-s-id-survives-the-adoption-and-a-real-client-render (lines 454-508) and the-hand-rolled-bytes-lose-the-id-through-the-same-door (lines 510-574) both call done in the .then callback's finally and then attach a .catch that calls done again.

That creates two distinct faults:
1. If sup/adopted! rejects before .then runs, .catch ends the row without unmounting the hydration handle or stopping the mismatch watcher. The control closes its console capture, but likewise omits unmount/watcher teardown.
2. If code inside .then throws, finally unmounts and calls done, the returned promise rejects, and .catch reports the error and calls done a second time. A failure can therefore advance the runner twice and make the following row's state/reporting unreliable.

The green success path and current sabotage controls do not exercise either branch. Keep the repair local to this test namespace; no runtime, SSR, disposition, or product API change is indicated.
acceptance_criteria: Each new async witness has one settlement path that reports a rejection, stops every watcher/capture, unmounts any created handle, and calls done exactly once on fulfillment or rejection. Add a deliberate rejected-adoption or thrown-body control that fails before the repair and proves the following row sees no retained root, frame, listener, or capture. Preserve the three witness readings and their node/browser coverage.
notes:
MAYOR VERIFICATION + WIDENING 2026-08-22, tip 2d064aec99. The audit's premise holds, verified by OPENING the file at the named lines rather than by grep intersection. And the same class exists at TWO MORE SITES the audit did not name — both inside this bead's own fence, so the widening does not breach it.

CONFIRMED AS DESCRIBED, both faults:
  :503-:508  finally calls (done) at :505, then .catch calls (done) again at :508
  :568-:574  same shape — finally (done) at :570, .catch (done) at :574
These are the two rows PR #8672 added, and they carry BOTH faults: double-finish on a throw
inside .then, and no unmount/watcher teardown when adopted! rejects before .then runs.

TWO MORE SITES, FAULT 1 ONLY, and they PREDATE #8672:
  :390-:398  (done) inside the .then body, .catch (done). Correct once-per-path idiom for done —
             NOT a double-finish — but the .catch stops no watcher and unmounts no handle.
  :655-:668  same: (done) at :664, .catch calls (remove!) and (done) but neither
             ((:stop! watch)) nor (h/unmount! handle).
So the leak-on-rejection half is a property of every async row in the namespace, not only of the
two the audit read. The double-finish half is genuinely confined to the new pair.

WHY I AM WIDENING RATHER THAN FILING A SIBLING. 'Bounded repair bounds the change, not the
search.' On this project one false sentence spawned four separate items by being repaired one
named site at a time, and the audit that reopens each of them is the same audit. The bead's own
instruction — 'keep the repair local to this test namespace' — is satisfied: all four sites are
in that one file.

WHAT DOES NOT WIDEN: no runtime, SSR, disposition or product API change. The acceptance criteria
already say one settlement path per witness, reporting rejection, stopping every watcher/capture,
unmounting any handle, and calling done exactly once.
SIBLING FILED AS rf2-x43z, 2026-08-22 02:2x AUSEST. The worker's out-of-fence report — identifier_prefix_ssr_dom_cljs_test.cljs at ~541 — is real and I re-derived it at source. It is NOT the same shape: that file has NO .catch at all (0 hits against 4 in this file's base 2d064aec99, control run in both directions), so its four adoption rows never settle on rejection rather than settling twice. Same leak, opposite settlement fault, and the failure surfaces as an opaque async timeout. Reporting it outside the fence rather than widening was the right call — the fence said one namespace and this is a second one.

All four async rows in server_render_ssr_dom_cljs_test now end with a single settle-row! path: one .then carrying both handlers, release and done on the far side of both, done in a finally. The audit's two named sites (the PR #8672 pair) carried both faults; two older sites carried leak-on-rejection only, and all four are inside the bead's own fence. Two new controls exercise the branches no green path reaches, and both were shown to fail before the repair by planted faults: the double-finish plant reds the throwing-body control (done ran 2 times) in the node lane, and the leak plant reds all four of the rejected-adoption control's retained-nothing assertions (root, frame, listener, capture) in the browser lane, five failures confined to the two new controls. title: docs(method): the read-the-item rule points at the newest note, which can itself re-import superseded text
description:
METHOD-REREAD DRIFT FINDING, mayor, 2026-08-21. The rule is sound and INCOMPLETE, and the

must order by tracker timestamps and 'WALK ADJACENT PAIRS NEWEST-FIRST UNTIL THE FIRST CHANGE TO
A TEXT-BEARING FIELD'.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY, AND WHAT COST A WORKER CYCLE TONIGHT. A note that is newest BY TIMESTAMP can
be a faithful re-derivation of superseded text. Timestamp order then points straight at it, and
following the rule PERFECTLY still yields the wrong instruction.
