Neither fires at the FILING decision, and filing is where the claim becomes durable: a bead description outlives the worker, the chat and the mayor, and the next reader has no way to tell a verified premise from a relayed one. A false premise in a bead is worse than a false premise in a message, because it looks like a finding.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS CHEAP TO FIX. Verifying costs one grep or one file read at filing time. Not verifying costs a worker's whole investigation — and it is a worker who is under a fence, on someone else's evidence, spending its context proving the mayor wrong before it can start.

THE PRACTICE:
- Before filing a bead from someone else's report, open the file at the named path and line. If the claim is about absence ("X does not exist", "nothing records Y"), run the search yourself — absence claims are the ones that fail, because the reporter searched for what they expected rather than what is there.
- If you cannot verify it in the moment, FILE IT AS A CLAIM IN THOSE WORDS: "reported by <worker>, NOT verified at source — verify before acting". That is honest and costs nothing.
- The two claim shapes that failed here are both worth naming in any brief you build on them: a FREEZE or manifest constraint (read the manifest; they shrink as things retire), and a NEVER-RECORDED / UNCITED claim (search the docs tree, not just the code).
- Tell the receiving worker explicitly that the bead text is yours and may be wrong. The line "my bead text is a claim, not a fact — verify every path, line number and structural claim before acting on it, and report anything that did not hold" turned both of these into corrections instead of wasted work.

CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION MUST BE QUERIED PER-BRANCH. A GLOBAL 'gh run list --limit N' TRUNCATES AND REPORTS 'NO LIVE RUNS' FOR A BRANCH THAT HAS FOUR (observed 2026-08-07, PR #7626).

WHAT HAPPENED: I evaluated 'are there queued/in-progress runs on this PR's branch' with a single 'gh run list --limit 40' grouped by headBranch. worker/shellbytes-2rtt6-82 did not appear, so I reported it had no live runs. Querying it directly — 'gh run list --branch worker/shellbytes-2rtt6-82' — showed FOUR runs queued on the PR's head sha (tests, portability, docs, lint). They fell outside the 40-item window because other branches' runs filled it.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT AGAIN: clause 4 exists because statusCheckRollup can report pending==0 while runs are queued. I added a second source of truth and then read it through a truncating window, so the second source acquired the same failure mode as the first — it reported the absence of evidence as evidence of absence. Five variants of one bug in a single session: empty rollup passes '0 fail and 0 pending'; status==COMPLETED counts CANCELLED as passed; pending==0 while runs are queued; a rollup total that shrinks after a re-run still looks plausible; and now a truncated run list that omits a branch entirely.

THE RULE: for a MERGE DECISION, query the head branch DIRECTLY — 'gh run list --branch <headRefName> --limit 25' — and confirm no run is queued or in_progress, AND that the runs present are on the PR's current head sha (compare against 'gh pr view --json headRefOid'; stale-sha runs are not evidence about this head). Never use a global limited listing to decide a merge. A grouped overview is fine for a dashboard; it is not fine for a gate.

COROLLARY worth remembering: a rollup can show ONE check while four workflows sit queued on the same sha, because a queued run's checks are not yet attached to the commit. total==1 with 'no live runs' is therefore not 'this PR has one check' — it is 'look again, properly'.

MERGE-LOOP BUG (2026-07-18): my merge-loop's if-gate checks PRE-merge CI state but does NOT verify gh pr merge SUCCEEDED before running bd close + git branch -D + git push origin --delete. When a PR is 'not mergeable' (behind main / needs rebase), gh pr merge --admin FAILS but the loop still deleted the branch → PR AUTO-CLOSED + work stranded + bead wrongly closed (hit on zef0e #6214). Recovery: git branch <name> <tip-SHA from the 'Deleted branch (was SHA)' line>; git push origin <name>; gh pr reopen; bd update --status open. FIX: gate branch-delete on verifying gh pr view <pr> state==MERGED AFTER the merge call, never on the pre-merge check alone.

MERGE-LOOP CAVEAT (mayor, 2026-07-25): a merged PR does NOT necessarily close every bead named in its TITLE. Because briefs now tell workers to open the PR as soon as any commit exists (so work becomes visible and durable rather than waiting on a long local gate), a PR can be deliberately PARTIAL when the mayor sweeps it — title lists three beads, diff contains one file. Observed live: PR #6940 was titled for rf2-na9p0 + rf2-x4jda + rf2-rhg4q and contained ONLY spec/API.md; the two B5 beads were still uncommitted in the worker's tree at merge time. This is not a worker error and the early-PR instruction is still right — incremental delivery is fine and the merge was correct. The fix is on the MAYOR side: before closing beads after a merge, read the PR's actual FILE LIST (gh pr view <n> --json files) rather than trusting its title, close only the beads the diff really delivered, and tell the worker its branch is now partly merged so it rebases and opens a second PR for the remainder rather than assuming its work is lost.

MERGE LOOP — derive the bead from the BRANCH NAME, never from a guessed PR number. On 2026-07-19 I hardcoded a PR-number case statement (6373 -> rf2-2hkfy) by assuming PRs open in the order I dispatch. They do not: #6373 was worker/guide-register-bbdbs2 and rf2-2hkfy had not opened a PR at all. Merging would have closed the WRONG bead with a "shipped #6373" reason, corrupting state for two beads at once and being nearly invisible afterwards. FIX: read `gh pr list --state open --json number,headRefName` and map branch -> bead, since every worker branch is named worker/<desc>-<BEAD_ID>. The bead id is the branch suffix. Verify before every merge batch, not once per session — PRs open and close continuously while multiple workers run. GENERAL FORM: this is the same class as the stale ready-pool that made me dispatch a closed bead (rf2-lvrkp) — a cached mapping that was true when I built it and silently went stale. Any lookup table I construct from a moment in time needs re-derivation each tick, not reuse.

MERGE-LOOP HAZARD — I remove a worker worktree the instant its PR merges, but the WORKER MAY STILL BE RUNNING. On 2026-07-19 rf2-k8l1m reported: "The PR was merged by you, not me... The worktree and branch were cleaned up underneath me mid-command." It had finished writing and was only verifying CI, so nothing was lost — but a worker that is still editing, or about to amend and force-push, would lose work or fail confusingly. The window is real because workers commonly push, then poll CI, then write their final report; my loop sees pend=0/nf=0 and merges + removes during that poll. MITIGATIONS, in order of preference: (1) merge the PR but DEFER worktree/branch removal to the next tick — by then the worker has almost always reported; (2) if removing immediately, check the worktree is clean AND that no live agent is associated with it; (3) never remove a worktree whose branch has an OPEN PR (already the rule) or that holds gitignored-but-unique content (see retro-extended-context, 17KB invisible to git status). NOTE the merge itself was correct — CI was genuinely green; the defect is only in the eager cleanup. Also: my gh merges appear authored as mike-thompson-day8 because I use his gh auth, so a worker seeing "merged by Mike" may actually be seeing the mayor.

MERGE-LOOP JSONL CHECKOUT SILENTLY REVERTS WORKER BEAD CLOSES (observed 2026-07-25, re-confirmed). The mayor merge loop does 'git checkout HEAD -- .beads' before 'git pull --ff-only' (needed: an uncommitted issues.jsonl aborts the pull and silently freezes HEAD). But that checkout DISCARDS the bd auto-export of any close a worker performed since the last commit — and a later 'bd import' of the reverted file resurrects the bead as open/in_progress. Observed: rf2-kqxe6.17 and rf2-b617w both closed by their worker on PR #6895, both back to in_progress after the post-merge checkout; misdiagnosable as a reviewer reopen. MITIGATION: after every merge+pull, re-verify the merged PR's beads with 'bd show' and re-close any that reverted, citing the merge commit. Better: commit the .beads export BEFORE merging rather than checking it out — commit-before-pull, never checkout-before-pull, when a worker has just closed something. DISTINGUISH FROM A REAL REVIEWER REOPEN: a genuine reopen carries a MERGED-PR AUDIT / AUDIT-REOPEN note naming an unmet defect at a code site; a checkout-race revert has NO such note and the bead simply reads in_progress with its pre-close state.

MERGE-LOOP: NEVER "git checkout HEAD -- .beads" — IT HAS NOW DESTROYED NINE BEAD CLOSES (2026-07-25). The mayor merge routine says: after each merge, "git checkout HEAD -- .beads" then "git pull --ff-only". That checkout DISCARDS the bd auto-export of every close performed since the last commit, and bd tracked post-checkout/post-merge hooks then RE-IMPORT the stale file into the Dolt DB, so the close is undone in the database itself, not merely in the working file. CONFIRMED VICTIMS this session: rf2-a32r7 (three times), rf2-kqxe6.17, rf2-drpa3.178, rf2-8ewl1, rf2-zt65l, rf2-vxgfnd.99.4, rf2-qwsmv. Each showed ZERO AUDIT-REOPEN notes, which is the discriminator: a genuine reviewer reopen always carries a MERGED-PR AUDIT / AUDIT-REOPEN note naming an unmet defect at a code site. CORRECT MERGE SEQUENCE — export, commit, THEN pull; never checkout: (1) bd export --all -o .beads/issues.jsonl  (2) guard wc -l >= 2000  (3) git add + git commit  (4) git pull --ff-only (or rebase)  (5) merge the next PR. The reason the checkout was in the routine at all is that an UNCOMMITTED issues.jsonl aborts a pull — committing it first solves that without destroying anything. WHY THIS KEPT RECURRING: I fixed the CHECKPOINT flow early and left the MERGE flow alone, because the loop prompt literally instructs the checkout. Deviating from that literal instruction is correct — it demonstrably destroys tracker state — and the deviation must be applied in the merge path too, not only at checkpoint time. AFTER EVERY MERGE, re-verify the merged PR beads with bd show and re-close any that reverted, citing the merge commit.

MERGE-ORDER BEATS --admin ON THE BAKED LANE: when two PRs both rebuild docs/cljs/playground-rf2.js, a PUSH by one cannot invalidate the other — only a MERGE can. So the escape from the rebase-deadlock is to control MERGE ORDER (let A finish CI and merge, then merge B, which rebases once onto A), NOT to --admin past pending checks. I merged rf2-qg98y (#6302) past 4 pending checks on 2026-07-18 to break a 5-cycle deadlock; it worked and main stayed green, but sequencing would have achieved the same without the risk. Rule going forward: on the baked lane, hold every candidate, merge strictly one at a time on GENUINE green, and tell the next worker it is sole occupant so it rebases exactly once. Root fix is rf2-tzy13 (stop committing the bundle, build in CI).

MERGE-TIME RULE (post #6677 contamination): before merging ANY worker PR, eyeball its file list for .beads/ — a worker-worktree commit of .beads/issues.jsonl is a stale full-DB snapshot that time-travels the tracker (reopens closed beads, deletes new ones, replaces memories). Reject/strip it; never --theirs/--ours on .beads — resolve-then-regenerate. Standing until rf2-ia8o7's guards land.

A MERGED-PR AUDIT THAT REOPENS THE EXACT SOURCE OWNER APPENDS ITS FINDINGS AS A NOTE AND LEAVES THE TITLE AND DESCRIPTION INTACT. Never rewrite a bead's title/description into the follow-through defect. Evidence (rf2-twpp6, 2026-07-26): the EP-0037 R1 and R2 slice beads (rf2-kqxe6.5, rf2-kqxe6.6) each had title AND description destructively replaced by their own merged-PR audits (commits 1e2627315c and 7528f0b84b). 'bd search "EP-0037 R2"' then returned nothing, and review gate 2 could not check those two slices against the tree at all -- while rf2-kqxe6.3 (R0b) and rf2-kqxe6.7 (R3), which APPENDED, were checkable. The named casualty: the EP's R2 tooling clause ended up with no bead carrying it. Recovery is possible but expensive -- .beads/issues.jsonl is a full-database export, so the original text is readable with 'git show <sha>:.beads/issues.jsonl | jq "select(.id==\"<id>\")"' -- do not create the need for it. Related: 'bd update --notes' REPLACES; use --append-notes or 'bd note'.

MERGING ON GREEN CAN LAND A BRANCH STATE OLDER THAN ITS TIP (2026-07-25). Twice today a PR merged while its worker was still pushing, so the merge captured an EARLIER commit than the branch's tip: #6975 landed one commit short (the worker opened #6982 to carry the remainder), and #6973 landed the v/html code half while its worker was still writing the acceptance suites (which then landed as #6980).

MECHANISM: the merge sweep reads 'fail=0 pend=0' and merges. Between that read and the merge, a live worker can push. GitHub merges the ref as it stood, so the delta silently becomes a follow-up PR — or worse, is briefly absent from main while the bead reads closed.

NEITHER CASE LOST WORK, and the reason is worth keeping: both workers were pushing as they went and both noticed, so each opened a follow-up rather than assuming its work had landed. Push-as-you-go plus a worker that verifies its own merge is what made this benign.

WHAT IT IS NOT: a reason to stop merging on green. Waiting for workers to declare done would idle the pipeline, and a green partial genuinely is worth more than a perfect whole later — that policy is correct and stays.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD: (1) when merging a PR whose worker has NOT reported terminal, expect a follow-up PR and do not treat the bead as discharged on that merge alone — read the worker's eventual report; (2) tell workers in the brief that a merge may land a state older than their tip, so if their last push is not in the merge commit they should open a follow-up rather than assume it landed (both workers did this unprompted — make it explicit so it is not luck); (3) when a merged PR's beads stay open or in_progress, that is often this, not a partial delivery — ask before inferring.

RELATED, SAME ROOT: three times today I pruned a worktree from under a live worker because the merge sweep had 'PR merged' in hand while terminality lived in task notifications. The pattern across all four incidents is the same — the merge sweep is where mayor actions and live worker state collide, so every destructive or finalising step inside it needs a liveness signal read rather than inferred.

MERGING ON GREEN LANDED A STALE TIP AGAIN -- THIRD INSTANCE, AND I NOW HAVE A ONE-COMMAND MITIGATION (2026-07-26). PR #7091 merged at c67fe52a91 while the worker branch tip was aa824a27b5. Five of six commits rebase-landed; the sixth (the FH-CTRL-018 browser row) did not, leaving the slice INCOMPLETE ON MAIN while the PR read merged. Prior instances: #6975 landed one commit short, #6973 landed the v/html code half while its acceptance suites were still being written.

WHY IT KEEPS HAPPENING: the merge sweep reads fail=0 pend=0 and merges. Between that read and the merge call, a live worker can push. GitHub merges the ref as it stood. The policy of merging on green is CORRECT and stays -- waiting for workers to declare done would idle the pipeline, and a green partial is worth more than a perfect whole later.

THE MITIGATION, cheap enough that there is no excuse: before merging a PR whose worker has NOT sent a terminal report, compare the PR head against the remote branch tip --
  gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid   vs   git ls-remote --heads origin <branch>
If they differ, the PR object is stale: re-read it and merge the current head. This is the same identity-not-name discipline that governs worktree pruning -- read the tip, do not assume the PR object is current.

WHAT MADE ALL THREE BENIGN, and it is the thing to keep briefing: every worker was pushing as it went AND checked whether its own work was in the merge commit. Each opened a follow-up PR rather than assuming it had landed. So the brief line "a merge may land a state older than your tip; if your last push is not in the merge commit, open a follow-up rather than assume it landed" is doing real work -- keep it, and note that all three workers did it UNPROMPTED before it was in the brief.

MAYOR-SIDE COROLLARY: when a merged PR beads stay open or in_progress, suspect THIS before inferring a partial delivery or a worker error. And do not close a bead on a merge whose worker has not reported -- read the file list, not the title.

The next checkpoint then re-exports from Dolt, which is why some closes survive and some do not: it depends on whether bd re-exported after the revert.

CLAUDE.md prescribes the exact opposite order and I read it repeatedly without applying it to my own loop: checkpoint FIRST (scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, which re-exports from Dolt rather than trusting the working file), THEN git checkout HEAD -- .beads, THEN pull. THE FIX, adopted now: in the merge sweep, run the checkpoint BEFORE any checkout of .beads. Better still, do not check out .beads at all unless a pull actually aborts — the checkout is a workaround for a specific failure, not a routine step. Sequence: sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, then (only if needed) git checkout HEAD -- .beads, then git pull.

If the reasoning lives only in a bead, the answer is invisible exactly when it is most needed — and the next person carefully re-derives a decision that was already carefully made.

MY PR SWEEP COLLAPSES FAILURE AND CANCELLED INTO ONE LABEL, AND I NEARLY DISPATCHED A FIX-WORKER FOR NOTHING (2026-08-11).

THE INSTRUMENT BUG. My sweep's jq is:
  select(.state=="FAILURE" or .state=="CANCELLED") | "  FAIL "+.name
Grouping them is CORRECT for the merge decision — the criterion says CANCELLED is not passed, and both block. But printing both as "FAIL" is wrong for the DIAGNOSIS, and the two have opposite remedies:
  FAILURE  -> the gate ran and said no. Dispatch a fix-worker to the same branch that runs the ACTUAL failing gate.
  CANCELLED -> the gate did not run to a verdict, usually superseded by a newer run. Wait or re-run. THERE IS NOTHING TO FIX.

WHAT HAPPENED: PR #7831 showed "FAIL Beads PR boundary". I went looking for a real defect, checked the branch's three-dot diff (clean of .beads), read the checker script and the CI invocation (both correctly use merge-base, and the YAML even documents this exact hazard), and started toward a fix-worker. Then the run log said "still in progress" — and the check's real state was CANCELLED, with the `tests` run in progress at that head. Nothing was wrong. The earlier attempt had been superseded.

Cost: several minutes and nearly a wasted dispatch, on a PR whose only problem was that CI had not finished.

THE FIX, one word: print the state instead of a fixed label.
  select(.state=="FAILURE" or .state=="CANCELLED") | "  " + .state + " " + .name
Then a CANCELLED reads as CANCELLED and I wait, and a FAILURE reads as FAILURE and I dispatch.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, which is the same one this repo keeps finding in its own gates: A SUMMARY THAT MERGES TWO STATES WITH DIFFERENT REMEDIES IS A SUMMARY THAT WILL EVENTUALLY PRESCRIBE THE WRONG ONE. My instrument was built for the merge question, then reused for the diagnosis question, and it is only correct for the first. Exactly the fault I have been recording in workers' witnesses all session — a claim broader than what the instrument distinguishes.

MY WORKTREE-BOUNDARY BLOCK CAUSES A CI FAILURE — add the counter-warning to every dispatch. On 2026-07-18 THREE PRs (#6360 sy7zr, #6361 sdeae, #6362 vxgfnd.290) all failed the same gate, "No hardcoded personal/home paths" (scripts/check-no-hardcoded-paths.sh, run by .github/workflows/portability.yml). The gate passes clean on main, so each PR genuinely introduced the path. ROOT CAUSE IS MINE: the mandatory worktree-boundary block repeats the literal absolute path C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2-worktrees/<name> four or five times in every brief, and workers paste it into test fixtures and helper code. The block is necessary — it prevents edits landing in the mayor checkout — but it hands the worker the exact string the portability gate forbids. FIX, now standard in every editing dispatch: add a line saying the worktree path is for NAVIGATION ONLY and must never appear in committed content; resolve paths at runtime instead (relative fixtures, System/getProperty user.dir, a temp dir, or whatever the surrounding tests already do); and note that scripts/check-no-hardcoded-paths.sh git-greps the tracked tree and will block the PR. Also worth saying explicitly: do NOT fix it by weakening or allow-listing the gate. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE THREE PRs: the gate exists because Mike is on Windows and the ecosystem is on Mac/Linux — a committed personal path is a portability defect for every contributor, not a cosmetic one.

NARROW THE BROWSER BUILD TO REPRODUCE A DOM DEFECT — a full lane becomes a ~23s compile (2026-08-14).

THE TECHNIQUE. To reproduce a real-DOM defect, narrow the :browser-test build's namespace selector to the one suite under test rather than running the full lane. A worker measured this today: a full-lane reproduction became a ~23 second compile, and it produced a verbatim reproduction — 9 tests, 35 assertions, 10 failures, captured exit 1 — including React's own InvalidStateError text out of setInitialProperties.

That matters because the browser lane exceeds the harness ceiling and forces detaching, which is where workers strand. A 23-second reproduction runs in the foreground.

THE TRAP THAT COMES WITH IT: --config-merge CANNOT CARRY A BACKSLASH ESCAPE on this setup. One backslash level is eaten between the node wrapper and the JVM, and the EDN reader then dies with `Unsupported escape character: \.`. So use a BACKSLASH-FREE regexp for the narrowed selector.

That is the same failure mode as the plant mangled by a bash-to-python round trip earlier the same day: a shell is not a neutral carrier of a pattern, and every layer between the command line and the reader may eat an escape. When a pattern must survive several layers, prefer one with no escapes at all over one you have carefully escaped.

USE IT FOR: reproducing an operator-reported DOM symptom, red-then-green on a single browser suite, and any bead where the acceptance is one behaviour in one namespace. Do NOT use it as the final gate — the full lane still decides, because a narrowed build cannot see a cross-namespace regression.

ATTRIBUTE A MEASURED CONSTANT, NEVER ASSERT ONE I CANNOT VERIFY — second instance of the same failure in one session (2026-08-14, method-reread loop).

INSTANCE 1, the node_modules canary: I pasted "101 immediate entries, 2933 recursive files" into briefs and tick reports. The real signature is 103/2933/2 — three parts, and my first term was wrong because I counted with ls rather than reading the removal script own CANARY line. Fixed by telling briefs to read the script output instead of quoting a number.

INSTANCE 2, the hicasso warning count: I have pasted "implementation/hicasso/ currently carries 8 pre-existing compiler warnings that are not yours" into at least four briefs. That number is NOWHERE IN THE TREE — grep of docs/design/hicasso/ and implementation/hicasso/ returns nothing. It came from one worker report about two hours earlier, and PRs #8163, #8175 and #8177 have landed on that surface since.

THE FAILURE DIRECTION IS THE DANGEROUS ONE. A worker told "there are exactly 8 pre-existing warnings, do not fix them" who then sees 9 can either chase a warning it did not introduce, or — worse — assume all 9 are pre-existing and ignore one it DID introduce. The second makes my helpful number a fail-open on the worker own change.

THE RULE: if I cannot verify a number at dispatch time, ATTRIBUTE it and hand the worker the method rather than the value. Say "a worker measured N earlier today; establish your own baseline before you change anything and compare against that" — which is what the gate-mechanics block already tells them to do for test counts, and it generalises. If I CAN verify it cheaply, verify it and cite how.

THE COMMON SHAPE OF BOTH INSTANCES: a number that was true when someone measured it, repeated by me long enough that it read as a property of the repository. Both were caught by the method-reread loop grading my own briefs rather than by any worker, which is what that loop is for.

NEVER PUT `git checkout` ON A FILE YOU ARE EDITING INTO A BACKGROUND JOB — it can land minutes late and silently revert verified work (2026-08-14, rf2-gatearm worker).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker ran a script that backgrounded a `git checkout HEAD -- <file>` as part of its own cleanup. The script failed, but the backgrounded checkout survived it and executed MINUTES LATER — after the worker had made further edits to that same file and verified them present. The edits vanished. The worker caught it only because a `git diff` it expected to be non-empty came back empty, and re-applied them; the re-applied blob hashed identical to the original.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY ANNOYING. The revert is SILENT and DELAYED. Every check the worker made — file content, diff, hash — passed at the moment it looked. The failure lands afterwards, in a window where nothing is being watched. A worker that commits during that window commits the reverted file and its own verification is worthless.

THE RULE: a `git checkout`, `git restore` or `git stash` naming a file you are actively editing must run in the FOREGROUND, synchronously, and its effect must be verified immediately afterwards. Never inside a background job, never inside a script whose failure path you have not read, never chained behind a long-running gate.

THE SAME CLASS AS TWO OTHER HAZARDS ALREADY RECORDED. A backgrounded gate that outlives its shell keeps writing to a log a restart is already using — same shape: an orphan process acting on state its owner believes it controls. And this repository's `.beads` rule exists for the same reason: a checkout that follows a tracker mutation within one tick reverts the mutation.

DETECTION, if you suspect it: a diff you expect to be non-empty comes back empty, or a file you just verified reads as HEAD. Re-apply and hash-verify rather than assuming you imagined the edit.

NEVER 'bd import' A JSONL YOU JUST REVERTED — IT CORRUPTS THE DOLT DB (root-caused 2026-07-25). The Dolt database is the SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH; .beads/issues.jsonl is a derived export. The mayor's conflict-reconcile procedure was: git checkout HEAD -- .beads (to unblock a pull) -> git pull --rebase -> rebase --skip -> bd import .beads/issues.jsonl -> bd export. The import step feeds the REVERTED (pre-close) file back INTO the database, resurrecting beads that were legitimately closed minutes earlier. Confirmed on rf2-a32r7: closed with a full reason, zero AUDIT-REOPEN notes, back to OPEN after one reconcile cycle. Also hit rf2-kqxe6.17 (twice), rf2-8ewl1, rf2-x4jda. CORRECT PROCEDURE — the file is downstream of the DB, data only ever flows DB -> file: (1) git checkout HEAD -- .beads  (2) git pull --ff-only  (3) bd export --all -o .beads/issues.jsonl  (4) guard wc -l >= 2000  (5) git add + commit + push. On a push rejection, repeat from (1) — NEVER 'bd import'. Import is ONLY for restoring a database that is itself lost or empty, never as a merge step. DIAGNOSTIC that distinguishes this from a genuine reviewer reopen: a real reopen carries a MERGED-PR AUDIT / AUDIT-REOPEN note naming an unmet defect at a code site; a procedure-revert has ZERO reopen notes and the bead simply reads open with its pre-close state. Grep the notes before re-closing.

NEVER DELETE A BRANCH THAT ANOTHER PR TARGETS AS ITS BASE — it silently CLOSES the dependent PR (2026-08-03, my error).

WHAT HAPPENED: PR #7376 (worker/shell58-2rtt6-58) carried rf2-2rtt6.58's R=0 boundary-shell measurement — the +106 B / +9.3% figure the OPERATOR RULED ON for the HD-028 value-equality default. It TARGETED worker/cascade-2rtt6-52 rather than main, because two of its three files existed only on that branch. When #7375 merged I deleted worker/cascade-2rtt6-52 in the routine post-merge cleanup. GitHub auto-closed #7376. Its branch and commits survive; its measurement is NOT on main.

WHY THE EXISTING RULE DID NOT COVER IT: the standing rule is 'never delete a branch BEFORE its own PR merges' (deleting auto-closes it). This is the mirror case — the branch's own PR HAD merged, but a DIFFERENT PR pointed at it as base. The post-merge cleanup checks the merged PR's state, not whether anything else depends on the branch.

THE CHECK, before deleting any worker branch: does any open PR name it as baseRefName? One call answers it:
  gh pr list --state open --json number,baseRefName --jq '.[]|select(.baseRefName=="worker/<name>")|.number'
If it returns anything, RE-TARGET those PRs to main first (gh pr edit <n> --base main), then delete. The dependent will usually need a rebase afterwards — that is a worker's job, not a blind resolution.

WHY STACKED PRs EXIST HERE AT ALL: a measurement PR must measure the branch that would merge, so it is cut FROM that branch and targets it. That is correct and will recur. The hazard is entirely in the cleanup order.

RECOVERY IS CHEAP IF CAUGHT: the branch survives deletion of its base, so the work is never lost — reopen or re-raise against main and rebase. The cost is latency and a confusing audit trail, not data.

NEVER dispatch two workers to the SAME git worktree/branch concurrently — even for two DIFFERENT fixes both needed on one PR. They share the worktree index + merge state and corrupt each other. Observed 2026-07-07: a bead-id-leak fix-worker AND a docs-reconciliation merge-worker both sent to the lxwpob #5234 worktree (worker/frame-lifecycle-collapse-rf2-lxwpob) -> the merge-worker's git merge origin/main collided with the fix-worker's concurrent commit, left the worktree stuck mid-conflict. Recovered ONLY because the merge happened to capture both commits (parents = both), but it was fragile. RULE: when a PR branch needs a second fix, SEQUENCE it — dispatch the second worker only AFTER the first has pushed and you have verified; or fold both into one worker's brief. One worktree = one live worker, always.

NEVER `git checkout HEAD -- .beads` AFTER AN OPERATION THAT CHANGED THE DOLT DATABASE — re-export from Dolt instead. Learned the hard way 2026-07-23 during a bead GC.

THE NORMAL REFLEX IS CORRECT AND THAT IS THE TRAP. The mayor loop runs `git checkout HEAD -- .beads/issues.jsonl` before every pull, because an uncommitted export otherwise aborts the pull and silently freezes HEAD. That reflex is right on an ordinary heartbeat and I run it dozens of times a session.

WHAT HAPPENED: after `bd gc --older-than 14 --force` deleted 462 closed beads (2610 -> 2148 issues, export 2774 -> 2313 lines), my very next checkpoint began with the usual `git checkout HEAD -- .beads` — which RESTORED THE PRE-GC 2774-LINE EXPORT over the freshly shrunk one. Dolt now said 2148 while the git export claimed 2774. The commit reported success. Nothing looked wrong.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS, not merely untidy: bd RE-IMPORTS the JSONL in various flows (a fresh worktree first-touch, a checkpoint re-import). Re-importing that stale export would have RESURRECTED ALL 462 DELETED BEADS. This is the same mechanism as the older reference_bd_close_reverted_by_jsonl_checkout memory, but at 462x the blast radius.

THE RULE, unconditional and safe in BOTH contexts:
  bd export --output .beads/issues.jsonl     # regenerate FROM the source of truth
  git add .beads/issues.jsonl
  git show :.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -l      # size guard BEFORE committing
  git commit && git push
Never restore the export from git over a database that has moved. Dolt is the source of truth; the JSONL is a projection of it. Regenerate the projection, never resurrect it.

HOW I CAUGHT IT: by VERIFYING the result rather than trusting the "committed + pushed" line — compare `bd stats` Total Issues against `wc -l` on the export. A git success message tells you a commit happened, not that it committed the right thing. Make that comparison part of any checkpoint following a bd operation.

ALSO FROM THE SAME GC (useful defaults): `bd gc --older-than N --dry-run` previews all three phases; the real run needs `--force`; it deletes ONLY closed issues older than N days and preserves every open/in-progress/blocked bead AND all memories (165 survived intact). Verify a handful of live bead ids and the memory count after any GC before committing the shrunk export.

I STATED A NAMING RECOMMENDATION AS A SETTLED RULING, TWICE IN ONE BRIEF, AND IT WOULD HAVE RE-COMMITTED THE DEFECT (2026-08-11, rf2-5l7l).

WHAT I WROTE. Briefing the `h/fn` sweep, I told the worker — twice — that "rf2-hic-065's row-1 ruling settled the callback macro as `h/event` and rejected `h/handler`", and instructed it to correct docstrings to the ruled name.

WHAT SOURCE SAYS. In naming-ledger.md row 1, `h/event` sits in the RECOMMENDATION column with STATUS = open, and the cell reads "Both candidates stand for the sitting (rf2-84w6)." rf2-hic-065's own note says "ALL NAMING ROWS RESERVED TO MIKE'S SITTING" and calls the appended recommendation "advisory, adopted nowhere as a naming ruling."

WHY IT MATTERED RATHER THAN BEING A PEDANTIC CORRECTION: `h/event` DOES NOT RESOLVE EITHER. Had the worker followed my brief, it would have replaced a name that does not exist with ANOTHER name that does not exist — re-committing the exact defect the bead was filed to remove, in the same files, under the authority of a ruling that was never made.

THE ACTUAL NAME IS `hfn`, so `h/hfn`. The worker established it three ways rather than assuming: the `(defmacro hfn ...)` and its self-refer in hicasso.cljc; `hfn`'s own docstring explaining WHY ("spelled `hfn` here because `h/fn` is qualified in the product and a bare `fn` would shadow cljs.core/fn on a :refer"); and a PASSING WITNESS in public_door_macros_cljs_test.cljs that writes `(h/hfn [e] ...)` under "Witness A — h/hfn, the one callback form".

THE RULE: A RECOMMENDATION IN A LEDGER IS NOT A RULING. Before citing one in a brief, read the STATUS column, not the recommendation text. In this repo a ruled row says so explicitly and names the operator and date; an advisory row says "open" and names the sitting it is reserved to. The two look alike in a summary and are opposite in force.

AND THE WIDER FORM, which I have now broken in three variants across one session: DO NOT ASSERT FROM MEMORY WHAT A RULING, A GATE OR A METHOD FILE CONTAINS. Grep it, read the status field, and quote it. The earlier variants were naming the wrong gate for a surface, and asserting the method already carried a discipline it had never contained. Same failure, three levels.

READING A BEAD WITH "bd show <id> | head -N" STRUCTURALLY GUARANTEES MISSING THE RULING (2026-08-18).

It cost a full worker cycle tonight. I briefed rf2-xa8wo to BUILD a p95/p99 estimator, quoting the description-s claim that lane.cljs computed none. The bead-s NEWEST comment opened with the words "DELIVERABLE 1 LANDED (PR #8481)". The estimator had shipped. The description had never changed across all 110 history entries, so a top-down read was guaranteed to return the oldest text and miss the only line that mattered.

WHY head IS WORSE THAN tail AND BOTH ARE WRONG. bd show prints DESCRIPTION first, and the description is the oldest text on a bead — corrections accrete below it as comments. So head reads the oldest material by construction. tail is not the fix either: audit notes append INTO the description block while dated comments render after it, so the last lines on screen can be older than material higher up. Grepping the prose for dates does not work: a date in the text is CONTENT, not a mutation time, so an undated correction is invisible and an edited description can be the newest field.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKS, and it is two commands:
  bd comments <id> --json   -> sort by created_at, read the newest first
  bd history <id> --json    -> walk adjacent pairs newest-first to the first change in a text-bearing field
Plus: re-enumerate children (a ruling is sometimes a new CHILD bead), and read DEPENDS ON links with their status and close reasons (a ruling that discharges a slice is often the CLOSE REASON of an already-closed dependency, which no child enumeration and no id-prefix filter will find).

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS BITE THE MAYOR SPECIFICALLY. Every brief I send already tells the WORKER to do this — it is in the pasted common preamble. The gap is at the one moment a brief is WRITTEN FROM a bead, where the mayor is reading fast to dispatch fast. I pasted that paragraph into the very brief whose premise I then got wrong. The worker obeyed it and caught me; that is the licence-to-refuse clause paying for itself, not a control.

RULE: never pipe bd show into head or tail when the output will become a brief. Read the comments as JSON, ordered, newest first, BEFORE writing a single line of the dispatch. It costs one command and it is cheaper than a worker cycle every time.

I REAPED A LIVE WORKER'S WORKTREE THREE TIMES IN ONE NIGHT. I WROTE THE RULE DOWN TWICE AND BROKE IT AGAIN TWENTY MINUTES LATER (2026-08-10).

THE THREE. rf2-hic-009: agent had reported, I resumed it, reaped on the stale report. rf2-hic-016: agent had NEVER reported; I merged its PR and reaped in the SAME COMMAND. rf2-x874: agent reported, I resumed it with a GO signal, it worked for 30 minutes, I merged and reaped with no report after the resume. Each time the worker was mid-gate. Each time the reap deleted .git and the running log underneath it.

WRITING THE RULE DID NOT WORK. TWICE. The reason is that the rule lives in my head at hygiene time, and the violation happens at MERGE time. Merge and reap are adjacent in the loop: the PR lands, the branch looks spent, the directory looks like litter, and the reap rides along on the same impulse. A memory that says "check for a report" is consulted during hygiene, which is exactly the tick where I am not making the mistake.

SO THE FIX IS MECHANICAL, NOT A REMINDER. NEVER REAP IN A MERGE TICK. Merging a PR and reaping its worktree are two decisions with two different signals, and putting them in one turn is what makes the error. Reap only during a hygiene pass, where the survey forces me to look at each worktree and ask what authorises removing it. If the merge tick makes a directory look spent, leave it; hygiene will take it next pass, and a stale directory is the entire cost of waiting.

THE SIGNAL, unchanged and simple: only the agent's own report authorises a reap. A resume voids an earlier report. No report at all authorises nothing. A merged PR is not a report; it says the code is done, not that the agent is. A worker routinely keeps running after it pushes, finishing the very gates its PR body promises.

WHAT SAVED ME EACH TIME, and it will not always. All three had pushed. The third still had its node_modules junction in place when the reaper ran, and the mayor's tree survived at 101 — scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh took the safe path and unlinked rather than following it. That script is the only reason three violations cost nothing. A bare `git worktree remove` would have emptied the mayor's real node_modules, which has happened twice historically.

NEVER RUN `git fetch --depth=N` INSIDE A WORKER WORKTREE — IT SHALLOWS THE OBJECT STORE SHARED WITH THE MAYOR AND EVERY OTHER WORKER (2026-08-14, reported by the rf2-4sl9 worker, which avoided it deliberately).

THE HAZARD: every worker worktree here is a LINKED worktree sharing one .git. A depth-limited fetch converts a complete clone into a shallow one — measured on real re-frame2 history: is-shallow false to TRUE, walkable history 21890 commits down to 100. Run inside any worktree, that truncation hits the shared object store, so it would silently break history-dependent work for the mayor and every concurrent worker, not just the one that ran it.

THE SAFE FORM when you must demonstrate depth behaviour: run the control in a THROWAWAY CLONE outside the worktree tree, then delete it and verify the mayor object store is still complete. That worker did exactly that and checked afterwards.

RELATED AND ALREADY ACTED ON: `git fetch --depth=N` under a `fetch-depth: 0` checkout is a defect wherever it appears in CI, because it discards the history the full checkout just paid for. Four instances found in one day — docs.yml (rf2-ihfw, fixed), lint.yml (rf2-4sl9, fixed), and .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh (rf2-om08, filed). The fourth family member was found by sweeping .github/ rather than guessing, and the tree already argued against it: test.yml says "the fetch-depth: 0 above is what makes the base resolvable without a fetch: it can be arbitrarily deep" while the script it calls truncates that to 100 one line in.

THE DISCRIMINATOR FOR A LEGITIMATE USE: a `--depth=1` fetch of a SPECIFIC SHA under a deliberately shallow `fetch-depth: 2` checkout is correct and documented (portability.yml, post-merge-workflow-sanity.yml). The defect is only a depth cap applied on top of a FULL checkout.

NEW CI FLAKE CLASS: GOOGLE FONTS 503 FAILS 'mkdocs build --strict' (2026-07-25). The docs job aborted with: "ERROR - Couldn't find font family 'IBM Plex Sans' on Google Fonts (503: Service Unavailable)" then "Aborted with a BuildError!". The Material theme fetches the font family AT BUILD TIME and --strict promotes the fetch failure to a BuildError, so an entirely unrelated diff (a spec/012 documentary edit) reds on an external service outage.

HOW TO TELL IT APART FROM A REAL DOCS FAILURE, which matters because the two present identically as 'Docs required + MkDocs build' both red: read the log. A real failure names a FILE and a TARGET — e.g. 'BROKEN ANCHOR: skills/re-frame2-pair/SKILL.md:200 -> references/ops.md#...' from the 'Validate doc links' step, or a nav/strict error naming a page. The font flake names a font family and a 503 in the 'Build site (strict)' step and lists no file at all. Both were observed within minutes of each other today on #6978 (real: 8 broken anchors from one renamed heading) and #6981 (flake: the 503).

CORRECT RESPONSE: 'gh run rerun <run-id> --failed'. Do NOT --admin past it. The method permits --admin only for a check that structurally cannot touch the diff and is PENDING; this one is FAILED, and a re-run gets an honest green rather than a bypassed one. If Google Fonts is degraded for a sustained period every docs PR will red the same way, so expect a cluster and re-run rather than dispatching fix-workers.

MAYOR-SIDE: pulling the CI log is cheap and it is the difference between a 2-minute re-run and a wasted fix-worker dispatch. Do it before deciding what a red docs job means — I diagnosed both of today's cases from 'gh run view <id> --log-failed' in one call each.

New CLJS test suites that share the node-test bundle (npm run test:cljs runs every *-cljs-test ns in ONE Node process / process-global runtime) MUST use re-frame.test-support/make-reset-runtime-fixture (the rf2-7hwnu run-order-independence fixture — snapshots load-time registrar baseline, restores registrar + disposes adapter on teardown). A bare (registrar/clear-all!) + (rf/init!) fixture with no snapshot/restore leaves the runtime dirty and contaminates the ALPHABETICALLY-LATER suite (e.g. derivation-conformance broke the Reagent reg_view_react_key suite via a null reagent_component read — rf2-jn7frs/#3943). JVM-only (.clj) tests do not hit this (no shared bundle). Brief test-authoring workers to adopt the fixture; reply-conformance/ + security/ are the precedents.

NEW FALSE-GREEN SHAPE: A CROSS-DOOR TEST THAT EXERCISES ONE DOOR TWICE CANNOT DETECT A CROSS-DOOR DISPARITY (2026-07-26, self-caught by the rf2-kqxe6.23 worker, which is why it is worth recording).

WHAT HAPPENED: the bead defect was that the named-address door and the three URL doors resolve different targets for one destination. Its acceptance test was hover-then-click on one link, expecting ONE cache entry. The first draft dispatched a hand-written [:rf.route/navigate {:to ...}] for the click — the same NAMED door the hover already used — so both halves landed on the same wrong value, agreed with each other, and the arm PASSED AGAINST THE UNFIXED CODE. A parity test whose two sides go through the same seam tests nothing about parity.

IT WAS CAUGHT ONLY BY THE REVERT-IN-PLACE NEGATIVE CONTROL. That is the whole argument for making the negative control mandatory rather than encouraged: a test that passes before the fix is indistinguishable from a test that passes after it, unless you actually run the before case. The house standard held.

THE FIX SHAPE: drive each side through the seam a REAL caller uses. Here that meant taking both halves off one props map through prefetch-payload and link-model :payload — the two paths an actual anchor exercises — rather than hand-writing the dispatch. Hand-writing the event is what collapsed two doors into one.

GENERALISE INTO BRIEFS for any parity, round-trip or cross-path acceptance: state explicitly that each side must go through a DIFFERENT real entry point, and that the negative control is what proves it. This is adjacent to the fixture-blindness family (a gate that cannot see the case) but distinct: here the gate looks right, exercises the right number of steps, and is blind because both steps are the same step.

NEW "Ran 0 tests" VARIANT — `clojure -M:test -v ns/a ns/b ns/c` SILENTLY RUNS ONLY THE FIRST VAR. Found by the rf2-vy2hj/z53ph worker (#6419) on 2026-07-19, caught only because it noticed an ASSERTION COUNT OF 6 WHERE 16 WERE EXPECTED. Multi-var selection does not error, does not warn — it just quietly ignores every var after the first, and the run reports green.
RULE: verify each var INDIVIDUALLY, or verify the expected assertion count. Never trust a multi-var `-v` invocation to have run what you listed.

THIS IS THE FOURTH DISTINCT WAY "green" HAS MEANT "nothing ran" in this repo:
  1. A bare `clojure -M:test -n <ns>` from implementation/ silently runs 0 tests and prints "Ran 0 tests".
  2. A CLJS runner selecting nothing after a namespace rename (the :ns-regexp "cljs-test$" trap — renaming *-cljs-test to *-test deletes it from the suite silently).
  3. A clojure.test MAP FIXTURE — a map is IFn, so {:before f} composes to a fn returning nil and the body never runs. (cljs.test DOES support map fixtures; the trap is clojure.test only.)
  4. THIS: multi-var `-v ns/a ns/b ns/c` running only ns/a.
THE ONLY RELIABLE DEFENCE, and it works against all four: demand a NON-ZERO AND PLAUSIBLE count, and know roughly what the count should be. #6419 caught this by expecting 16 and seeing 6. A worker who only checked "non-zero" would have shipped it.

ALSO FROM #6419, the counterpart discipline: it VACUITY-PROBED by flipping an assertion and confirming the FULL gate redded NAMING ITS TEST, then restored and verified the tree byte-identical. That probe is what distinguishes "my namespace ran and passed" from "my namespace was never selected".

DIAGNOSIS: "intermittent timeout under load" is a THEORY, and a recorded one can be wrong for years while every remedy it suggests fails. Corrects my earlier entry on the http supersede-stale flake, which repeated that theory.

WHAT EVERYONE BELIEVED, including the test source comment, the bead, my brief and my own memory note: an async supersede landed after the poll window, so the test was timing the machine. The remedy that follows is a bigger bound, and it had already been applied once (5s -> 30s) without removing the failure.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY TRUE (measured 2026-09-01, rf2-o9e15 / PR #8889): the path is not async at all — supersede! and the stale-trace emit run INLINE in the fx phase, and the row lands before the second dispatch-sync returns; probed present with zero wait. The real failure was ABSENCE, not lateness. supersede! returns nil when nothing is in flight, and the test gate was a no-op: a CountDownLatch(1) whose first act INSIDE the handler was its own countDown, so the following await returned immediately and held nothing. Request #1 could complete its whole round trip before the second dispatch, so no supersede ever occurred and the poll waited out its backstop for a row that could not arrive.

THE SENTENCE TO REMEMBER: no bound is large enough for an event that is never emitted. That is why the 5s -> 30s raise reduced the rate without removing the mode — a larger window only widens the race it cannot fix.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, cheap and decisive: before accepting "it timed out under load", probe whether the awaited event happens AT ALL with zero wait. If it does, the problem is not timing, and a bigger timeout is treating a missing precondition as slowness. The repair here made the precondition hold (a held server keeping every exchange until released), turning the supersede from a race into a guarantee, and the stale row is now asserted with no wait at all.

AND CHECK THE GATE ITSELF WHEN A TEST GATE IS THE SUBJECT: a latch that counts itself down, a promise resolved before the thing it guards, a fixture asserting its own setup — these read as synchronisation and provide none.

NODE AND CHROME DISAGREE ON HEAP ABSOLUTES BY ~2x, BY CONFIGURATION. `v8_enable_pointer_compression` is 0 in Node and 1 in Chrome — 8-byte vs 4-byte tagged slots. Measured directly: the same narrow write read 854,788 B under Node against the browser's 457,181 B = 1.87x, exactly what an uncompressed heap does to pointer-dominated CLJS. SHARES AND RATIOS TRANSFER; ABSOLUTES DO NOT. State the engine beside every heap figure, and never compare a Node absolute against a Chrome absolute. This is the third runtime-transfer trap on this surface, after JVM-vs-CLJS (dynamic `binding` allocates ~760 B on the JVM and nothing in CLJS) and dev-vs-production DCE.

ONE ARGUMENT THREADED INTO TWO PAYLOADS ACQUIRES TWO DIFFERENT DECLARED TYPES (2026-08-06, found while fixing rf2-j4bg3, filed as rf2-am6qs).

THE INSTANCE: `require-frame-provider-target!` threads ONE `where` argument into BOTH payloads. rf2-j4bg3 tightened `NoFrameContextTags`s `:where` slot from `:any` to `:symbol`. `BadFrameProviderArgTags` still declares `:any`. So the SAME VALUE, from the SAME call site, is now declared two different ways depending on which record it lands in. Two more slots are still `:any` (`FrameDestroyedTags`, `ResourceSsrBlockingTimeoutTags`).

THE GENERALISATION WORTH CARRYING: when tightening a schema slot, ask WHERE THAT VALUE COMES FROM, not just what this record does with it. If one producer feeds several records, the slot is a property of the PRODUCER and tightening one consumer creates a disagreement rather than removing one. That is the same identity-function lesson as fixing a by-name law at the naming boundary rather than per check.

WHAT THE CORPUS ACTUALLY SAID, and it settled a question the audit had left open: the audit described the accepted contract as "sym-or-kw". A census of the real producers found 48 DISTINCT `:where` VALUES, ALL QUOTED SYMBOLS, ZERO KEYWORDS, across core, http, machines, routing, flows, resources, ssr, freehand and ui. So `[:or :symbol :keyword]` would have CONTRADICTED the schemas own comment two lines above the slot ("a SYMBOL … not a keyword"). Two `frame.cljc` docstrings carrying the sym-or-kw claim were the source of the audits framing and were corrected in the same pass — leaving them would have re-created the bead.

THE TYPE-MUTATION WITNESS IS THE POINT, because the catalogue conformance gate COMPARES KEYS ONLY and is blind to types by construction. Reverting the slot to `:any` produced 6 failures, four reading `actual: (not (not true))` — a string, a number, a map AND a bare keyword all validated. I REAPED A LIVE WORKER'S WORKTREE TWICE IN ONE NIGHT, AND THE SECOND TIME I USED THE FORBIDDEN PROXY DIRECTLY (2026-08-10).

CASE 1, rf2-hic-009. The agent HAD reported. I then resumed it, and reaped later on the strength of that stale report. I wrote a memory about it: resuming invalidates an earlier completion report.

CASE 2, rf2-hic-016, and it is worse. The agent had NEVER reported. I merged PR #7757 and reaped its worktree in the same command. The signal I acted on was PR-MERGED STATE - the exact proxy the hygiene rule names first and forbids. The worker was running its last gate. Deleting the worktree took .git and its log out from under a spine run at 1125 lines with zero real failures. Its report arrived twenty minutes later and told me what I had done.

SO THE RULE IS SIMPLER THAN I WROTE IT, AND I OVER-COMPLICATED IT BY PATCHING ONE CASE. Only the agent's own report authorises a reap. Not a merged PR. Not a clean tree. Not elapsed time. Not "the work is obviously done". A resume voids an earlier report, and no report at all means no authorisation of any kind.

WHY MERGING MAKES THIS EASY TO GET WRONG. Merge and reap feel like one motion: the PR lands, the branch is spent, the directory looks like litter. But merging says the CODE is done. It says nothing about whether the AGENT is done - and a worker routinely keeps running after it pushes, because it is finishing the very gates whose results the PR body promises.

THE CHECK, BEFORE ANY REAP: has THIS agent reported since its last resume? If no report has arrived at all, do not reap, however finished the PR looks. Merging a PR and reaping its worktree are two decisions with two different signals; never put them in the same command.

WHAT IT COSTS. Nothing was lost either time - both workers had pushed. But a worker holding unpushed commits would lose them, and one worker tonight sat on three unpushed commits for over an hour. A stale directory is the entire cost of waiting.

Workers have reported 103 and 105 for the dotfile-inclusive count on the same healthy tree. A bare number with no command invites a worker to measure differently and conclude the tree is damaged.

AN ORACLE CROSS-CHECK MUST TEST WHAT THE ORACLE ACCEPTS, NOT ONLY WHAT IT REFUSES — otherwise it confirms your intent rather than the truth. Found by the rf2-drpa3.90/.97/.98 worker (PR #6733, 2026-07-23), and it is the sharpest refinement of the verify-the-verifier discipline this project has.

THE SETUP: the Freehand compile checker hand-rolls reader-conditional branch selection, so the established technique is to cross-check that selection against `clojure.tools.reader` at `:features #{:clj}` and `#{:cljs}` — an oracle independent of the code under test.

THE INSIGHT, in the worker own words: "the oracle only caught it because I cross-checked the ACCEPTING cases, not just the refusing ones... that is what separated the reader refuses this from MY RULE refuses this."

THE CONCRETE CASE IT SAVED: `{#?(:clj :a) #?(:clj 1)}` reads as `{}` for `:cljs` under tools.reader — perfectly legal. A naive "refuse any entry with an elided side" rule would have REFUSED it. That is a FALSE-RED, and false-reds are HARDER to notice than false-greens because the tool looks like it is working — it is confidently rejecting something, and nobody investigates a refusal that matches their expectation. The fix was to DROP an entry whose key AND value both elide, matching the real reader. Neither that case nor the companion `{#?(:clj :a) 1 :b #?(:clj 2)}` (which re-pairs to `{1 :b}` for the real reader) appeared anywhere in the bead.

THE RULE FOR ANY ORACLE-BACKED WORK: enumerate BOTH directions before trusting the cross-check —
  (a) cases the oracle REFUSES that your rule must also refuse (guards against false-green), AND
  (b) cases the oracle ACCEPTS that your rule must NOT refuse (guards against false-red / over-refusal).
Only (a) is the instinctive half, and only (a) is what a bead usually enumerates. A cross-check limited to (a) is not an independent oracle at all — it is a restatement of the intent you already had.

RELATED, SAME FAMILY, ALREADY RECORDED HERE: a probe that has never flagged anything has not been tested; run it against a KNOWN-PRESENT and a KNOWN-ABSENT instance. A blanket mutation that reds three fixtures while leaving two green certifies falsifiability it has not established. A guard proven on cases can still fail on SEQUENCES. This adds the missing axis: a guard proven on refusals can still fail on ACCEPTANCES.

BRIEF LANGUAGE THAT WORKS: "cross-check against <independent oracle>, and enumerate what it ACCEPTS as well as what it refuses — a rule that only reproduces your intended refusals has not been checked against anything."

os.loadavg() RETURNS [0,0,0] ON WINDOWS, SO A LOAD RIDER BUILT ON IT SILENTLY RECORDS NOTHING (2026-08-21, rf2-24o2z, PR #8596).

WHY THIS BITES HERE SPECIFICALLY. Windows is the box every measurement window in this repo is taken on. rf2-24o2z asked for 'the box's load at window open' to be recorded in the allocation datasets, so that the mode-rate's mechanism — thermal state against V8 tier accumulation against heap fragmentation — could eventually be separated. The obvious implementation is os.loadavg(). On Windows Node returns [0, 0, 0] unconditionally: not an error, not a throw, just three zeros. Every window would have recorded a perfectly well-formed load field of zero, and the census built on it would have concluded the box was idle for every run ever taken.

THE FAILURE SHAPE IS THE ONE THIS REPO HUNTS EVERYWHERE ELSE: a reading that is PRESENT and WRONG, indistinguishable from a real one, underwriting a conclusion nobody would re-check. It is the sibling of 'a search that returns ZERO is not a check that passed'.

WHAT WAS BUILT INSTEAD: a CPU-times snapshot PAIR — os.cpus() times at window OPEN and again at CLOSE — whose delta gives the busy fraction the run actually saw. That is better than a loadavg on two counts beyond portability: it costs no sleep, and it measures the window's own interval rather than a trailing 1/5/15-minute average that mostly describes what happened BEFORE the window started.

THE GENERAL RULE: before recording any environment fact into a dataset, check what the API returns ON THIS PLATFORM, with a positive control. Cross-platform is a standing constraint here — Mike is on Windows, maintainers are on Mac and Linux — so a value that is merely well-formed on one of the three is not evidence.

OUTAGE PLAYBOOK — CORRECTION TO MY OWN NOTE FROM AN HOUR EARLIER (2026-07-26). I recorded that during a sustained 529 window the right move was to STOP resuming because resumes die on contact. Then I observed resumes DOING REAL WORK (two branches advanced, one worker reported a full Freehand JVM suite green at 1206 tests / 8042 assertions immediately before being killed), concluded the earlier note was too pessimistic, and resumed six workers plus dispatched two.

BOTH READINGS WERE RIGHT FOR THEIR MOMENT, AND THAT IS THE ACTUAL LESSON. The outage had PHASES. Between roughly 19:38 and 19:44 workers were killed AFTER producing work — resuming was clearly correct. From roughly 19:50 onward they died BEFORE THEIR FIRST TOOL CALL: measured, four consecutive resumes of the same worker left its branch tip, local HEAD and uncommitted count all byte-identical, and three freshly dispatched workers never even created their worktrees.

SO THE RULE IS NOT "resume" OR "do not resume" — IT IS: MEASURE WHETHER THE LAST ATTEMPT PRODUCED ANYTHING, AND LET THAT DECIDE THE NEXT ONE. The discriminator is cheap and objective: after a resume, did the remote branch tip move, did the local HEAD move, did the uncommitted count change, or (for a fresh dispatch) does the worktree exist? If none of those moved, the window is in its dead phase and further attempts are pure loss. If any moved, keep resuming — each turn buys real progress even though it ends in a kill.

WHAT DOES NOT WORK AS A SIGNAL: the SendMessage response. It returns "resumed from transcript in the background" identically whether the agent then does ten minutes of work or dies immediately. It confirms delivery, not viability.

AND WHAT STAYS TRUE IN EVERY PHASE, because it is the only thing that made two hours of this survivable: the mayor job is DURABILITY, not throughput. No unpushed commits anywhere (verified per worktree by comparing local HEAD against git ls-remote). Every at-risk uncommitted diff copied OUT of its worktree to a location outside the repo — seven patches by the end, including a 387-insertion core-walker change and a 32-file docs restructure. Never commit them: only that worker knows whether its files form a coherent change. And mark those worktrees EXEMPT from the hygiene reap on their beads, because the reap gate (zero commits, clean, no PR) matches an interrupted worker exactly.

THE TRACKER'S 'parent' FIELD IS IN USE — 37 BEADS CARRY ONE — AND ENUMERATING CHILDREN BY ID PREFIX MISSES 40% OF THEM (measured 2026-08-23 11:04 AUSEST, tip 88362471d4). This CORRECTS an earlier reading of my own that recorded the field as unused.

THE CENSUS, over all 1001 open + deferred + closed beads: 37 carry a non-empty 'parent'. Every one of the 37 is CLOSED. No open bead is a child, and — checked in the other direction, which is the one that matters for a backlog pass — NO OPEN BEAD HAS CHILDREN. The three parents named are rf2-0yp7w (the ui/freehand retirement epic), rf2-0yp7w.9 (its prose sweep) and rf2-2rtt6 (the Hicasso programme epic), all closed.

SO THE CORRECT STATEMENT IS NOT 'the field is unused'. It is 'the mechanism exists and is used, and it currently touches nothing on the board' — which is stronger, because it says the re-enumeration is a real check that happened to return empty rather than a check against a field nobody populates.

THE PREFIX TRAP, REPRODUCED WITH NUMBERS RATHER THAN QUOTED. rf2-0yp7w.9 has TEN true children by the parent field. A prefix scan for 'rf2-0yp7w.9' finds SIX and misses FOUR: rf2-5z6bb, rf2-c95do, rf2-n9hno, rf2-v14sq. Those four are generated ids that share no prefix with their parent.

AND THE MISS IS THE REASSURING KIND, which is why it is worth writing down. The six the prefix scan DOES find are .1 through .6 — a contiguous, gapless run that reads as a complete set. Nothing about the result looks truncated, so there is no prompt to go looking for the other four. That is the same failure shape as every other well-formed wrong answer in this tracker: right-looking, confidently returned, 60% complete.

HOW TO ENUMERATE: read the 'parent' field off the JSON listing and group by it. Never derive children from the id string.

WHAT HAPPENED. Checking quotes I had been attributing to the method tree, a case-sensitive single-line grep returned NOT FOUND on four of five. Three of the four were VERBATIM PRESENT and my probe missed them:

* "cite the check you made" — the tree begins the sentence "Cite the check you made, or say plainly that you are summarising and from what."
* "where a reader-side rule has failed repeatedly" — the tree has "Where a reader-side rule has failed repeatedly, more text is usually not the repair."

The fourth, a principle I attributed to the tree in a merged PR body, read as INVENTED under a 180-character context window and turned out to be stated THREE TIMES once I widened the window and varied the phrasing.

THREE COMPOUNDING CAUSES, all mine. (1) Case: re-typing a phrase from memory drops the sentence-initial capital, and grep is case-sensitive by default. (2) Window: a fixed -oE context window centred on a short term misses the statement that sits just outside it. (3) Wrapping: these files wrap near 95 characters, so ANY quoted sentence longer than a clause spans a line break and a single-line grep cannot see it — flatten with tr '\n' ' ' first.

DIRECTION OF THE ERROR IS ALWAYS THE SAME AND ALWAYS THE EXPENSIVE ONE: absent-when-present. It reads as discovering drift, and acting on it means "fixing" a document that is already correct, or filing a correction against a merged PR that needs none. I was one step from both.

PIPING A GATE INTO tail OR grep DISCARDS ITS EXIT CODE — a false-green generator affecting EVERY worker. Found 2026-07-24 by the worker whose PR it burned, and refined by that same worker afterwards.

THE MECHANISM: `npm run test:browser | tail -20` exits with the status of `tail`, not the runner. A worker reads "0 failures, 0 errors", sees a zero exit, reports green. The runner had exited NON-ZERO the whole time.

THE BRIEFED FORM — REQUIRE THIS IN EVERY DISPATCH:
  npm run test:browser > /tmp/gate.log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -20 /tmp/gate.log
Capture to a file, ECHO THE EXIT CODE, then read. A worker reporting a gate green must include the EXIT CODE, not just the counts.

⚠️ GREP IS WORSE THAN TAIL, not equivalent. Tail masks the exit code; grep masks the exit code AND hides the explanatory line — because a pattern chosen BEFORE you know what the failure looks like cannot match it. The real message here was "cljs.test summary was green, but the browser emitted 1 uncaught pageerror(s)" and it matched none of the workers `FAIL|failures` patterns. Capture-then-read fixes both: the file keeps everything and you can grep it as many times as the diagnosis needs.

⚠️ SCOPE THE COMPANION RULE CORRECTLY — do NOT over-generalise it. implementation/scripts/run-browser-tests.cjs fails a run on ANY uncaught pageerror even when every assertion passes (rf2-mwx08). That is BROWSER-LANE-SPECIFIC; the JVM and node lanes have no equivalent, and there the summary IS the verdict. State that distinction in briefs, or workers will start distrusting counts everywhere and re-derive exit codes from scratch each time. THE EXIT CODE IS THE UNIVERSAL ANSWER; the pageerror rule is merely why a green summary was never sufficient in that one lane.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY FALSE GREEN: the test summary is GENUINELY green. cljs.test reported 0F 0E inside a job that failed. Every human-readable signal says pass; the failure lives only in the discarded exit code.

A DISCIPLINE THAT PROVABLY WORKED, worth keeping: my brief for the fix DELIBERATELY REFUSED TO NAME A CAUSE (per the standing symptoms-not-causes rule, adopted after three of my asserted causes were wrong). A BYTE-DELTA ASSERTION CANNOT PROVE A PLANT LANDED — hash the line, do not measure it (2026-08-15 15:35 AUSEST).

WHAT I HAVE BEEN BRIEFING, and it is incomplete: 'these files are CRLF, so a patch matching \n writes nothing and the gate comes back green on unmodified bytes — assert the match count before and after the write, AND ASSERT THE BYTE-LENGTH DELTA.' The byte-delta half is the weak one.

MEASURED by worker/records-mha1r (rf2-mha1r cluster, PR #8297). It planted '#7-planted-bogus-anchor-mha1r' on dispositions.md:66, replacing an anchor of EQUAL LENGTH. THE BYTE DELTA WAS EXACTLY 0. A worker following my advice literally would have read delta==0 as 'the write did not land', aborted a plant that had in fact landed perfectly, and either retried pointlessly or concluded the gate was untestable. What proved the write was a sha256 of the single line, which changed.

SO THE DELTA CHECK IS NECESSARY-BUT-NOT-SUFFICIENT IN ONE DIRECTION AND OUTRIGHT WRONG IN THE OTHER:
  - a NON-ZERO delta does prove bytes changed;
  - a ZERO delta proves NOTHING — it is equally consistent with a no-op patch and with an equal-length substitution.
Equal-length substitutions are not exotic here. Swapping one anchor slug for another of the same width, flipping a digit, or exchanging two same-length identifiers all produce delta 0.

THE CORRECT ASSERTION, in order of strength:
  1. HASH THE SINGLE LINE before and after (git hash-object on the file, or sha256 of the line). A changed hash proves the write; an unchanged hash proves the no-op. This works for every case including equal-length.
  2. Assert the match count moved 1 -> 0 for the pattern you replaced.
  3. Use the byte delta only as a cheap corroboration when you EXPECT it to be non-zero, and never as the primary test.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE PLANT: the whole point of the plant is to prove the gate reads YOUR tree. If the plant silently no-ops, the gate comes back green and that green is meaningless — the 'a patch that never applied reads clean too' trap. An assertion that itself gives a false negative on a legitimate write pushes a worker toward abandoning the only proof it has.

FOUR WORKERS HIT THE CRLF NO-OP TRAP TODAY AND THE ASSERTION CAUGHT IT EVERY TIME — the mechanism is right; only my choice of measurement was sloppy. Brief the HASH, mention the delta as corroboration.

THE PR'S OWN CHECK RUN CAN FALSIFY THE PROSE IN ITS DIFF, AND THAT CONTRADICTION IS VISIBLE AT MERGE TIME. Measured 2026-08-22, on a clause I merged and the audit reopened an hour later.

WHAT HAPPENED. PR #8678 added one paragraph to the method saying "documentation and prose changes typically arm no gated surface at all", resting on report-changed-surfaces.sh returning 0 of 28 keys for the path. Three of us took that measurement independently -- two workers and me -- and all three read it as "no gates". The merged-PR audit found it false: report-changed-surfaces.sh is the test.yml classifier, and docs.yml has a SEPARATE Detect docs surface step that maps docs/* to docs_surface=true and gates a MkDocs build on it.

THE EVIDENCE WAS ON MY OWN SCREEN AT MERGE TIME AND I DID NOT CONNECT IT. The rollup I read to clear clause 2 showed "docs: success" -- that job is docs.yml's, and its running at all is a live demonstration that the path arms a gated surface. The diff said the opposite four lines away.

THE GENERAL FORM, which is what makes this worth keeping. The merge criterion says to read the FILE LIST against the item, and I extend it: when the diff makes a factual claim about GATING, the PR's own check run is a free control on that claim, and it is already open in front of you. A claim that a path arms nothing, beside a rollup showing a surface-gated job that ran, is a contradiction you can see without running anything.

THE NARROWER TRAP UNDERNEATH IT. "0 of 28" is one classifier's answer, not a census of gates. This repo has at least three independent gating paths -- test.yml's report-changed-surfaces.sh, docs.yml's own Detect docs surface step (which report-changed-surfaces.sh:44 NAMES in its own comment as a path it does not cover), and lint.yml's. A zero from one of them says nothing about the other two. Ask for the COMPLETE covering set, never one classifier's keys.

AND THE COUNTEREXAMPLE THAT MAKES IT CONCRETE: implementation/hicasso/spec/budgets.md is in docs.yml's docs_surface case list AND arms five test.yml surfaces including three Chromium lanes and an ~11-minute compile. It is prose, and it is the heaviest change in the repo.

The original worker had not exited -- it was still resolving that very conflict. Its worktree's .git file was deleted underneath it and a new worktree appeared holding its branch at its own rebased SHA. It handled this better than I did: it verified the branch tip carried its complete resolution and pushed a ref-only update from the mayor checkout rather than racing, then flagged the orphaned directory. Nothing was lost, but only because the worker was careful.

THE COMMON ERROR: I treated the PR opening as the worker's last act. It is its last REPORTED act. After opening a PR a worker may still be running gates, updating the PR body, answering a message, or -- as here -- resolving a conflict I asked about.

THE RULES:
1. BEFORE REAPING A WORKTREE: require the worker to be finished, not the PR to be merged. The cheap approximation is to reap on the NEXT tick, once the tree is quiescent.
2. BEFORE DISPATCHING ONTO AN EXISTING BRANCH: confirm no live worker holds it. If a PR needs a rebase or a fix and its worker may still be alive, SEND THAT WORKER A MESSAGE instead of dispatching a second one. Resuming an existing worker is cheaper and cannot race.
3. A branch with a live worktree is CLAIMED. Treat a worktree the way you would treat an IN_PROGRESS bead.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE WASTED RUN: both failure modes produce evidence that looks real. A deleted worktree yields a gate failure naming real files that are present; a hijacked branch yields two agents with divergent views of the same tip. Neither announces itself as an infrastructure fault, and both invite a "fix" for a defect that does not exist.

PR visibility + merge SLA (Mike, 2026-07-13): remote PR head is authoritative. After a coherent checkpoint passes fast deterministic checks, commit/push before any test expected over 10 minutes; active PR must not lag a clean local worktree by more than 15 minutes. Draft may be incomplete but never stale/local-only. Run long CI and independent review in parallel on the pushed SHA. Mayor reconciles local HEAD vs PR HEAD every 5 minutes. Exact-head green + independently cleared merges within 5 minutes, followed immediately by mayor pull. If blocked, report named blocker + exact SHA. This prevents stale green GitHub ticks hiding hours of local work.

A PR CAN BE PERMANENTLY UNMERGEABLE BY A MAYOR WHOSE OWN LOOP MOVES main (2026-08-07, PR #7637, 28 attempts).

THE SYMPTOM: 'Base branch was modified. Review and try the merge again.' on every attempt, with the PR reading 86/86 SUCCESS, all five workflows completed/success at the head sha, mergeable=MERGEABLE, and behind=1.

BOTH TRANSPORTS AGREE, so it is not a client quirk: GraphQL mergePullRequest gives the message, and REST 'PUT /repos/{o}/{r}/pulls/{n}/merge' with an explicit sha gives HTTP 405 with the identical message. Do not spend attempts hunting a different call.

THE MECHANISM, and it is self-inflicted: the beads audit hook and the mayor's own checkpoint pushes each add a commit to main. So the cycle is — gh pr update-branch takes the branch to behind=0, CI restarts (~10 min) on the new head, a checkpoint push lands during that window, the branch is behind=1 again, and the merge refuses. The mayor is the thing staling it.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKS: clear the whole queue first, THEN update-branch, THEN merge NOTHING and PUSH NOTHING until its CI completes. A nominal 'this PR has priority' makes it worse, because priority without an empty window just means more attempts against a moving base. That inversion — merge everything else FIRST so the straggler gets a genuinely empty window — is the counterintuitive part.

WHEN TO STOP: this cost far more attention than the PR was worth (a docs/bench change). If a PR refuses more than about three times and nothing else is blocked on it, shelve it and merge it opportunistically when the tree is quiet for other reasons. Persistence on a blocked item is its own kind of gold-plating.

A PRECEDENT IS A CONCLUSION, NOT A SENTENCE TO COPY — and copying one writes a new falsehood (2026-08-05, learned on rf2-j4bg3).

WHAT I BRIEFED: rf2-e28wl had fixed the ambient-refusal row by STATING THE RULE rather than enumerating operations - "the category is defined by the DOOR, because every ambient resolution goes through require-current-frame!". I told the next worker to follow that precedent on the sibling row.

WHY THAT WAS WRONG, and it is not a near miss: THE REFUSAL ROW CAN SAY "ONE DOOR" BECAUSE THERE IS EXACTLY ONE. Absence has FIVE EMIT PATHS ACROSS THREE NAMESPACES AND 56 CALL SITES - require-current-frame! (21), require-frame-stamp! (27, the carried-stamp seam covering framework fx, timers, HTTP replies, history listeners, SSR hydration and machine lifecycle, WHICH CAN NEVER BE REFUSED because it never consults the resolver), require-frame-provider-target! (8), plus re-frame.ui.frames/resolve-frame which builds the payload and calls the emitter DIRECTLY, bypassing all three, and re-frame.resources' flat throw-error! guards. The worker contracted the CONDITION instead, with primitives as illustration.

SO THE PRECEDENT WAS "DO NOT ENUMERATE WHAT IS OPEN - STATE WHAT IS INVARIANT". The SENTENCE that expressed it was true only of the sibling. Had the worker copied it, the row would have asserted a single door where five exist, which is a WORSE error than the enumeration it replaced, because it reads as authoritative.

THE RULE FOR MY BRIEFS: cite a precedent by its REASONING and the problem it solved, never by its wording, and say explicitly that the wording may not transfer. "Do the same here IF the defect is the same" was in the brief and is what saved it - the worker checked. Without that clause I would have shipped a falsehood through a worker doing exactly as told.

RELATED, SAME BEAD: I also told it to follow the sibling's payload-key fix. It found the right move was WORDING, NOT A KEY - 009's own Dispatch-correlation section already states :rf.trace/parent-dispatch-id is :rf.event/dispatched-only, so the rows CONTRADICTED THEIR OWN DOCUMENT, and HandlerScope has no parent slot to thread. And it DECLINED the audit's :recovery finding on measurement: 134 active rows list that key, so striking it from two would make them the odd ones out - the very deliberate-distinction trap the bead argues against.

PROBE A BEAD NOTES FIELD WITH bd show --json, AND NEVER LET THE PROBE STRING CROSS A NEWLINE (2026-09-01, mayor session 9a; refined twice in one session).

CLAUDE.md says to confirm an --append-notes landed by probing for known content at start, middle and end. There are TWO ways to get that probe wrong, and both report data loss that did not happen -- the alarming direction, whose documented remedy is to reconstruct from a git checkpoint, which would DUPLICATE an intact note.

TRAP ONE, the renderer. bd show renders notes into a fixed-width column and LINE-WRAPS. Any probe longer than the wrap width straddles an inserted newline and cannot match however intact the data is. Measured: two of three probes returned 0 through bd show; the raw field via bd show --json measured 10858 chars with all five probes returning 1.

TRAP TWO, YOUR OWN SOURCE, and it SURVIVES the fix for trap one. Reading the raw field does not help if the probe string spans a newline you typed yourself. Prose written with hard line wrapping contains real newlines, so a probe copied from a rendered version of your own sentence crosses one. Measured on a note appended minutes after trap one was recorded: probe "only ever decided the fate of dead code" returned 0, while the raw field held "0dcoa only\never decided the fate of dead code." -- present, correct, and unmatchable. Two other probes on the same note returned 1, which is what makes the single zero read as partial truncation.

THE RULE: read the RAW field (bd show --json, which returns a LIST -- index [0]), and choose probe strings that cannot contain a newline. A distinctive fragment of a SINGLE line is the right unit -- roughly three to six words -- not a whole clause. If a probe returns 0, find the fragment with a substring search and print its neighbourhood before concluding anything: str.find plus a slice settles it in one command.

WHY BOTH TRAPS ARE THE SAME ERROR: a probe is an instrument that can answer "nothing here", and any such instrument gives that answer when misused, with no error raised. Trap one measures the renderer instead of the data; trap two measures your line breaks instead of the content. Neither is a fact about bd. And a length comparison is not the fallback -- chunked appends shift lengths by a byte or two, which CLAUDE.md already warns about.

PRODUCTION BYTES — a var whose :doc is REIFIED by a #' read ships its docstring into the :advanced bundle.
