Roughly one reopen per merged PR looked like an immovable property of running an audit; a meaningful share of it is gate beads closed on arming rather than on catching. That is fixable from my side.

WHEN A GUARD IS WARRANTED UNDER "TRUST THE PROGRAMMER" — the principle that reconciles three decisions I made today (2026-07-26).

The three look contradictory on their face:
  1. rf2-bk7z5 — CLOSED, refusing to validate :role against its documented closed set.
  2. rf2-8o66x — DEFERRED, refusing a performance regression gate.
  3. The empty-export finding — FILED, asking for a row floor in the pre-commit hook.

Two refusals and one request, all under the same posture. The distinguishing principle is not size, cost or priority. It is:

  A GUARD IS WARRANTED WHEN THE FAILURE IS SILENT AND HAS ALREADY HAPPENED. IT IS NOT WARRANTED WHEN THE PROGRAMMER CAN SEE THE FAILURE, OR WHEN THE FAILURE CANNOT OCCUR.

Applied:
  1. :role validation — the failure CANNOT OCCUR. Every producer is in-namespace; no caller can pass an invalid role. Enforcing it adds a failure mode, a message to maintain and a test to keep green, and catches nothing. That is a nag-diagnostic.
  2. The perf gate — the failure would be NOISE, not signal. The no-substrate floor drifted 37% across rounds, larger than most effects being measured, so the gate would red on nothing. And a false red is expensive here precisely because the standing rule is that a failing test on a touched surface is never a flake.
  3. The row floor — the failure IS SILENT AND HAS HAPPENED TWICE, six weeks apart, by the same mechanism. An empty tracker with a CLEAN git status is exactly what a programmer cannot see. That is not distrust; it is the only way the fact becomes visible at all.

SO "TRUST THE PROGRAMMER" IS NOT "ASSUME NOTHING GOES WRONG". It is: DO NOT GUARD AGAINST WHAT THE PROGRAMMER CAN ALREADY SEE. A loud crash needs no guard — it is already a signal. A wrong value that renders visibly needs no guard. What needs a guard is the state that looks correct: an empty file with a clean status, a gate green on a defect it was built to catch, a test armed on two lanes and selected by neither.

THE COROLLARY IS THE ONE I HAVE BEEN UNDER-USING: this principle is also a REJECTION criterion with teeth. Most proposed guards fail it, because most proposed failures are either impossible or loud. Ask which of the three cases a proposal is in before pricing it, and the answer usually decides the bead without further analysis.

AND IT EXPLAINS WHY THE ERGONOMICS CLAUSE IS A DETECTOR RATHER THAN A BRAKE: a bad diagnostic is the same defect class inverted. The failure IS visible, but it points somewhere useless — an author told to add a key the source already has, or handed a JSON encoding error naming a reified malli class. That is a signal that lies rather than a signal that is missing, and both are worth fixing where a merely-absent convenience is not.

WHERE A FINDING BELONGS WHEN ITS PREMISE IS AN OPEN RULING (2026-07-25, articulated by the R6 worker and worth adopting): a finding whose premise depends on how an OPEN P1 gets ruled belongs on the PR, NOT in the tracker, until that ruling lands.

Concrete case: R6's guide audit found seven canonical recipes omitting an explicit {:sensitive ...} map and recorded the roster on its PR rather than filing beads. rf2-kqxe6.20 then shipped option A — the framework retains its own carrier classification — and the finding DISSOLVED COMPLETELY: those seven recipes had been describing the correct spelling all along; the framework was what needed fixing. `.claude/commands/*.md` AND `CLAUDE.md` ARE GATED — BY check_readme_links.py, NOT by check_doc_slugs.py (2026-08-11, rf2-j689 / PR #7887).

I HAVE BRIEFED THIS WRONG. Twice in one day I told a worker that `.claude/commands/*.md` "may have no automated gate at all" and to verify by hand. That is false, and the worker on rf2-j689 established the real mapping at source:

- `scripts/check_readme_links.py` OWNS repo-root markdown — its docstring names `CLAUDE.md` — and, per rf2-1yy75, also resolves markdown path references inside `.claude/commands/*.md`.
- `scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` EXPLICITLY DOES NOT COVER `CLAUDE.md`. Its own notes warn that briefs have nominated it and received a GREEN EXIT VERIFYING NOTHING — the precise fail-open defect this project spends its days hunting, arriving through the brief rather than through the code.
- `docs/the-mayor-method/` IS inside the mkdocs site build (proved by `python -m mkdocs build --strict` producing `site/the-mayor-method/`), and `check_doc_slugs.py` enrols that tree explicitly via FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES.

THE COVERAGE IS REAL BUT NARROW, and the worker proved the boundary rather than assuming it. Its FIRST negative control was INVALID and it said so instead of burying it: a bogus `scripts/*.sh` path planted in `mayor-merge.md` was NOT flagged, exit 0, because the resolver matches `.md` references only. Re-run with a `.md` path, it failed correctly and named the file and line. So the gate catches broken MARKDOWN references in those files and nothing else — it will not notice a wrong command string, a broken shell path, or prose that contradicts itself.

WHAT TO PUT IN A BRIEF FROM NOW ON, for a diff touching CLAUDE.md or .claude/commands/**:
  Run `python scripts/check_readme_links.py` — it owns repo-root markdown and resolves `.md` references inside `.claude/commands/*.md`. Do NOT nominate `check_doc_slugs.py` for `CLAUDE.md`; it does not cover it and exits green having verified nothing. Prove the gate reaches your file with a negative control that breaks a MARKDOWN reference — a broken script path will not be caught, and a control that fails to fail proves nothing.

Windows unclean-shutdown can ZERO-FILL .git/config (12KB of \0), breaking ALL git ('fatal: bad config line 1'). Diagnose: od -c .git/config shows all \0; scan .git top-level for other all-null files (only config was hit). A WITNESS DERIVED FROM THE FIX INHERITS THE FIX'S BLIND SPOTS — five instances in one session (2026-08-10/11, hicasso).

THE SHAPE: a test or table whose STATED SCOPE EXCEEDS THE CASES IT ACTUALLY DRIVES. Each was green, each was honest, each claimed more than it checked.

1. rf2-hic-020 — a runtime/kit parity table claiming both arms of the raw escape, driving only the VALID raw component.
2. rf2-hic-007 — a completeness test claiming all six constructor fields unforgeable, running only where declaring! had already supplied real values; outside every extent the guarantee did not hold.
3. rf2-hic-012 — a comment recording the EXPECTED result as though it were the measured one, contradicted by the very row it annotated.
4. rf2-hic-021 — a round-trip check whose both directions ranged over ids THAT EXIST, so thirteen taught refusals with no id at all satisfied it VACUOUSLY (fail-open).
5. rf2-hic-022 — a shadow-detection walker whose letfn arm reads [nm params] and collects params only when the second node is a VECTOR; in multi-arity letfn it is a LIST, so every arity is missed. PR body and README both claimed letfn was covered.

WHY IT RECURS, and it is not carelessness: the witness is written FROM the fix, so it drives the shapes the author had in mind while fixing. The shapes that break it are exactly the ones the author did not think of — the same set. Test-after-fix is structurally biased toward passing.

THE COUNTERMEASURE, now standing in briefs: DERIVE THE WITNESS FROM THE GRAMMAR OF THE THING, NOT FROM THE FIX. Enumerate the legal shapes of the construct (for letfn: single-arity vector, multi-arity lists, docstring/prepost variants) and drive each. Require the PR body to state which shapes of the grammar were driven AND which were not — the second list is the valuable one, and writing it is what surfaces the gap.

SISTER RULE: see sweep-generator-defines-reachable-failure-directions — a generator's excluded shapes make a whole error DIRECTION invisible. Same disease at a different scale: coverage is defined by what the instrument can express, not by how much of it you ran.

A DEFECT-WITNESS TEST AND ITS FIX ARE MUTUALLY INVALIDATING — merging both without flipping the witness REDS MAIN, in either order. Cost a P0 red-on-main on 2026-07-24.

THE MECHANISM: a validation pilot reproduces a known hazard and writes it down as a LIVE TEST asserting the CURRENT (broken) behaviour. A separate slice FIXES that hazard. Each PR is green against a main lacking the other. Merge both and the witness test fails, because the defect it documents no longer exists.

THE CONCRETE CASE: the dropdown pilot independently reproduced the ref-composition hazard and shipped `a-behavior-and-a-top-layer-state-on-one-element-lose-a-ref` — a test that PASSES ONLY WHILE THE BUG IS PRESENT. I merged the pilot, then merged the ref-composition fix, and main went red with 2 failures. Every other gate stayed green, so it read like a mystery regression in a slice that had been CLEAN as a PR.

⚠️ WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH A MEMORY IS THAT I HAD ALREADY IDENTIFIED THE PATTERN AND FAILED TO APPLY IT. Days earlier I wrote into a different brief: "both pilots assert the current REFUSAL in a test, so the blocked cell re-opens loudly. THOSE ASSERTIONS WILL START FAILING WHEN YOU SUCCEED — update them deliberately as part of this slice." I understood it for the compiled-browser refusal and did not carry it to the very next fix I merged. Recognising a hazard in one place does not transfer it to another unless it becomes a CHECK.

THE CHECK, now standing — BEFORE MERGING ANY FIX, ASK: does a merged test currently ASSERT THE DEFECT THIS FIXES? If yes, the flip belongs in the SAME PR as the fix, or main goes red the moment both are in.
  git grep -l "<hazard keyword>" implementation/**/test/
Pilot and validation suites are the usual home, because documenting current-state honestly is exactly what they are FOR.

THE REPAIR IS A FLIP, NOT A DELETE, and it has three parts:
  1. Assert the FIXED behaviour positively (both participants ran), never loosen to tolerate either outcome — that discards the only coverage of the combination.
  2. RENAME the test. A name asserting the opposite of its body is a trap for the next reader.
  3. Sweep for SIBLING witnesses in the same suite rather than discovering them one merge at a time.

⚠️ AND THE DIAGNOSTIC LESSON: the failure looked like a regression in the fix. The worker got it right by READING CI OWN LOG for the failing test NAME and MESSAGE — the name said "lose-a-ref" and the message said "one of the two refs was lost", which is the test DOCUMENTING a defect, not detecting one. A test name that describes a BUG rather than a PROPERTY is the tell. My own grep for the failure lines used a pattern chosen before I knew what the output looked like and returned only the namespace roster — capture the log to a file and read it.

GENERAL FORM: this WILL recur wherever validation pilots run alongside active development, which is the whole point of running them. It is a property of the arrangement, not a mistake by either author.

WORKER 'BACKGROUND-GATES-THEN-END-TURN' PATTERN: several workers (xray-tail, m90brg-finish, schemas-5a5qwp) did the full implementation + committed-or-staged it, then spawned their gate runs (npm run test:cljs, JVM suites) as BACKGROUND tasks and ENDED THEIR TURN saying 'I'll pick up when the background tests report' — leaving the work uncommitted/unpushed with the bead still IN_PROGRESS. The harness fires a completion notification but there's no PR. RECOGNITION: worker 'completed' but result says 'background test runs still executing / I'll wait for completion' + worktree shows modified>0, commits/pushed=0. RECOVERY (fast, no work lost): SendMessage-resume the SAME agent → tell it to run gates in the FOREGROUND (wait inline), commit, rebase, push, gh pr create, bd close. Its WIP survives. PREVENTION: put 'run gates in the FOREGROUND — do NOT background them or end your turn waiting on a background task' in dispatch briefs (already added to recent ones; the pattern still recurs, so keep the resume-recovery reflex). NOT a stall — the work is done, just the push step remains.

READ A WORKER'S LIVENESS CLOCK IN ITS OWN METADATA DIRECTORY, NOT AT <worktree>/.git -- AND ALWAYS PRINT THE DATE (2026-08-23, two sweeps wrong on the first, one on the second).

TRAP 1 -- THE PATH. In a LINKED git worktree, .git is a FILE containing "gitdir: <path>", not a directory. So "find <worktree>/.git -maxdepth 1 -type f -printf %T@" measures the mtime of that one-line pointer and reports it as the worker's metadata clock. It fails quiet: a plausible timestamp comes back, no error. MEASURED: on worktree pr-audit-8445 the wrong form read 2026-08-23 03:13:05 while the real gitdir clock was 21:14:02 -- an 18-hour error, in the direction that reads as DEATH. I nearly recorded a live, actively-fetching worker as quiescent.

RESOLUTION: gd=$(git -C "$wt" rev-parse --git-dir); find "$gd" -type f -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS %f\n' | sort -r | head. For a linked worktree that resolves to <main>/.git/worktrees/<name>/, holding that worktree's OWN FETCH_HEAD, HEAD, index and ORIG_HEAD.

TRAP 2 -- THE FORMAT. Printing %TH:%TM without %TY-%Tm-%Td makes a four-week-old file read as tonight. MEASURED: three frozen husks printed "20:45" beside a live worker's "22:07" in the same table, and the 20:45 was 2026-07-25. The conclusion survived only because the number contradicted an earlier reading and I re-measured with dates. In a liveness table -- where the whole question is how old something is -- a bare time is not a timestamp. ALWAYS carry the date.

WHICH FILE ANSWERS WHAT, measured on pr-audit-8445:
* FETCH_HEAD -- moves on every fetch, so it is the POLLING clock. Movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration; stillness proves nothing. Read it twice 30-60s apart.
* index -- moves when the worker actually stages work. Its index wrote at 11:41:02 and the commit "chore(beads): audit PR #8721" landed at 11:43:26, two minutes later. That gap VALIDATES index-mtime as the "is it producing?" clock, distinct from the fetch clock.

THE METHOD TREE ALREADY SAYS THE FIRST HALF, better than I was practising it: the fetch-head file lives in "that item's OWN metadata directory, which each linked worktree gets its own copy of", and "movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration". Both failures were mine, not the document's, so the repair is this memory rather than more text in the tree.

DO NOT confuse the mayor's .git/FETCH_HEAD with the worker's. Both move; only the worker's proves the WORKER is alive. Check the path you actually measured.

MEASURING WHETHER A WORKER IS ALIVE: compare the TIP REVISION ID, never a commit count (2026-08-13, corrected same day by an audit).

BE PRECISE ABOUT WHICH COUNT — the first version of this memory was wrong and the error reached main:
  git rev-list --count <branch>              counts EVERY reachable commit. Measured 21677.
                                             REBASING ONTO AN ADVANCED TRUNK MAKES THIS GROW. Not invariant.
  git rev-list --count origin/main..<branch> the AHEAD count. Measured 3.
                                             INVARIANT under rebase — the same commits are replayed.

The ahead count is the one a mayor naturally reads, and it is the one that misleads.

WHAT MOVES AND WHAT DOES NOT, under rebase:
  ahead count        NO
  %ar author date    NO
  %cr committer date YES
  tip revision id    YES

So record the tip id each tick and compare ids. Committer date is a usable second signal.

AN UNCHANGED TIP AUTHORISES NOTHING ON ITS OWN. That half is load-bearing: it is what stopped a healthy worker being called stranded across two ticks. The next step after an unchanged tip is to MESSAGE, and the reply shape is the real read — 'queued for delivery' means alive, 'had no active task; resumed from transcript' means idle.

SECOND TRAP IN THE SAME MEASUREMENT: do NOT read FETCH_HEAD after a fetch whose exit code you suppressed. Linked worktrees share one .git and therefore one FETCH_HEAD, so a raced or failed fetch leaves a stale value that reads as fresh. Prefer 'git ls-remote --heads origin refs/heads/worker/*' — one command, no shared state, no exit code to check.

WHEN TWO AGENTS DISAGREE ABOUT A COMMIT'S AGE, suspect two clocks before suspecting an error. One reported 75 seconds where another read 43 minutes; one read committer date, the other author date. Neither misread.

WORKER LIVENESS (Windows mayor loop): TaskList can return 'No tasks found' for background agents launched in a PRIOR turn even while they are actively running, AND their output-file mtime does NOT advance during a run (transcript flush is buffered). Both gave false 'dead' signals — a realm worker that TaskList showed as absent + mtime static for 9min actually completed a 624s run. NEVER infer a worker is dead from TaskList/mtime; NEVER recycle/--force-remove a worker's worktree on that basis (it clobbers live workers mid-edit). The ONLY reliable liveness signal is the completion/kill <task-notification>. To recycle, wait for that notification or confirm via a pushed branch with the expected commits.

Background workers and review agents MUST NOT create, claim, or close beads. Beads are mayor action only — filing them makes the mayor think they own the work. Worker outputs go in chat and ai/findings/ (local). Use background workers freely for parallel drafts/research; never bd create for that.

Worker path-leak mechanism (CONFIRMED 2026-07-17, rf2-r09qj + flagged by rf2-klyw5): a subagent that Reads MAYOR-checkout absolute paths during exploration can have its SUBSEQUENT Edit tool-calls carry that mayor path — so edits land in the mayor checkout, NOT the worktree. LESSON: in worker briefs, tell workers to create the PR with a SIMPLE body or '--body-file', avoid backticks/parens/heredocs in the inline body; and if a worker is committed+pushed but PR-less + idle, the mayor can open the PR for it (git -C <wt> push; gh pr create --head <branch>) rather than killing the work.

worker/receipts-hic081 IS NOT STRANDED -- do not delete it, and do not re-file it as hygiene residue (rf2-fuuqd, triaged 2026-08-15).

It is a DELIBERATELY RETAINED spike record. rf2-hic-081 ('Spike: capability receipts') closed with the verdict SPLIT and its close reason ends: 'Spike commits are pushed on worker/receipts-hic081 and retained as the experiment's record; nothing from them lands on main.' The 3 commits are pushed, have no PR and never will -- that is the design, not an oversight.

The conclusions are fully promoted and verified on main: the capability-receipt DESIGN is in docs/design/hicasso/product/specification.md, decision-brief.md and lanes/left-field-ideas.md (rf2-eoo9, PR #7898); the erasure-gate reachability rule is in check_production_erasure.cjs and siblings (rf2-nkr3, PR #7878); impl/receipt.cljs is correctly ABSENT from main.

THE GENERAL LESSON for the hygiene loop: 'pushed + unlanded + no PR' is a heuristic, not a verdict. Before filing a branch as stranded, check whether a CLOSED bead retained it on purpose -- spike branches are the class where the finding lands on main and the diff deliberately never does.

Worker recovery hazard (learned 2026-06-22, the #4910/#4913 xray-testbeds incident): (1) A worker coming to rest is NOT proof it finished. The xray-testbeds worker came to rest waiting on a gate it launched; the mayor misjudged it as done, committed its UNCOMMITTED partial work as a recovery PR (#4910) — but it had not yet written standard_epochs/core.cljs, so #4910 merged an incomplete state that crashed the two-frame surface on load and left a red gate on main. RULE: only recover/commit a worker's work after a genuine final report with a PR URL; an idle worktree mid-task is not a completion signal. (2) NEVER git worktree remove --force a worktree whose worker may still be live — it destroyed the live worker's workspace AND emptied the mayor implementation/node_modules via the node_modules junction cascade (the worker had to npm install to restore the mayor tree). RULE: only remove a worktree for a worker that has genuinely completed (final report received); the junction-rmdir-before-remove step does not protect against removing a still-active worktree.

"WORKTREE-LOCAL" IS ONLY HALF THE RULE FOR WORKER SCRATCH FILES — IT MUST ALSO BE GITIGNORED (2026-08-09).

THE SEQUENCE. Earlier in the day two concurrent workers overwrote each other's helper files and PR-body drafts in the SHARED scratchpad, and one nearly published another bead's PR body. The fix put into later briefs was "write every file you create inside your own worktree". Both workers complied exactly. Both worktrees then REFUSED to reap: REMOVE_REFUSED_DIRTY, each holding one untracked pr-body-<bead>.md that the disposability classifier will not accept as build output.

SO THE TWO HAZARDS TRADE OFF AND THE BRIEF MUST CLOSE BOTH. dispatch-prompt-template.md already says it: put EVERY gate artefact where git ignores it, and warns that one leftover is enough to make a tree unreapable (nine accumulated that way once). The ignored extensions are *.log, *.exit and *-exit.txt. A file named pr-body-something.md is worktree-local, safe from collision, and still blocks the reap.

THE COMPLETE INSTRUCTION FOR A DISPATCH BRIEF: write every file you create inside your own worktree AND give it an ignored name (*.log / *.exit), or delete it before you report done. Never a shared temp directory; never an unignored leftover.

RESOLVING IT WHEN IT HAPPENS IS CHEAP BUT MUST NOT BE BLIND. --dry-run prints each offending path tagged [KEEP] or [build output]; a PR-body draft whose content is already published on the merged PR is genuinely disposable, so --force is correct AFTER looking. Do not reach for --force-disposable (it refuses anything not recognised as build output) and never spray a blanket --force across a sweep list: when that guard was written, one worktree held four analysis files for an OPEN bead and three others carried uncommitted source and doc edits.

A WORKTREE YOU DID NOT EXPLICITLY DISPATCH MAY BE YOUR OWN WORKER SPAWNING A SECOND WORKTREE — not a concurrent session. Misdiagnosed 2026-07-24. I dispatched a 4-bead cluster to ONE worker; it did 3 beads in worktree A (PR one) then created worktree B for the 4th bead (PR two). My hygiene scan found worktree B, had no record of creating it, and I concluded a concurrent session was also dispatching workers. WRONG — it was my own worker branching per bead. THE COST: the false belief made me over-cautious about that surface being externally contested. THE DISCRIMINATOR before concluding concurrent-session: a branch named worker/<desc>-<beadid> whose bead you assigned to a live worker IS that worker, even as a second worktree. Check worker completion reports and open PRs first — a worker report names every worktree and PR it created. Track by BEAD ownership (who did I give this bead to), never by worktree count: one worker is NOT necessarily one worktree or one PR. The genuinely-separate process here (the pr-audit loop) FILES beads, it does not dispatch code-editing workers, so it never contests a code surface. No harm done — I correctly did not touch the worktree or re-dispatch the bead.

A WORKER STRANDS BY ENDING ITS TURN ON A BACKGROUNDED GATE, AND IT WILL DO IT REPEATEDLY UNLESS THE BRIEF SAYS HOW TO WAIT. Observed again 2026-08-08 on rf2-2rtt6.142, twice in a row after a resume.

THE SHAPE. A gate exceeds the tool's foreground time ceiling. The worker detaches it — correctly — and then ENDS ITS TURN "waiting" for a completion notification. Nothing is guaranteed to wake it. It reports "still progressing, continuing to wait", the turn ends, and the same thing happens on the next nudge. The work is usually fine; only the waiting is broken.

WHAT DOES NOT FIX IT: telling the worker again that gates must be foreground. It already believes that, which is exactly why it detached and then waited politely. The instruction it is missing is what to do INSTEAD of waiting.

WHAT FIXES IT — put this in every brief, not just the ones with long gates:
  "If a gate exceeds the tool's time ceiling, run it detached and BLOCK ON IT INSIDE THE SAME TURN by polling its exit file in a loop. Never end a turn with a gate outstanding."
and give the literal shape:
  for i in $(seq 1 240); do [ -f gate-<id>.exit ] && break; sleep 15; done; cat gate-<id>.exit

TWO RIDERS THAT MATTER AS MUCH AS THE LOOP:
- The detached invocation must use an ABSOLUTE path to the gate script. These scripts derive their repo root from BASH_SOURCE, and a relative invocation that gets detached adopts whatever cwd the shell really has — one did that inside ANOTHER live worker's checkout and produced a complete, internally consistent verdict about somebody else's diff. Check the run's "gate root:" first line names your own worktree.
- If the invocation writes no exit file at all, that is the real defect, not the waiting. Re-run as: sh <ABS>/scripts/test-fast-pr.sh > g.log 2>&1; echo "$?" > g.exit

MAYOR-SIDE RECOVERY, cheap and reliable: check the ground truth yourself rather than nudging twice. `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` and a remote-vs-local sha comparison in the worktree tell you whether the work is durable; `ls *.log *.exit` plus the log's mtime tell you whether the gate is genuinely still running or dead. On this occasion the work was already committed AND pushed, so nothing was at risk — the only outstanding step was reading an exit code.

DO NOT MISREAD THE SPINE LOG WHILE CHECKING. test-fast-pr.sh prints lines like "ok  unexpected extra dependency -> FAILED" from a negative-test harness confirming its own mutations fail correctly. Those are PASSES. The verdict is the echoed exit code, never a line in the log.

WORKER TRAP — git mv then edit (2026-07-25, found by the misc-cluster-a worker on PR #6946): after 'git mv old.cljc new_cljs_test.cljc', a subsequent 'git add <path>' does NOT pick up content edits made after the mv. The worker's first pushed commit therefore carried the RENAMED file with the OLD ns name still inside it — a commit that would not compile. It was caught only by noticing a stray 'M' in git status, then fixed by rebuilding both commits from the base and force-pushing with --force-with-lease. This is the exact shape of the rf2-dn6v7 / rf2-lgozq lane-suffix work (rename file + edit ns in one change), so it will recur. Put in briefs for any rename-plus-edit bead: after a git mv, re-run 'git add' on the path AFTER the content edit, and verify with 'git diff --cached' that BOTH the rename and the content change are staged before committing; a rename-only commit of a .cljc test file is a non-compiling commit.

A FRESH WORKER WORKTREE CANNOT RUN THE FAST-PR SPINE'S NODE TIER WITHOUT THE node_modules JUNCTION (measured 2026-08-13).

A worker on a clean worktree captured exit 1 at 'FAIL CLJS node integration' with 'Cannot find module shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js'. Nothing in its diff could reach shadow-cljs resolution. THE CAUSE WAS THE MISSING implementation/node_modules. Creating the junction turned the SAME spine green with no source change.

SO THE BRIEF'S INSTRUCTION 'run scripts/test-fast-pr.sh' IS INCOMPLETE for a doc-only worker that never expected to need npm. The failure looks like a real red, and a worker that trusts it will hunt a defect that does not exist - or worse, report a red PR as blocked.

SAY THIS IN BRIEFS THAT NOMINATE THE SPINE: if the node tier fails on module resolution, create the implementation/node_modules junction, re-run, and REMOVE THE LINK with cmd /c rmdir as your last act. Never a recursive delete - it follows the junction and empties the mayor's real tree, which has happened twice. Re-verify the canary with the script's own instrument either side.

THE SAME WORKER ALSO HIT THE HARNESS-DISAGREEMENT TRAP ON THAT RUN, which is the sixteenth observed instance: the harness reported 'completed (exit code 0)' while the runner's own .exit file read 1. It quoted the file. Had it trusted the harness it would have shipped a red spine as green. EVERY observed disagreement so far has surfaced as a harness-reported 0.

A FRESH WORKER WORKTREE HAS NO `implementation/node_modules`, AND THE SPINE FAILS ENVIRONMENTALLY THERE — the harness then misreports it (2026-08-11, rf2-gxry).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker ran `scripts/test-fast-pr.sh` in a newly-created worktree. It captured exit **1** on `CLJS node integration`, with `Cannot find module 'shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js'` — nothing compiled, because the worktree had no `node_modules`. **The harness announced "completed (exit code 0)" against that captured 1.** The worker junctioned `node_modules` at the mayor's real one, deleted the stale `.exit` and `.log`, re-ran the gate whole, and captured **0** with `[:node-test] Build completed. (2307 files, 2306 compiled, 0 warnings)`.

THE HAZARD IS NOT THE FAILURE, IT IS THE SHAPE OF IT. A missing-module error is not a test failure, but it PRESENTS as a red gate, and if a worker reads the harness's number instead of the captured one it presents as a GREEN gate over a build that never ran. Both readings are wrong in opposite directions, and the second is the dangerous one: a green that compiled nothing.

WHAT TO PUT IN A BRIEF for any worker that will run a compiling gate:
  - A fresh worktree has NO `implementation/node_modules`. If a gate needs one, create the junction to the mayor's real tree, and REMOVE THE LINK (never its target) as your last act — a later `git worktree remove` follows it and empties the shared tree. Canary the mayor's count before and after.
  - `Cannot find module` or `command not found` from a gate is ENVIRONMENTAL, not a verdict. Fix the environment and RE-RUN THE GATE WHOLE. Do not report the first number, and do not report it as a failure of the diff.
  - DELETE the stale `.exit` and `.log` before the re-run. A stale `.exit` survives the next run's `>` on its log, so the pair can disagree and the older verdict is the one you quote.

TWELFTH SIGHTING TODAY of the harness reporting a captured 1 as exit 0. The rule stands and is now in the method: THE NUMBER YOU QUOTE IS THE ONE YOU CAPTURED.

Worker worktrees have NO node_modules, so browser/shadow-cljs gates cannot run there by default. Do NOT junction into the mayor checkout's node_modules to fix it — that is the configuration that destroyed the mayor's real node_modules once and nearly again. THE SAFE ANSWER IS `npm ci` INSIDE THE WORKTREE (one worker did exactly this today, exit 0, no junction created, canary unmoved). Cost is a few minutes; the alternative is deferring every browser gate to CI. Put this in any brief whose gate menu includes `npm run test:browser`, a shadow-cljs build, or an adapter testbed spec.cjs — otherwise the worker hits 'shadow-cljs is not recognized', concludes the gate is unrunnable, and defers coverage that actually matters (the real-DOM gate catches repaint bugs test:cljs structurally cannot see). Related: [[windows-junction-detection-two-wrong-answers-before-the]].

Workers can get stuck in a monitor-wait loop on slow test suites (rul3ov burned ~770K tokens over 3 segments re-arming a Monitor for the full CLJS conformance run before committing). Recovery: SendMessage the agentId with a firm 'do NOT arm another Monitor — commit FIRST, push, gh pr create NOW; CI runs the full suite so CI is the gate, not your local terminal.' Over-cautious 'won't PR until local green' is the anti-pattern; the PR's CI is the real gate.

CONCURRENT WORKERS SHARE THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD AND OVERWRITE EACH OTHER'S FILES — including PR bodies (2026-08-09).

WHAT HAPPENED. Six workers ran in parallel on the hic-* Wave A set. The rf2-hic-004 worker reported that its verify.py and pr-body.md were BOTH overwritten mid-run by the rf2-hic-005 worker. Same filenames, same shared scratchpad directory. Its PR body survived only because gh had already read the file before the overwrite landed. A slower run would have published another bead's PR body under its own PR number.

WHY THE EXISTING RULE DID NOT COVER IT. The brief said 'use worktree-local log paths', and every worker complied FOR GATE LOGS — they all wrote gate-slugs.log inside their own worktree. The collision was in the HELPER FILES nobody thought to fence: scratch scripts, PR-body drafts, temp verification output. The known hazard was written narrowly as a gate-log hazard; it is really a shared-temp-directory hazard and applies to every file a worker writes outside its worktree.

THE FIX FOR FUTURE BRIEFS. Say: write EVERY file you create - gate logs, helper scripts, PR-body drafts, scratch output - inside your own worktree, never in a shared temp or scratchpad directory. If you must use a shared directory, prefix every filename with your bead id.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A WRONG GATE LOG. A clobbered gate log yields a plausible-but-wrong exit code, which the echo-the-exit-code rule catches. A clobbered PR body is published verbatim to GitHub under the wrong PR and nothing checks it.

THREE WORKERS IN ONE NIGHT STALLED WAITING FOR A "COMPLETION NOTIFICATION" THAT DOES NOT EXIST (2026-08-10).

WHAT THEY EACH DID. rf2-8a6s: "Still running. I'll stop here and resume when the watcher fires - no more polling." rf2-hic-009: "The spine is still running ... I have a waiter armed on its exit code and will report the moment it lands." rf2-hic-016: "The fast-PR spine is still running; I'll wait for its completion notification rather than end the turn" - and then the turn ended. All three had briefs that said, in terms, run gates in the foreground to completion and never background one.

THE BELIEF IS SPECIFIC AND WRONG, WHICH IS WHY THE EXISTING WORDING DOES NOT PREVENT IT. They do not think they are abandoning the task. They think a watcher/notification will wake them. Nothing does. A stopped subagent resumes ONLY when the mayor sends it a message, and the mayor only knows to because the completion report reads oddly. "Run gates in the foreground" does not contradict the belief - a worker can believe it ran the gate in the foreground AND that something will tell it the answer later.

THE WORDING THAT ADDRESSES THE BELIEF, not the behaviour: "There is no completion notification. No watcher wakes a stopped worker. If you end your turn waiting for a gate, the task stops until a human notices. Run the gate in the foreground, block on it, read its exit code yourself. A long foreground gate is fine; an unfinished turn is not."

THE REAL COST IS UNPUSHED WORK, AND IT VARIES. rf2-8a6s had committed AND pushed - fully durable, only the PR was missing. rf2-hic-009 had pushed and opened a PR - only the spine result and PR body were missing. rf2-hic-016 had THREE COMMITS AND HAD NOT PUSHED - one lost worktree from losing an entire three-engine browser suite. So the recovery order is: check `git log origin/main..HEAD` and `git ls-remote` FIRST, and if it is unpushed, make PUSH step 1 of the resume message before anything else.

RECOVERY IS CHEAP AND RELIABLE: SendMessage to the agent id resumes it from its transcript with full context. All three resumed and continued correctly. Do not re-dispatch a fresh worker - it would redo work that is already committed.

DETECTION: a completion report that says "still running", "I'll report when", "waiting for", or "watcher armed" is a stall, not a status. Treat it as a resume trigger immediately, and check push state before replying.

Workers strand because the long gate outlives their TURN budget, not because they disobeyed 'run foreground'. Three workers in one session (dispatch-sync, ci-test-lanes, tags-ratchet) ended their turn mid-gate with 'Waiting on the spine/watcher' — commits pushed, NO PR, nothing mergeable. A brief that says 'run test-fast-pr.sh foreground to completion, THEN open the PR' makes stranding likely on a loaded box, because the spine can exceed the budget. BETTER BRIEF ORDER: commit -> run only the FOCUSED, fast, arm-specific gates (plus any non-vacuity/mutation proof, which is cheap and is the evidence that actually matters) -> OPEN THE PR -> name the slow gates as 'deferred to CI' in the ## Quality gates section. CI runs the same surface and IS the merge gate; the local spine never was. Recovery is SendMessage-resume, which works and keeps the worker's context.

Workflow rule (Mike, 2026-06-10): beads marked in_progress are LOCKED - never update their title/description/notes/scope (a worker is executing against them). To add findings or scope to in-progress work, CREATE A FOLLOW-UP BEAD (dep on the in-progress one if sequenced). Check status with bd show before any bd update.

`git worktree add` CAN BE KILLED BY THE HARNESS FOREGROUND TIMEOUT MID-CHECKOUT, LEAVING A STALE LOCK (2026-08-11; hit by two workers in one tick).

This repo's checkout is ~5308 files, and a fresh `git worktree add` can exceed the harness's 2-minute foreground limit. When it is killed partway (~25% in one observed case) it leaves BOTH a stale `.git/worktrees/<name>/index.lock` AND a `locked` marker reading `initializing`. The worktree exists, is registered, and is unusable; the guard script fails.

RECOVERY, in this order:
1. remove `.git/worktrees/<name>/index.lock`
2. `git reset --hard HEAD` from inside the worktree, BACKGROUNDED - it re-runs the full checkout and took ~9 minutes on this box
3. `git worktree unlock <path>`
Then the worker guard passes normally.

PUT THE MITIGATION IN THE DISPATCH BRIEF: every brief I write opens with `git worktree add`, so this is a first-command failure that costs a worker ten minutes before it has done anything. Tell workers to run the create BACKGROUNDED by absolute path and poll, exactly as they are already told to do for the 25-minute test spine - the same 10-minute ceiling applies to it and nobody expects it to.

Two workers hit this in a single tick (thirdsite-fbi4 and presence-5gka), so it is not rare. Both recovered without data loss, and both reported it rather than silently retrying - which is what made it diagnosable.

Worktree cleanup: a directory can be REUSED and re-pointed at a different branch mid-session, so a name-based safe-list goes stale while you are acting on it. Observed live: a hygiene agent was handed 'ci-test-lanes-cluster - safe to remove, PR #7116 merged', but between the list being written and the removal, a worker reused that same directory on a NEW branch (worker/xray-fuzzy-regression-pin) carrying an open PR #7119. Removing by name would have destroyed an in-flight PR worktree. Re-read `git worktree list --porcelain` IMMEDIATELY BEFORE each removal and re-verify the branch AND its PR state at that moment; never trust a safe-list compiled minutes earlier. Corollary: 'PR merged' is a fact about a BRANCH, not about a DIRECTORY. Related: [[rebase-merge-makes-a-worker-branch-look-unmerged]].

Worktree hygiene: `git status` ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH to decide whether a worktree holds work. The `/ai/` tree is GITIGNORED, so findings docs, gate logs, PR-body drafts and ad-hoc probes are INVISIBLE to git status — a worktree that looks pristine can hold real content. Sweep `ai/` (and any `.worker-logs/`, `.wt-logs/`) separately and READ any non-log file before discarding. Observed: three worktrees held hidden content (20 gate logs, a pr-body.md draft, an ad-hoc probe .clj) — all correctly judged residue, but only because they were looked at. Corollary for the other direction: a hygiene brief that says 'clean tree = safe to remove' is wrong on this repo.

A WORKTREE'S INDEX CLOCK MEASURES THAT WORKTREE, NOT THE FUNCTION IT WAS DISPATCHED FOR (2026-08-24, correcting my own reading across ~six sweeps).

WHAT I HAD BEEN SAYING. Every stranded sweep reported the pr-audit worktree as "alive, polling on a ~40s cadence, index still 11:41, so nothing audited since 11:43". The first half is right. The second half quietly asserted that the AUDIT FUNCTION had produced nothing, and that does not follow.

WHAT THE PARENT CHAIN SHOWS.
* 10ade546c4 "audit PR #8721", 11:43:26, parent ebc7e737bd -- which IS that worktree's HEAD and its branch tip. So that commit was made from that revision, and the index write at 11:41:02, two minutes earlier, is genuine evidence of it staging. That inference was sound.
* d1c824098d "audit PR #8730", 01:22 the next morning, parent 3c9e358a0f -- a revision that worktree has NEVER been at (its branch reflog has exactly two entries: created, then one fast-forward to ebc7e737bd, and `git cherry` reads 0 ahead).

SO AUDITS KEPT HAPPENING WHILE THAT WORKTREE DID NOTHING BUT FETCH. Tonight's audit filed a bead against my own merge and pushed a commit, from a checkout at main's tip, not from there. At least two things perform this role, and the worktree I was watching is not the one that has been working.

THE CORRECTION, and it is about the shape of the claim rather than the number: an index mtime is evidence about ONE CHECKOUT. Reading it as a health signal for the capability that checkout was dispatched to provide is a category error, and it fails in the reassuring direction -- "nothing has been audited" was false every time I said it, while the audit was in fact catching my own defects.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE PARENT CHAIN, not the clock: take a commit the function produced and ask whether its PARENT is a revision that checkout has actually been at. Its branch reflog answers that in one command and cannot be faked by a fetch.

STILL TRUE, and worth keeping: FETCH_HEAD movement proves that worktree is alive (measured twice, 40 seconds apart, against a mayor clock that stayed still), and it remains unreapable and unmessageable because no dispatch row records an agent id for it.

THE 'NEVER WRITE THE WORKTREE PATH INTO A COMMITTED FILE' RULE IS NARROWER THAN THE RISK, AND THE CI GATE DOES NOT CLOSE THE GAP (2026-08-18).

Adopted into mayor dispatch practice on the report of the worker on rf2-f5cma, which was fixing that very rule and is the best-placed reader of it.

THE GAP: a PR body and a bead close reason are both DURABLE and PUBLIC, and neither is a committed file. The 'No hardcoded personal/home paths' CI gate does not see either. So a worker that obeys the rule as written can still publish an absolute home path where it persists. That worker kept paths out of both only by extending the rule on its own initiative.

ADOPTED WORDING for every dispatch: report the printed WORKTREE_ROOT to the mayor in your completion message, and never write it, or any absolute home path, into any COMMITTED FILE, PR BODY OR TRACKER TEXT.

AND CARRY THE POSITIVE FORM, which the template now has and my briefs lagged a revision behind: if the deliverable is itself a written record, what makes the guard evidence is that it RAN and exited 0, not the machine-specific path it printed. A worker told only what not to write still has evidence to produce and will improvise something.

SEPARATE OBSERVATION FROM THE SAME REPORT, not yet actioned: the guard prints an MSYS-style root (/c/Users/...) while the boundary block in every brief states the worktree as C:/Users/.... A worker comparing the two LITERALLY sees a mismatch, on the one rule where a directory-level error is expensive. Every worker so far has resolved it from context. If it ever bites, the fix is to state both forms in the boundary block rather than to change either producer.

GENERAL SHAPE: the worker fixing a rule is the best reviewer of the brief that carries it. Ask. Two of the three improvements here came from asking one worker whether its own setup instruction was well worded.

WSL bash.exe DOUBLE-EXPANDS a -c command string. Found by rf2-sefx0 (#6357, 2026-07-18) with a decisive probe: bash -lc with FOO=hello then printf of the escaped dollar-FOO prints the literal dollar-FOO under Git Bash (single pass) but prints hello under WSL bash (an outer pass already substituted it). CONSEQUENCE: any -c string that READS BACK a variable the SAME string assigns is broken under WSL — the outer pass substitutes the not-yet-assigned name to empty. That is how a PATH= assignment referencing a FIXTURE_DIR assigned immediately to its left silently produced /bin:<real PATH>, so stub executables were never found and 15 of 15 cases failed before reaching the code under test. Pre-existing vars (PWD, PATH) survive both passes, which is why the bug looks selective. FIX SHAPE: build one env-prefixed command whose every dollar-NAME already exists in the parent environment; let the child script read the rest from its own environment rather than from the command string. DISPROVED on the way: the semicolon separator is fine, and double-quoting is fine — do not chase those. TESTING LESSON (the important half): a BEHAVIOURAL test for this cannot protect you, because Git Bash and the Ubuntu CI runner both expand ONCE — a reintroduced self-reference stays green on CI while breaking only for Windows contributors. sefx0 pinned the STRUCTURE instead (assert the command references only pre-existing variables) with a non-vacuity guard. Generalise: when a defect is invisible on the platform your CI runs, a structural pin beats a behavioural one.

A RULING DETAIL WAS EMPIRICALLY WRONG: notifications CAN arrive before dispatch returns on the stock-Reagent adapter (found 2026-08-07, rf2-ynved).

THE RULING SAID (item 8) that notifications never arrive before dispatch returns. FALSE on this adapter: :flush-render! is (fn [f] (f) (r/flush)), so dispatch-sync DRAINS THE QUEUE ITSELF. A test written to assert the ruling literally went red.

HOW IT WAS HANDLED, and this is the part to copy: the worker did not quietly conform the test to observed behaviour, and did not quietly conform the docs to the ruling. It reported the ruling was wrong, and changed the DOCS to say the re-feed rides a Reagent flush rather than an inline callback inside the app-db write — while telling the author to code as though it lands on the FOLLOWING commit. That last clause is the useful part: teach the WEAKER guarantee even when the stronger one currently holds, because the stronger one is an implementation detail of one adapter.

SECOND FINDING from the same run: a sibling unmount COMMIT re-runs a surviving tracker against an unchanged value, so the survivor takes one idempotent re-feed. The DOM-free counterpart drives the identical release with NO React commit and sees no duplicate. So it is a property of the commit cycle, not of the recipe — and the assertion was rewritten property-based with the reason recorded.

GENERAL RULE: when a test contradicts a recorded ruling, the ruling is a hypothesis like anything else. Report the contradiction, establish which is true FROM THE ADAPTER SOURCE, and fix whichever is actually wrong. Do not assume the ruling wins; do not assume the observation wins.

title: surface-review(epoch): make strict replay a one-call epoch-id gesture
description:
## Scope

Close the gap between the epoch runtime's recorded replay material and the public/Tool-Pair replay gesture. Cover the smallest coherent slice across `implementation/epoch/**`, the optional core facade/late-bind hook, Pair-MCP runtime/tool wiring, Tool-Pair/API/spec prose, descriptor manifest, and focused CLJ/CLJS/tool tests.

## Findings

- Every ordinary `:rf/epoch-record` already captures the complete ingredients for a faithful strict replay: `:trigger-event`, the post-generation `:rf.cofx` token (including mid-run minted facts), and the envelope's serializable `:fx-overrides` / `:interceptor-overrides`.
- The normative Tool-Pair replay contract requires replay to re-supply all of those fields and hard-wire `:rf.cofx/mint-policy :strict`; missing facts and `:rf/fn-override` must fail loud.
- No epoch public API or late-bind hook performs that gesture from an epoch id. `re-frame.epoch` exposes history, restore, replace, listeners, config, and egress projection; Pair-MCP exposes `restore-epoch`, while its `dispatch {replay true}` merely sets strict mode and requires the caller to copy the event/cofx/override fields manually.
- That manual route is not generally available to an off-box agent: `projected-record` deliberately replaces every `:trigger-event` argument with `:rf/redacted` by default, and `:include-sensitive?` is orthogonal to `:include-event-args?`. Pair-MCP's epoch egress threads only the app-db `include-sensitive` axis, so `trace-window` / `watch-epochs` cannot return the raw arguments needed to replay a normal argument-bearing event. The remaining escape is raw `eval-cljs` over `rf/epoch-history`, which bypasses the structured privacy and tool envelope.
- Existing replay tests prove the ingredients by hand-extracting a record and calling `rf/dispatch-sync`; none proves that a programmer or tool can name one retained epoch and replay it in one supported call.

## Recommended Action

Provide one dev-only replay-by-epoch-id operation, preferably `replay-epoch!`, owned by the epoch artefact. It should resolve the retained raw record in-process, build the strict dispatch opts from the record in one place, and dispatch the recorded event without exporting its arguments/coeffects/overrides. Make source-frame and target-frame semantics explicit (same frame by default; an optional explicit target only if needed), and make clear that replay runs against the target frame's current state/code unless the caller separately restores a starting epoch.

Expose the operation through the normal optional-artefact facade and as a dedicated Pair-MCP `replay-epoch` tool (or an equally direct epoch-id mode on the existing dispatch tool). Return a structured consequence/failure envelope. Fail before dispatch for an unknown/aged-out id, a non-replayable record (synthetic/halted/missing trigger or replay token), or any recorded `:rf/fn-override`; preserve the existing strict missing-cofx failure rather than minting. Use the existing dispatch authority/annotation posture—do not invent another permission system.

## Evidence

- `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch/assembly.cljc` builds `:trigger-event`, post-generation `:rf.cofx`, `:fx-overrides`, and `:interceptor-overrides` into each record specifically for Tool-Pair replay.
- `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch.cljc` publishes no replay hook or public replay function; its Tool-Pair mutations are restore and replace only.
- `implementation/epoch/src/re_frame/epoch/tool_pair.cljc` independently redacts trigger-event args; `implementation/epoch/test/re_frame/epoch_egress_redaction_cljs_test.cljc` pins that `:include-sensitive? true` still leaves them redacted unless the separate `:include-event-args?` opt is supplied.
- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/epoch_egress.cljs` threads only `:include-sensitive?` into projected epoch pages and explicitly leaves the orthogonal event-args axis closed.
- `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/src/re_frame2_pair_mcp/tools/dispatch.cljs` accepts caller-supplied event/cofx/overrides plus `replay true`; it performs no epoch-id lookup. `registry.cljs` and generated `tool-descriptors.edn` contain restore but no replay-by-id tool.
- `spec/Tool-Pair.md` Replay and `tools/re-frame2-pair-mcp/spec/003-Tool-Catalogue.md` Strict replay instruct callers to read and copy the four recorded fields manually.
- `implementation/epoch/test/re_frame/epoch_test.clj`, `epoch_override_capture_test.clj`, `machine_minted_cofx_replay_token_test.clj`, and `join_strict_mint_epoch_replay_test.clj` all demonstrate replay through manual record extraction/re-dispatch.
- `implementation/epoch/deps.edn` confirms epoch is an optional, dev-elided artefact with an existing real production-gate lane; the new seam belongs under that same boundary.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. From only a retained epoch id plus explicit frame targeting, a public dev API can replay an ordinary argument-bearing event using the raw in-process `:trigger-event`, recorded `:rf.cofx`, and both recorded override maps under hard-wired `:strict` mint policy.
2. An end-to-end test records a generator-backed/mid-run coeffect and serializable fx/interceptor overrides, then replays by id and proves the generator/host is not consulted and the recorded effective chain is used. Include an event argument that the off-box projected history exposes only as `:rf/redacted`.
3. Pair-MCP offers the same one-call epoch-id gesture without requiring raw event, cofx, or override payloads on the wire; the descriptor, generated manifest, catalogue, and skill routing all agree.
4. Unknown/aged-out ids, halted/synthetic/incomplete records, and `:rf/fn-override` records return stable structured failures and do not dispatch. Missing declared recordable facts remain the canonical strict `:rf.error/missing-required-cofx`; no live mint fallback is introduced.
5. Docs state the state semantics plainly: replay does not implicitly restore, external effects may fire again, the target's current code/frame config applies, and the replayed dispatch records a new ordinary epoch.
6. Existing `projected-record` privacy defaults remain unchanged; no raw event-argument egress knob is added to make replay work.
7. Focused JVM/CLJS epoch tests, Pair-MCP tool tests, descriptor-manifest drift checks, and the existing epoch production-elision lane pass with non-vacuous assertions.

## Non-goals

- A branching timeline, redo stack, or general event-log framework.
- Automatic restore-before-replay or a promise that replay matches the historical `:db-after` when starting state/code differs.
- Replaying opaque fn-valued overrides, virtualising/undoing external effects, or weakening off-box redaction.
- Compatibility aliases, a generic command abstraction, or a second permission/gating system.

## Related beads

No open duplicate was found after title and full-description searches for replay-by-epoch-id, strict replay, trigger-event replay, and `include-event-args`. Historical implementation lineage visible in source/commit history: rf2-1xdotm (post-generation cofx capture), rf2-yigokd (override capture), rf2-v52xsr (strict replay flag), rf2-m7x0qb (Pair-MCP override re-supply), rf2-s3qjlw (epoch/restore strict-replay composition proof), and rf2-nm611o (fail-closed trigger-event args).

title: machines/SSR: hydration leaves pre-existing timers absent from the replacement snapshot
description:
## Scope

Repair the SSR-to-client handoff for state-machine `:after` transitions. The scope is active singleton and spawned snapshots under `[:rf.runtime/machines :snapshots]`, including flat/compound states, active paths in root-parallel regions, and a root-parallel `:after`. Keep ordinary transition semantics and epoch restore semantics unchanged.

## Correctness finding

The server intentionally suppresses machine wall-clock timers, but the client hydration path only installs the serialized runtime-db snapshot. It does not reconstruct the host-side timer table for active `:after` declarations and does not re-run machine entry. A machine hydrated while sitting in an `:after`-bearing state therefore has the right durable `:state`, `:data`, and `:rf/after-epoch`, but no live timer. It can remain in that state forever unless some unrelated external event moves it.

This contradicts the local contract that timers begin on the client after hydration. It is also the relevant conformity lesson from XState v6 persistence: durable state and host work are distinct, and restoring a snapshot must explicitly reconstruct the timer runtime without replaying historical effects.

## Evidence

- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/transition.cljc` (`build-after-fx`, around lines 2059-2144) emits `:rf.machine/after-schedule` only while processing newly-entered nodes. In server mode the effect carries `:server? true` and the timer is skipped.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/timer.cljc` keeps timer handles/watchers in a process-local timer table; they are not part of the hydration payload.
- `implementation/ssr/src/re_frame/ssr/hydrate.cljc` (`hydrate-event-handler*`) installs the payload's runtime-db and has one late-bound reconciliation hook for Resources. There is no Machines hydration/re-arm hook or machine scheduling effect.
- `implementation/core/src/re_frame/late_bind/directory.cljc` inventories Machines hooks for SSR projection, timer cleanup on frame destroy/epoch restore, and timer scheduling, but no hydration reconstruction hook.
- `implementation/machines/src/re_frame/machines/ssr.cljc` projects durable machine snapshots only; it cannot carry host timer handles.
- `spec/005-StateMachines.md` lines 1323 and 2444-2448 say server timers no-op and the client schedules them after hydration.
- `spec/011-SSR.md`, section “`:after` is no-op under SSR”, requires `:after` timers to begin running on the client against the preserved snapshot epoch.
- `docs/machines/automatic-transitions.md` states: “The client re-arms timers after hydration.”
- XState v6's official persistence contract includes timers in the durable snapshot shape and restores without replaying historical entry effects: https://stately.ai/docs/xstate/v6/persistence and https://stately.ai/docs/xstate/v6/how-xstate-runs-machines . Exact comparison baseline: `xstate@6.0.0-alpha.50` (`0b52534e`), released 2026-08-27.

## Steps to Reproduce

### Failure scenario/invariant

Given a server-rendered machine whose active state declares `:after {5000 {:target :timeout}}`:

1. Server entry bumps/stores the node's `:rf/after-epoch`, emits the skipped-on-server trace, and schedules no host timer.
2. The hydration payload carries the active snapshot and epoch.
3. `:rf/hydrate` installs that snapshot on the client without entering the state.
4. No client timer exists, so advancing beyond 5000 ms never dispatches the synthetic elapsed event and the machine remains stuck.

Required invariant: after a successful client hydration commit, every live active `:after` declaration represented by the hydrated snapshot has exactly one client timer/watch armed for that snapshot's existing epoch, without replaying unrelated entry behavior.

## Recommended minimal fix

Add one hydration-only Machines reconciliation seam, analogous in ownership to the existing Resources hydration hook:

- Have the Machines artefact publish a late-bound hydration hook/effect that runs only after a valid client `:rf/hydrate` has committed the payload runtime-db.
- Walk the hydrated live snapshots, resolve each actor's registered/inline machine definition using existing resolver paths, enumerate only the currently active nodes (plus the root-parallel node), and schedule their declared `:after` entries through the existing timer scheduler.
- Reuse the persisted `:rf/after-epoch`; do not bump it.
- Resolve literal/function/subscription delays on the client. Because the wire does not carry a schedule timestamp or due-at value, arm the full declared client-relative delay, matching the repository's existing SSR contract.
- Do not re-run `:entry`, actions, raises, spawns, or other effects. Do not reuse the epoch-restore callback: epoch restore deliberately cancels host work and must continue not to revive it.
- Make repeated hydration/scheduling idempotent by the existing timer-table key or an equally small guard, so it never leaves duplicate handles/watchers.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A focused hydration integration test registers an `:after` machine, produces/installs an SSR-shaped runtime-db snapshot, hydrates on a client frame, and proves exactly one timer is armed with the persisted epoch and its callback performs the declared transition.
- The test proves the timer was not armed on the server and that hydration does not re-run an entry action, raise, or spawn.
- Coverage includes a compound active path and root-parallel coverage sufficient to prove active region nodes and root-owned `:after` declarations are enumerated correctly.
- A dynamic subscription/function delay is resolved on the client through the existing scheduling path; watcher teardown/cancellation remains correct.
- Negative controls prove that a snapshot with no active `:after`, a rejected malformed/wrong-frame hydration, and a server-side hydrate arm no timers.
- Existing epoch-restore coverage continues to prove `:machines/on-frame-restored!` cancels timers and does not re-arm them.
- Existing timer traces remain coherent; hydration-created timers emit one normal scheduled trace (with actor, path/state, delay source, epoch, and frame) rather than a misleading state-entry replay.
- Relevant spec/docs wording and late-bind directory inventory match the implemented hydration-only seam.

## Non-goals

- A general durable workflow engine, snapshot migration framework, elapsed-time/due-at persistence, or cross-process clock reconciliation.
- Replaying all machine entry behavior during hydration.
- Reviving timers during epoch/time-travel restore.
- Serializing browser timer handles or subscription objects.
- Matching XState's actor API or persistence wire format.

## Related/duplicate search

All-status tracker searches covered titles/descriptions containing: `machine timer`, `after hydration`, `hydration timer`, `re-arm`, `rearm`, `skipped-on-server`, `after-epoch`, `hydrate`, `restore`, `SSR`, and `rf.runtime/machines`. No bead owns this outcome. Closed `rf2-1vlyg` concerns reverse-creation teardown after restore, not hydration timer reconstruction; closed `rf2-ys42` is a documentation review that repeated the client-rearm promise but did not implement it.
acceptance_criteria: After client hydration, the frame's host timer table contains exactly the timers implied by the installed machine snapshots: stale pre-hydration/previous-hydration entries and dynamic-delay watchers are cancelled, live declarations are armed once at their persisted epochs, and no entry/cascade is replayed. A changed-snapshot regression distinguishes this from the existing identical-snapshot idempotence test; restore semantics and other frames remain untouched.
notes:
AUDIT PR #8915: reopened after the three-lens review. The new hydration seam reconstructs every live declaration correctly, but it does not reconcile away host timers that are absent from the replacement snapshot. :rf/hydrate replaces runtime-db wholesale; timer/after-timers is separate host state. rearm-after-timers! only walks the newly installed snapshots and calls schedule-after-timer! for their active declarations. That function supersedes an old entry only when the new declaration has the same {actor, invoke-id, delay-key}; there is no frame-level cancellation or set difference. The idempotence test repeats the identical snapshot, so it proves only the same-key case.

A frame with a pre-hydration timer, or a documented direct second :rf/hydrate, can therefore replace an :after state with a no-:after state, remove an actor, or shrink a delay set while leaving the old host handle in after-timers. Literal handles linger until firing; subscription-delay entries can keep a reaction/watcher alive and reschedule. Epoch/active-path checks may suppress the eventual stale transition, but they do not release the host work or give the replacement operation coherent scheduled-to-cancelled tracing.

Minimal repair: after the payload runtime-db commit, reconcile this frame's timer table to the exact declaration keys enumerated from the installed snapshots: cancel entries not in that set, then retain/supersede or arm the live set. Preserve the client/payload/hook gates, existing epochs, no-entry-replay rule, and epoch-restore semantics. Add a changed-snapshot control (active :after to no :after or absent actor) and a dynamic-delay watcher/ref-count control; do not add a general persistence layer or public API.

---

AUDIT REPAIR (2026-09-01 21:47 AUSEST) — PR #8930, branch worker/timerrec-jqvgp.

PREMISE VERIFIED AT TIP BEFORE BUILDING. Both halves of the audit note hold exactly as
written. schedule-after-timer! computes its slot as
(after-timer-key parent-id invoke-id delay-key) => {:parent <actor> :spawn (vec invoke-id)
:delay <delay-key>} and issues ONE cancel-after-timer-entry! against that single key with
:reason :on-supersede — so the supersede is keyed on {actor, invoke-id, delay-key} and
there is no frame-level cancellation and no set difference anywhere in the arm path.
rearm-after-timers! walked only the newly installed snapshots. And
hydration-re-arm-is-idempotent in machine_after_hydration_rearm_cljs_test.cljc installs the
SAME runtime-db value twice into one frame, so it proves only the same-key case.

THE REPAIR. rearm-after-timers! is now a two-phase reconcile.
  1. hydrate/live-declarations (new, pure) enumerates the live declarations of every
     resolvable snapshot ONCE, each carrying its :actor-id and its :snapshot. Both halves
     read that one list, so a table entry is cancelled if and only if the walk did not

title: surface-review(template): collapse the generator to one small runnable SPA contract
description:
## Scope

Reduce `tools/template/**` to one deliberate product contract: scaffold a small client-side counter SPA that a programmer or agent can read, run, test, and replace. Keep the Reagent default and the UIx substrate selector because that choice changes authored source and adapter wiring. Remove feature/style modes and the generated policy/toolchain bundle. Update the generated resources, hook API, tests, and normative spec together; touch directly coupled template release-gate assertions only where the smaller contract requires it.

## Findings

1. The default Reagent scaffold is not minimal. Before compiled output or `node_modules`, it emits 20 files, 75,816 bytes, and 1,579 lines. The generated README alone is 677 lines; `events.cljs` is 232 lines for two tiny handlers; `deps.edn` is 76 lines. The actual counter cycle is a handful of forms.
2. The default installs decisions the app has not made: schemas, a git-pinned Xray tool plus `@xyflow/react` and `elkjs`, a trace error sink, a whole-app-db schema, a long commented HTTP handler, CSP and production-hosting policy, GitHub Actions, Lefthook, cljfmt, clj-kondo, `dev/user.clj`, and a REPL scratch namespace. These are useful recipes, not requirements for the first SPA.
3. The generator exposes three feature/style flags (`:include-story?`, `:include-ssr?`, `:css`) on top of the substrate axis, yielding eight accepted output cells and mutual-exclusion/capability machinery. `hooks.clj` is 774 lines; the template tests are 5,608 lines; the spec is 3,295 lines. Much of the suite pins explanatory prose, badges, CSP snippets, Xray layout details, and variant combinations instead of the first-run contract.
4. The shared README teaches Story even when Story was not requested. The generated source teaches HTTP, privacy/egress, production schema elision, Xray, and deployment hardening before the reader has replaced the counter. This makes both humans and agents distinguish essential code from a framework handbook on their first edit.
5. The public descriptions have already drifted under the matrix: `template.edn` advertises Story but omits the live SSR and Tailwind modes; Principles P3 says React and ReactDOM are the only npm dependencies while the default Reagent path injects Xray's two additional npm packages. The canonical Clojure name `acme/my-app` is copied verbatim into `package.json`; npm 11's bundled `validate-npm-package-name` rejects that unscoped slash form.
6. History shows accretion, not an intentional current baseline. The initial scaffold at `2313a8d85a` emitted 10 files / 8,966 bytes / 272 lines. Subsequent commits separately added the dev bundle (`d9830dc2fc`), cljfmt (`3cdc6f3b26`), Lefthook (`bfe4aa3ee8`), Xray's predecessor (`efbdd60a94`), CSP/production hardening (`f61b816163`), best-practice demos (`f6f770bfc0`), and CI (`b04c304614`). Correct later fixes hardened that accumulated shape, but no product pass re-asked what belongs in a starter.
7. Public distribution is a separate known blocker: `.github/workflows/template-release.yml` states that it rewrites emitted framework coordinates to local roots and that the advertised public template coordinate is not yet usable. Existing publication beads own that. Adding another invocation mode or a `:minimal?` flag would compound both problems.

## Recommended Action

- Make the template emit one SPA shape per supported view substrate. `:name` remains required; `:substrate :reagent|:uix` is the only template-specific option, with Reagent as the obvious default.
- Delete `:include-story?`, `:include-ssr?`, and `:css` from the hook API, resources, errors, docs, and matrix tests. Story, SSR, and Tailwind remain learnable through their focused examples/guides; do not replace the flags with a wizard, profiles, or separate compatibility modes in this task.
- Emit only the files needed to run, test, release, and understand the counter: `.gitignore`, a short README, `deps.edn`, `package.json`, `shadow-cljs.edn`, the HTML/CSS shell, `core.cljs`, `events.cljs`, `subs.cljs`, `views.cljs`, and one focused event-flow test. Remove generated CI, hook-manager/editor/formatter/linter configs, REPL scratch scaffolding, and schema source.
- Keep direct dependencies to the runnable counter: Clojure/ClojureScript, re-frame2 core, the selected adapter and view library, shadow-cljs, React, and ReactDOM. Do not preload Xray or pull schemas/tool coordinates into every Reagent app.
- Keep comments local and brief. Preserve the measured-correct `^:dev/after-load` lifecycle, but move HTTP, schema, privacy, CSP, production-host, Xray, Story, SSR, migration, and tooling tutorials to existing public docs and link to them from a compact next-steps section.
- Derive an npm-valid package name from the Clojure project coordinate instead of copying `acme/my-app` verbatim.
- Replace prose- and combination-heavy tests with a small black-box contract: exact emit manifest, parseable/valid manifests, compile/test/release, real browser boot and 0→1 counter interaction for both substrates, and absence of retired files/dependencies/options. Keep history in git rather than carrying completed migration/validation reports as live normative surface.

## Evidence

- `tools/template/test/day8/re_frame2_template/template_test.clj:37-66` enumerates the 20-file default; lines 364-712 assert the generated handbook, CI, Xray host, CSP, privacy, schema, and HTTP prose.
- `tools/template/resources/day8/re_frame2_template/root/README.md` is 677 lines and includes Hot reload, Story, Production hardening, REPL, schemas, privacy/egress, HTTP, migration, and future skill-install sections.
- `tools/template/resources/day8/re_frame2_template/_shared/events.cljs` is 232 lines; the counter handlers occupy only the small initialisation/increment blocks, while the rest is an error sink and commented HTTP exemplar.
- `tools/template/resources/day8/re_frame2_template/_reagent/deps.edn` adds schemas, Xray, cljfmt, clj-kondo, and tools.namespace around the base app; `_shared/package.json` injects Xray npm packages and uses `{{name}}` as the npm name.
- `tools/template/src/day8/re_frame2_template/hooks.clj:179-291,321-643,655-741` owns the flag gate, coercions, capability-conditioned substitution prose, and file-selection matrix.
- `tools/template/spec/000-Vision.md`, `API.md`, `001-Substrate-Variants.md`, and `002-Generated-Shape.md` claim a minimal counter while specifying the larger matrix and tooling bundle.
- `.github/workflows/template-release.yml:114-129,257-273` explicitly says the release smoke masks unresolved consumer coordinates; this task must not invent a second distribution route around that separate owner.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. The documented template API has exactly one template-specific selector: optional `:substrate` with Reagent default and UIx alternative. The removed Story, SSR, and CSS keys fail as unknown; there are no aliases, deprecation warnings, reserved gates, or compatibility shims for them.
2. Reagent and UIx emit the same small project manifest apart from `core.cljs`, `views.cljs`, and required dependency differences. The emitted tree contains the run/test/release essentials named above and does not contain `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, `lefthook.yml`, `.cljfmt.edn`, `.clj-kondo/`, `.editorconfig`, `dev/`, `schema.cljs`, Story files, SSR files, or Tailwind overlays.
3. The default direct dependency graph contains no Xray, Story, SSR, schemas, machines, cljfmt, clj-kondo, or tools.namespace coordinate and no Xray-only npm package. `package.json` has an npm-valid name derived deterministically from both qualified and bare Clojure project names.
4. Each substrate's generated app parses, compiles, runs its focused test, builds an advanced release, opens its real generated page, paints the counter, and moves 0→1 on click. The correct one-time init plus `^:dev/after-load` re-render lifecycle from `rf2-r0kk7` remains covered.
5. Generated source contains the counter dataflow and the lifecycle facts needed to edit it, without embedded HTTP/schema/privacy/security/tooling tutorials. The generated README gives the run, test, release, and guide/docs links without conditional sections for modes that were not emitted.
6. Template tests assert the behavioral and manifest contract, including red witnesses for a retired flag, an advanced dependency/file reappearing, an invalid npm name, and a broken browser boot. They do not pin badges, prose paragraphs, server-specific CSP snippets, or removed variant cells.
7. Normative template docs and metadata describe the same reduced surface. Completed migration/validation records are removed from the live contract or clearly historical; no document advertises a mode the generator no longer accepts.

## Non-goals

- No new wizard, `:minimal?` switch, profile system, second template, prompt sequence, or replacement feature flag.
- No compatibility layer for pre-alpha Story/SSR/Tailwind invocations; git history is the migration record.
- No runtime, adapter, Xray, Story, SSR, Tailwind, schema, HTTP, or security-policy redesign.
- No Hicasso substrate addition.
- No operator-owned repository split, coordinate rename, Clojars verification, tag, or publication work. The reduced scaffold must compose with that work when it lands, not duplicate it.
- Do not delete the focused examples or guides that become the on-ramp for advanced capabilities.

## Related beads

- `rf2-r0kk7` (closed): established the correct generated hot-reload lifecycle; preserve its behavior while shrinking the prose.
- `rf2-48rk3` (closed): made feature capability selection fail closed; most of that machinery becomes unnecessary when feature modes are retired, while the substrate registry can remain small.
- `rf2-8urba` (deferred): proposed a future Hicasso template variant; distinct and explicitly outside this minimal-contract change.
- `rf2-uelji` (deferred) and `rf2-fo4ng` (deferred): own verified-group/public-coordinate work; this task does not bypass or duplicate them.
- `rf2-k5r9t` (open): adapter-owned client-root work may later shorten generated Reagent boot code, but is not a prerequisite for removing template ceremony.

== 1. DECISION ==

(a) THE COLLAPSE IS AFFIRMED AS SCOPED. The template becomes one deliberate contract: `:name` (required) plus `:substrate` (`:reagent` default | `:uix`), emitting the same twelve-file runnable counter SPA for both substrates apart from `core.cljs`, `views.cljs` and the substrate's own coordinates. `:include-story?`, `:include-ssr?` and `:css` are deleted from the hook API, resources, error vocabulary, tests, spec and every public description; the retired keys fail as UNKNOWN through the existing unknown-key gate — no aliases, no deprecation warnings, no reserved gates, no compatibility shims.
